en: Before initiation, there is freedom of action, freedom of speech,
and freedom of consumption.
From what has not been offered in sacrifice;
he is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*);
his voiding of urine and feces is as it occurs naturally.
For him, the rule for sipping water (ācamana) does not exist,
except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling.
GDhS-A 1,2.7 / GDhS-St 2.3: There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse].

GDhS-A 1,2.8 / GDhS-St 2.4: But one should not employ him for the Agnihotra sacrifice or the offering of the bali-oblation. GDhS-A 1,2.9 / GDhS-St 2.5: He should not pronounce the Veda, except for the utterance of the *svadhā* at the pouring of the funeral libation.
GDhS-A 1,2.10 / GDhS-St 2.6: The rule begins with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). GDhS-A 1,2.11 / GDhS-St 2.7: Studenthood (*brahmacarya*) has been described.
GDhS-A 1,2.12 / GDhS-St 2.8a: [The duties are] tending the sacred fires and going for alms.
GDhS-A 1,2.13 / GDhS-St 2.8b: Speaking the truth.
GDhS-A 1,2.14 / GDhS-St 2.8c: Touching water.
GDhS-A 1,2.15 / GDhS-St 2.9: Some [prescribe] the gift of a cow and so forth.

GDhS-A 1.2.16 / GDhS-St 2.10: And [the performance of] the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) must take place outside [the village]. GDhS-A 1.2.17 / GDhS-St 2.11: He should stand during the former [twilight prayer] and sit during the latter, remaining silent until the stars appear while the light [of the sun] still remains, or until the stars are visible. GDhS-A 1.2.18 / GDhS-St 2.12: He must not look at the sun.

He shall avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, anointing the body, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, speaking, playing musical instruments, bathing for pleasure, cleaning the teeth,
exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. He shall not cover his neck,
sit with his thighs bound together, lean against a support, or stretch out his feet in the presence of his teacher.
Spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles [are forbidden]. Beholding or touching women when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse [is forbidden].
Gambling, service to the low, taking what is not given, and violence; [the names of] the teacher, his son, and a woman initiated for a sacrifice;
and those who speak of white [clothes].
{VAR_St: bitter words} GDhS-A 1.2.25b | GDhS-St 2.20: A Brāhmaṇa must always [avoid] intoxicants.
GDhS-A 1.2.26 / GDhS-St 2.21: He should sleep on a low bed and seat, rise before [his teacher], and go to rest after him.
He should restrain his speech, arms, and belly.
He should mention the name and lineage of his teacher with reverence. He should act in the same manner toward one who is honored and toward one who is superior.
GDhS-A 1.2.30 / GDhS-St 2.25: He should answer [the teacher's call] after leaving his bed, seat, or standing place.
GDhS-A 1.2.31 / GDhS-St 2.26: He should go toward the teacher when he is not visible [to him], at the teacher's command.
GDhS-A 1.2.32 / GDhS-St 2.27: He should remain standing or seated on the ground and avoid crosswinds; furthermore, he should rise upon seeing the teacher.
One should follow him as he goes; having informed him of the task and having declared it.
When summoned, he shall study; being disciplined,
he shall strive for what is pleasant and beneficial.
GDhS-A 1,2.37 / GDhS-St 2.31: The same applies to their wives and sons.
GDhS-A 1,2.38 / GDhS-St 2.32: [The student shall not perform] eating of the leftovers, bathing, dressing, washing the feet, massaging, or clasping the feet [of his teacher].
GDhS-A 1,2.39 / GDhS-St 2.33: After returning from a journey abroad, he should clasp the feet of his teacher’s wives.
Some [teachers] say that [one should not solicit alms] from young women who have attained marriageable age.
One should go about begging alms from members of all social classes, with the exception of those accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their caste.
The word *bhavat* (sir) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of a sentence] according to the order of the social classes (*varṇa*).
In the case of teachers, paternal kinsmen, and elders, it may be used elsewhere when they are not present.
Among these, one should avoid each preceding one [in preference for the following].
Having informed the teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat;
in the teacher's absence, [he should seek permission] from his wife, son, or fellow student.
Restraining his speech, being satisfied with what he receives and not being greedy, and keeping water close at hand; the instruction of a pupil is carried out without corporal punishment.
If he is unable [to strike], he may do so with a thin cord or a split bamboo cane. One who strikes with anything other than these shall be punished by the king.
One should practice studentship (*brahmacarya*) for twelve years for each Veda;
or twelve years for all [the Vedas] together;
or until [the Veda] has been mastered.
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher should be invited with a gift of wealth. Or, having performed the ritual bath, he may do so with the teacher's permission.
Among all gurus, the teacher is the most eminent.
"Mother," say some. {VAR_St: "matā," say some}.
[GDhS-A 1,3 = GDhS-St III]

GDhS-A 1,3.1 / GDhS-St 3.1: Some declare that there is an option regarding these stages of life (āśrama). GDhS-A 1,3.2 / GDhS-St 3.2: [The stages are] the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the mendicant (bhikṣu), and the hermit (vaikhānasa).
GDhS-A 1,3.3 / GDhS-St 3.3: Among them, the householder is the source, because the others do not produce offspring.

Regarding this, it has been stated concerning the religious student (*brahmacārin*): [GDhS-A 1,3.4 / GDhS-St 3.4] "Dependence upon the teacher lasts until the end. [GDhS-A 1,3.5 / GDhS-St 3.5] "He should recite [the Veda] during the remainder of his duties for the teacher.
[GDhS-A 1,3.6 / GDhS-St 3.6] "He should recite [the Veda] with the remainder of the work for the teacher."

GDhS-A 1,3.7a | GDhS-St 3.7: In the absence of the guru, one should follow the conduct toward his offspring. GDhS-A 1,3.7b | GDhS-St 3.8: In the absence of that, [one should do so] toward an aged fellow-student or toward the sacred fire.
One who conducts himself in this manner and has conquered his senses attains the world of Brahman.
And this [rule] is not in conflict with the subsequent [stages of life].
The mendicant (bhikṣu) is one who does not accumulate possessions;
he is one whose vital energy (retas) is drawn upward.
During the rainy season, he should remain in one place;
he should go to the village for the sake of alms;
he should wander about at the end of the day and without returning.
He should abstain from seeking alms. He should restrain his speech, eyes, and actions. He should wear a garment only for the purpose of covering his private parts.
Some say that [a garment] that has been discarded should be washed before being used again. One should not take for use any part of plants or trees that has not been separated [from its source].
He shall not stay in a village for a second night during the non-seasonal period. He shall either shave his head entirely or keep a tuft of hair. He shall avoid the destruction of seeds.
He should be equal toward all beings in both harming and favoring them.
He should refrain from initiating new undertakings. As a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), he should live in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and be devoted to austerity.
Having established the fire with the *śrāvaṇaka* rite,
he shall not eat village food.
He shall worship the gods, the ancestors, humans, beings, and the sages.
He shall entertain all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited. He may even consume the food of a Vaiśya.
He shall not stand upon land ploughed by a plow. He shall not enter a village.
He shall wear matted hair and dress in bark garments or skins.
He shall not eat more than once a year.
But the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life, because the householder’s state is explicitly prescribed.

GDhS-A 1,4.1 / GDhS-St 4.1: A householder should marry a wife who is of equal status, not previously married to another, and younger than himself. GDhS-A 1,4.2 / GDhS-St 4.2: Marriage is with those who do not share the same *pravara*. GDhS-A 1,4.3a / GDhS-St 4.3: Beyond the seventh degree on the father’s side [of kinship].
And from the progenitor [the kinship extends] as well. From the mother’s relatives, it extends to the fifth degree.
To one endowed with learning, good conduct, kinship, and character, he should give [his daughter] in the *brāhma* form, having clothed and adorned her.
In the *prājāpatya* rite, the formula for the union is: "Let dharma be practiced together.
In the *ārṣa* rite, one should give a pair of cattle to the groom.
The *daiva* rite consists of giving [the girl] to the officiating priest within the sacrificial enclosure after having adorned her.
The Gāndharva [form] is the union with a willing woman. The Āsura [form] is the honoring of women with wealth.
The Rākṣasa [form] results from taking her by force;
the Paiśāca [form] results from approaching her while she is unconscious.
The first four [classes] are lawful.
Some say there are six.
From women of the same caste (anuloma) who are immediate, one-removed, two-removed, or three-removed [in rank], [the sons] are known as Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Daushyanṭa, and Pāraśava.
The *pratiloma* [castes],
however, are the Sūta, Māgadha, Āyogava, Kṣattṛ, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla.
A Brāhmaṇa woman bears sons from men of the [three] castes in order: a Brāhmaṇa, a Sūta, a Māgadha, and a Caṇḍāla.
From those same [men], a Kṣatriya woman bears an Ūrdhvāvasiktha, a Kṣatriya, a Dhīvara, and a Pulkasa. From those same [men], a Vaiśya woman bears a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha, a Māhiṣya, a Vaiśya, and a Vaideha.

GDhS-A 1,4.17c | GDhS-St 4.21: Some say that the Pāraśava, Yavana, Karaṇa, and Śūdra are [all] simply Śūdras. {VAR_St: bhṛjya} GDhS-A 1,4.18a | GDhS-St 4.22: The transition to another caste occurs in the seventh generation through either advancement or degradation.
GDhS-A 1,4.18b | GDhS-St 4.23: Or on the fifth day, according to the teachers.
{VAR_St: saptamena; pañcamenācāryāḥ} GDhS-A 1,4.19 / GDhS-St 4.24:
And for those born from a different womb.
But those born in the reverse order (pratiloma) are devoid of dharma;
and so too is [the son] born of a Śūdra woman.
But from a Śūdra woman of a different caste, he has the livelihood of an outcast (patita). From one of the lowest caste, he is most wicked.
Virtuous sons purify [their ancestors] for three generations on account of the *ārṣa* rite; ten generations on account of the *daiva* rite.
GDhS-A 1,4.26b | GDhS-St 4.32: From the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman born of a Prajāpati rite, there are exactly ten [generations].
GDhS-A 1,4.27 / GDhS-St 4.33: The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman born of a Brāhmaṇa man purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself.
{VAR_St: ten descendants}
GDhS-A 1,5.1 / GDhS-St 5.1:
He should approach his wife during her season. GDhS-A 1,5.2 / GDhS-St 5.2: Or he may do so at all times, except on forbidden days.
He shall worship the gods, the ancestors, men, beings, and sages. He shall engage in the daily recitation of the Veda.
And he shall offer water to the ancestors.

GDhS-A 1,5.5b | GDhS-St 5.6: The other [rites] are according to one's capacity. GDhS-A 1,5.6 / GDhS-St 5.7: The fire is either that of the wife or that of the inheritance. GDhS-A 1,5.7 / GDhS-St 5.8: In that [fire], the domestic rites are performed.
The sacrifices to the gods, the ancestors, and humans, as well as the study of one's own Veda and the offering of oblations (bali), [constitute the five great sacrifices].
The oblation (homa) is offered with the words: "To Agni in the fire, to Dhanvantari, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt."
And [he offers] to the deities of the quarters, each according to its own [direction].
At the doors, [he offers] to the Great Ones.
Having entered [the house], [he offers] to the household deities;
in the center, to Brahman.
GDhS-St 5.15: [The offering] to the waters is in a water-pot.
GDhS-A 1,5.14a; GDhS-St 5.16: [The offering] to space is in the intermediate air; the bali-offering is to be cast upward. GDhS-A 1,5.14b.
And [he should offer] to the night-walkers in the evening.
(GDhS-A 1,5.15 / GDhS-St 5.17) Having caused the recitation of a blessing, the giving of alms is preceded by water.
(GDhS-A 1,5.16 / GDhS-St 5.18) And the same applies to righteous acts of giving. (GDhS-A 1,5.17 / GDhS-St 5.19)
The rewards for giving to a non-Brahmin, a Brahmin, a learned Śrotriya, and one who has mastered the Vedas are respectively equal, double, a thousandfold, and infinite (GDhS-A 1,5.18 / GDhS-St 5.20).

Outside the sacrificial altar, there shall be a distribution of goods to those who have come for the sake of their teacher, those entering a new house, those seeking medicine, those whose livelihood is exhausted, those about to sacrifice, those engaged in Vedic study, those on a journey, and those who have won a universal contest (GDhS-A 1,5.19 / GDhS-St 5.21).
Among those begging, cooked food should be given; to others, [raw] grain (GDhS-A 1,5.20 / GDhS-St 5.22).
Even after having given a promise, one should not give to one who is joined with unrighteousness.
The words of one who is angry, delighted, terrified, afflicted, greedy, a child, aged, dull-witted, intoxicated, or insane are false, yet they do not constitute a mortal sin.

One should feed first the guest, the youth, the sick, the pregnant woman, the newly married daughter living in her father’s house, and the elderly; these are the ones to be fed last [after the others]. (GDhS-A 1,5.23 / GDhS-St 5.25) The act of cooking must be announced to the teacher, the father, and friends. (GDhS-A 1,5.24 / GDhS-St 5.26) The madhuparka offering is required upon the arrival of officiating priests, the teacher, the father-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles. (GDhS-A 1,5.25 / GDhS-St 5.27)
After one year [the impurity ceases];
before [the completion of] a sacrifice or a marriage;
and also for a king and for a *śrotriya*.
For one who is not a *śrotriya*, [he should offer] only a seat and water.

But for a *śrotriya*, he should provide water for the feet (*pādya*), the guest-offering (*arghya*), and various kinds of food; or else, he should always provide that which is distinguished by its preparation.
The distribution of food from the center [of the row] is for one who is not learned but is of virtuous conduct;
for those of the opposite character, [one should provide] grass, water, and ground.
GDhS-A 1,5.33b | GDhS-St 5.36: A warm welcome [is due] at the very least.

GDhS-A 1,5.33c | GDhS-St 5.37: And likewise, honor and the offering of food. GDhS-A 1,5.34 / GDhS-St 5.38: Bedding, seating, lodging, following behind, and attendance are common to both equals and superiors.
Even if [the guest] is slightly inferior, [one should offer hospitality].
A guest from a different village who stays for only one night and waits for the sun behind a tree is considered a true guest.
GDhS-A 1,5.37 / GDhS-St 5.41: [The guest] should inquire after [the host's] welfare, health, and freedom from disease. GDhS-A 1,5.38 / GDhS-St 5.42: For a Śūdra, [this inquiry] is the last [item].
GDhS-A 1,5.39 / GDhS-St 5.43: A non-Brāhmaṇa is not a guest for a Brāhmaṇa.
If [the sacrifice] has been completed in a closed space,
[he may eat]. Regarding the meal for a Kṣatriya, however, it occurs after [the meal for] the Brāhmaṇas.
Others, together with his dependents, for the sake of compassion, for the sake of compassion.

One should clasp the feet of [elders] daily when meeting them; however, one must do so upon returning from a journey. This applies to mothers, fathers, their relatives, ancestors, teachers of knowledge, and the teachers of those teachers.

In the case of a collision [with another person], one should greet the other first. When greeting a group of people who do not know [one's name], one should announce one's own name, saying, "I am so-and-so."
GDhS-A 1,6.6 / GDhS-St 6.6: Regarding the greeting when a man and a woman meet, some authorities maintain there is no fixed rule.
GDhS-A 1,6.7 / GDhS-St 6.7: One should not perform this greeting for women who are not one's mother, paternal aunt, wife, or sister, even if they have not lived abroad.
GDhS-A 1,6.8 / GDhS-St 6.8: Nor should one perform the formal clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) for the wives of one's brothers or for one's sisters.
But one must rise for and salute officiating priests, fathers-in-law, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles who are younger than oneself;
[but not for those older].

Likewise, another who is senior, even if he is a Śūdra, [should be honored] by one who is at least eighty years old as if he were his own son. A noble man (Ārya), even if younger, [is to be honored] by a Śūdra.
One should avoid pronouncing his name.
And the servant of a king shall not address him without reciting the *ajapa* formula.
A companion born on the same day shall address one as "O, sir" (*bho bhavan*).

GDhS-A 1,6.15a | GDhS-St 6.15: A fellow citizen who is ten years older [is equal to a father]. GDhS-A 1,6.15b | GDhS-St 6.16: One who supports [him] with five parts [of his wealth is equal to a father]. GDhS-A 1,6.15c | GDhS-St 6.17: A Vedic scholar (śrotriya) who is a wandering minstrel (cāraṇa) [is equal to a father] by three [parts].
Those who perform the duties of a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya* are devoid of [Vedic] learning.
And so is one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) prior to the purchase [of the Soma].
Wealth, kinship, occupation, birth, learning, and age are grounds for respect, each subsequent one being more powerful than the preceding.
But sacred revelation (śruta) is weightier than all [other sources],
because dharma is rooted in it,
and because of the authority of revelation itself.
One should yield the right of way to a chariot, to one who is in his tenth decade of life, to one who is worthy of protection, to a bride, to a *snātaka*, and to a king.
But a king must yield the right of way to a *śrotriya*.
[GDhS-A 1,7 = GDhS-St VII]
GDhS-A 1,7.1 / GDhS-St 7.1: In times of distress, it is permissible for a Brāhmaṇa to acquire knowledge from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.
GDhS-A 1,7.2 / GDhS-St 7.2: Following him and serving him [are required]. GDhS-A 1,7.3 / GDhS-St 7.3: Once the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes his teacher.
Sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts are [the means of livelihood] for all [twice-born classes].
Each preceding one is more venerable than the following.
In the absence of these, the occupation of a Kṣatriya [is permitted].
In the absence of that [the occupation of a Kṣatriya], he may follow the livelihood of a Vaiśya. His merchandise [is as follows]: GDhS 1.7.8.
Scent, flavor, prepared food, sesame, salt, linen, and skins;
dyed and washed garments. (GDhS 1.7.9–10)
Milk and its derivatives;
roots, fruits, flowers, herbs, honey, meat, grass, water, and unwholesome substances;
and animals when associated with injury.

A man, a ram, a maiden, and a cow that has miscarried are always [to be avoided]. Some [teachers] say that land, rice, barley, goats, sheep, horses, bulls, milch-cows, and oxen are also [to be avoided].
But there is a restriction.
Flavors [are purified] by flavors; (GDhS-A 1,7.18) and so too are animals. (GDhS-A 1,7.19) But not salt or prepared food.
And [this applies] to sesame seeds as well.
But for cooked food, one may exchange it for an equal amount of uncooked grain when there is an immediate need.
In every way, if one is unable [to subsist], one may maintain oneself by means other than the Śūdra.
Some [teachers] say that even this [eating of forbidden food] is permitted when there is a danger to life; however,
there is a restriction regarding the mixing of castes and the consumption of forbidden food.
In a life-threatening danger, even a Brāhmaṇa may take up arms;
a Rājanya [may take up] the duties of a Vaiśya.

In this world, two are firm in their vows: the king and the Brahmin who is deeply learned. Upon these two depends the livelihood of the fourfold human race—those with internal consciousness, as well as those that move, fall, and crawl.
The protection of offspring and the avoidance of intermixture constitute dharma.
He alone is one who is deeply learned.
One who knows the worlds, the Vedas, and the Vedāṅgas; one who is skilled in the dialogues, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas.
Dependent on that, he lives according to that [way of life].
(GDhS-A 1.8.7 / GDhS-St 8.7) Refined by the forty sacraments. (GDhS-A 1.8.8 / GDhS-St 8.8)
He should be devoted to three duties;
or to six;
and he should be thoroughly trained in the rules of conventional conduct.
GDhS-A 1,8.12 / GDhS-St 8.12: He is exempt from being avoided by the king for six [reasons].
GDhS-A 1,8.13 / GDhS-St 8.13: He is not to be killed, nor to be bound, nor to be punished with a fine, nor to be banished, nor to be censured, nor to be avoided.
GDhH-S-A 1,8.14 / GDhS-St 8.14: [The sacraments are] conception, quickening a male child, parting the hair, birth-rite, naming, the first feeding of solid food, the tonsure, and initiation.
There are four Vedic observances:
bathing, union with a wife who practices the dharma together,
and the performance of the five sacrifices to the gods, ancestors, humans, spirits, and Brahmins.
And of these [the following]:

The Aṣṭakā, the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha, the Śrāvaṇī, the Āgrahāyaṇī, the Caitrī, and the Āśvayujī—these are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*. The Agnyādheya, the Agnihotra, the Darśapūrṇamāsa, the Āgrayaṇa, the Cāturmāsya, the Nirūḍhapaśubandha, and the Sautrāmaṇī—these are the seven forms of the *haviryajña*.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma— these are the seven Soma-sacrifices.
These constitute the forty sacraments.
Now, there are eight qualities of the self (ātma-guṇa):
compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of weariness, auspiciousness, generosity, and lack of possessiveness.
He who possesses these forty sacraments (saṃskāra) but lacks the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with Brahman (sāyujya) nor residence in the same world as Brahman (sālokya).

But he for whom even a single portion of the purificatory rites has been performed, and who possesses the eight qualities of the self, attains union with Brahman (*sāyujya*) and residence in the same world as Brahman (*sālokya*). [GDhS-A 1,9 = GDhS-St IX]

Having bathed according to the prescribed rule and having taken a wife, he who practices the duties of a householder as they have been described should observe these vows; such is the Snātaka. (GDhS 9.1–2)
He should be constantly pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing. If he possesses the means, he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
One should not wear a garment that is dyed red, gaudy, or worn by another;
nor should one wear a garland or sandals [if they have been so used]. However, if one is unable to afford new ones, one may wear such items after they have been washed.
GDhS-A 1,9.8 / GDhS-St 9.7: One should not have his beard grown unless there is a specific reason.
GDhS-A 1,9.9 / GDhS-St 9.8: One should not hold fire and water simultaneously.
GDhS-A 1,9.10 / GDhS-St 9.9: One should not drink from one's cupped hands.
GDhS-A 1,9.11 / GDhS-St 9.10: One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while standing with water that has been drawn up.
GDhS-A 1,9.12 / GDhS-St 9.11: Nor should one do so with water offered by a Śūdra, an impure person, or with water held in only one hand.
GDhS-A 1,9.13 / GDhS-St 9.12: Nor should one discharge urine, feces, or impurities while facing the wind, fire, Brahmins, the sun, water, deities, or cows.
One should not stretch out one's feet toward these deities. One should not remove urine or feces with leaves, clods of earth, or stones.
One should not step upon ashes, hair, nail-clippings, husks, potsherds, or impure things. One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or those who are unrighteous.
Having conversed [with someone], he should mentally meditate upon those who perform meritorious deeds;
or he should converse with a Brāhmaṇa. He should say of a non-cow, "She is a cow that will become one."
"An inauspicious thing is auspicious.
"A skull is a vulva.
"The jeweled bow is Indra’s rainbow."
One should not point out to another a cow suckling her calf.
Nor should one drive her away. Having engaged in sexual intercourse, one should not delay in performing purification.
And on that bed, he shall not engage in the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya).
Nor, having studied during the latter part of the night, shall he go back to sleep again. He shall not take pleasure with a woman who is not his wife.
Not one who is menstruating;
nor should he embrace her.

GDhS-A 1,9.31b | GDhS-St 9.31: He shall not [marry] a maiden. GDhS-A 1,9.32 / GDhS-St 9.32: He shall avoid blowing on the fire with his mouth, speaking while holding [food in his hand], wearing perfumes and garlands [outdoors], combing the hair, eating together with his wife, looking at himself while applying ointments, entering through a side door, washing the feet with the foot [on a stool], eating while seated on a bench, crossing a river by swimming with the arms, and climbing up or down trees or uneven places; as well as exerting oneself to the point of risking one's life.
One should not board a boat whose safety is uncertain. One should protect oneself from all dangers. One should not walk about during the day with one’s head covered.
Having covered himself at night; and likewise after voiding urine or excrement.
GDhS-A 1,9.38 / GDhS-St 9.38: Not on the ground without something intervening.
GDhS-A 1,9.39 / GDhS-St 9.39: Nor from water or from a dwelling.
GDhS-A 1,9.40 / GDhS-St 9.40: Nor on ashes, on cow-dung, on ploughed land, in shade, on a path, or in a place desired by others.
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day;
and likewise during the two twilights.
At night, he should face the south.
He should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, as well as sandals and a tooth-stick made of that same wood.
One who wears shoes should avoid sitting, saluting with joined palms, and prostrating.
One should not let the forenoon, midday, or afternoon pass fruitlessly, but should devote them according to one's ability to dharma, artha, and kāma.
But among these, he should be preeminent in dharma.
He should not look at another man’s wife naked. He should not drag a seat with his foot.
One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, speech, or the eyes.
One should not, without cause, perform cutting, piercing, scraping, crushing, or tearing.
One should not walk over a rope of calf-hides stretched out above.
GDhS-A 1,9.53 / GDhS-St 9.53: He should not be one who goes from family to family.
GDhS-A 1,9.54 / GDhS-St 9.54: He should not go to a sacrifice unless invited. GDhS-A 1,9.55 / GDhS-St 9.55: But he may go at will for the sake of seeing it.
One should not eat foods placed on one's lap. One should not [eat] at night what has been brought by a servant.
One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor molasses, nor oil-cakes, nor anything churned [into curds], nor other such items whose vital essence (*vīrya*) has been removed.
However, one should eat food offered in the morning and evening, honoring it and refraining from criticizing it.
GDhS-A 1,9.60 / GDhS-St 9.60: One should never sleep naked at night.
GDhS-A 1,9.61 / GDhS-St 9.61: Or one may bathe.
GDhS-A 1,9.62 / GDhS-St 9.62: Whatever those who are self-possessed, aged, properly disciplined, free from deceit, greed, and delusion, and learned in the Vedas declare, that one should practice.
For the sake of security and well-being, one should seek out a ruler;
however, one should not seek anyone else except for gods, teachers, and righteous men.

One should strive to dwell in a residence that has an abundant supply of fuel, water, fodder, kusha grass, and garlands; where there is easy access for going out; which is populated mostly by noble people; which is free from sloth and prosperous; and which is governed by a righteous ruler.
66. One should circumambulate to the right those things that are praised, auspicious objects, temples, and crossroads.
67. Or, in times of distress, one may observe this entire rule of conduct mentally.
One whose nature is truth;
one who follows the conduct of the noble.
He should be a teacher of the learned;
he should be disciplined in purity; he should be devoted to the sacred revelation (Śruti).
Always non-violent, gentle, firm in action, and characterized by self-restraint and generosity—

one who conducts himself thus, and who, desiring to liberate his parents and his ancestors and descendants from misfortunes, remains a *snātaka*, never falls from the world of Brahman; he never falls.
GDhS-A 2,1.1 / GDhS-St 10.1:
For the twice-born, study, sacrifice, and giving are [the duties]. GDhS-A 2,1.2 / GDhS-St 10.2:
For a Brāhmaṇa, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are additional [duties].
GDhS-A 2,1.3 / GDhS-St 10.3: But there is a restriction regarding the former [occupations].

GDhS-A 2,1.4 / GDhS-St 10.4: In the case of restrictions concerning the teacher, kinsmen, friends, elders, wealth, and learning, the gift of the Veda may be given by one other than those previously mentioned.
GDhS-A 2,1.5 / GDhS-St 10.5: Or agriculture and trade, provided they are not performed by oneself.
And [the king shall engage in] usury.
For the king, the protection of all beings is his primary duty.
2.1.8 / 10.8: The administration of just punishment.
2.1.9 / 10.9: He shall support Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
2.1.10 / 10.10: And [he shall support] Brahmins who are lacking in energy.
And those who do not perform the duties of a Brahmin;
and those who are students (upakurvāṇa).
And there is yoga for the sake of victory;
(there is) especially so in times of danger;
and the practice consists of the chariot and the bow.
In battle, there is staying one's ground and not retreating.
For there is no fault in causing injury in combat,

except in the case of those who are horsemen, charioteers, those with weapons raised, those with palms joined in reverence, those with disheveled hair, those with their backs turned, those seated, those standing on high ground, those mounted on trees, messengers, cows, Brahmins, and those who proclaim [the king's name].
If a Kṣatriya should live off another by means of that other's occupation,
he may take the wealth acquired in battle.
But the conveyance belongs to the king (GDhS-A 2.1.21; GDhS-St 10.21).
And there is a preferential share even when the victory is not distinct [between the king and his army] (GDhS-A 2.1.22;
GDhS-St 10.22).
But the king shall distribute the remainder as is appropriate. The tribute to be given to the king by farmers shall be one-tenth, one-eighth, or one-sixth [of the produce].
GDhS-A 2,1.25 / GDhS-St 10.25: Some [teachers] maintain that for cattle and gold, the share is one-fiftieth.
GDhS-A 2,1.26 / GDhS-St 10.26: The toll on merchandise is one-twentieth.
GDhS-A 2,1.27 / GDhS-St 10.27: For roots, fruits, flowers, medicinal herbs, honey, meat, grass, and fuel, the share is one-sixth.
Because it is his duty to protect them;
however, he should be constantly devoted to those [duties].
2.1.30 (GDhS-A) / 10.30 (GDhS-St): Their livelihood shall be by means of some surplus. 2.1.31 (GDhS-A) / 10.31 (GDhS-St): Artisans shall perform one day's work every month.
2.1.32 (GDhS-A) / 10.32 (GDhS-St): By this, those who subsist by their own labor are explained.
And those who live by boat-traffic;
one should give them food.
Merchandise may be sold by merchants at a price lower than its actual value. Having found lost property that has no owner, they shall announce it to the king.
GDhS-A 2,1.37 / GDhS-St 10.37: Having been publicly proclaimed, he is to be protected by the king for one year.
GDhS-A 2,1.38 / GDhS-St 10.38: After that period, one-fourth of the property belongs to the finder, and the remainder to the king.
GDhS-A 2,1.39 / GDhS-St 10.39: One becomes the owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or finding.
For a Brāhmaṇa, what is obtained [without effort] is additional;
for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered;
for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, what is earned through labor.
The discovery of a hidden treasure belongs to the king;
however, it belongs to a worthy Brāhmaṇa.

GDhS-A 2,1.45 / GDhS-St 10.45: Even a non-Brāhmaṇa who reports [the thief] shall receive a sixth part [of the recovered property], according to some. GDhS-A 2,1.46 / GDhS-St 10.46: Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place.
{VAR_St: avajitya}
Or he may pay from the treasury. The property of a minor must be protected until he reaches legal majority, or until his return [from his teacher's house].
GDhS-A 2,1.50 / GDhS-St 10.49: For the Vaiśya, there are additional [duties], namely agriculture, trade, animal husbandry, and moneylending.
GDhS-A 2,1.51 / GDhS-St 10.50: The Śūdra is the fourth caste; he is of a single birth.
GDhS-A 2,1.52 / GDhS-St 10.51: For him also, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and purity [are required].
GDhS-A 2,1.53 / GDhS-St 10.52: Some say that for the purpose of *ācamana*, one should merely wash the hands and feet.
GDhS-A 2,1.54 / GDhS-St 10.53: [This applies to] the *śrāddha* rite.
55. Supporting dependents. 56. Devotion to one’s own wife. 57. And service to those who are superior.
From them he should seek his livelihood;
among them, he should serve each preceding one more than the following.
Worn-out shoes, umbrellas, garments, mats, and so forth;
eating the remnants of another's meal.
And [he may live by] the profession of an artisan (GDhS-A 2,1.62 / GDhS-St 10.60).
And he who takes refuge with a noble person must be supported by him, even if [the noble person] is impoverished (GDhS-A 2,1.63 / GDhS-St 10.61).
{VAR_St: āśrayīta}
And by that [means], the subsequent [rite] is performed. (GDhS-A 2,1.64 / GDhS-St 10.62) His accumulation of wealth should be for that purpose.
(GDhS-A 2,1.65 / GDhS-St 10.63) The mantra of salutation is prescribed for him. (GDhS-A 2,1.66 / GDhS-St 10.64)
GDhS-A 2,1.67 / GDhS-St 10.65: Some say that one should perform sacrifices by means of *pākayajñas* oneself.
GDhS-A 2,1.68 / GDhS-St 10.66: And all [members of the family] should serve each other in ascending order [of seniority].
GDhS-A 2,1.69 / GDhS-St 10.67: In the case of an interchange between an Ārya and a non-Ārya, there is equality of ritual action.
{VAR_St: equality} GDhS-A 2.2.1 / GDhS-St 11.1:
The king has authority over all, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas.
One who performs good deeds and speaks well; one who is thoroughly trained in the three Vedas or in Ānvīkṣikī.
Pure, with his senses conquered, and endowed with virtuous assistants and means,
he should be impartial toward all subjects.
He should do what is beneficial for them. While he is seated above, others— other than Brāhmaṇas— should sit below him.

They too should respect him. He should protect the social classes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*) according to what is right. And he should establish those who have strayed from them in their own respective duties (*svadharma*).
"For he becomes a sharer in a portion of dharma," so it is known.

And he should appoint as his domestic priest (*purohita*) a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, noble birth, eloquence, beauty, age, and good character, who is upright in conduct, and ascetic. Impelled by him, he should perform the ritual acts.
For it is known from scripture: "The Kṣatriya power, when produced by the Brāhmaṇa, prospers and does not falter.
And whatever those who contemplate divine portents and omens might declare, that he should respect.
For some maintain that even one's acquisition and preservation of property (*yogakṣema*) depend upon him (the king).

One should perform in the *śālāgni* (domestic sacrificial fire) those rites associated with prosperity— such as those for peace, auspicious days, well-being, long life, and blessings— as well as those associated with causing enmity, subjugation, malevolent magic, and the ruin of enemies.
GDhS-A 2,2.18 / GDhS-St 11.18: As has been stated, the officiating priests [perform] the others.
GDhS-A 2,2.19 / GDhS-St 11.19: And his means of knowledge are the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), the Upavedas, and the Purāṇa.

GDhS-A 2,2.20 / GDhS-St 11.20: The laws of regions, castes, and families that are not in conflict with the sacred scriptures (āmnāya) are authoritative. GDhS-A 2,2.21 / GDhS-St 11.21: Farmers, merchants, cattle-herders, moneylenders, and artisans [shall each abide] by their own respective classes.
GDhS-A 2,2.22 / GDhS-St 11.22: Having ascertained the matters from them according to their respective jurisdictions, the settlement of legal affairs shall proceed.
In the acquisition of right reasoning, logic (*tarka*) is the means.
Having inferred by means of that [logic], one should lead [the matter] to its proper place.
In the event of a conflict of views, having brought it back from those who are learned in the three Vedas and are elders, one should lead it to a final conclusion.
For thus his supreme good comes to be. It is known from scripture: "Brahman, when joined with Kṣatra, sustains the gods, the ancestors, and human beings."
GDhS-A 2,2.28 / GDhS-St 11.28: They say that "daṇḍa" (punishment) is so called because of its power to subdue; therefore, one should subdue those who are unsubdued.

GDhS-A 2,2.29a / GDhS-St 11.29a: The social classes (*varṇas*) and stages of life (*āśramas*), being devoted to their respective duties, after death experience the fruits of their actions; then, by the remainder [of that karma], they are born with distinguished place of birth, caste, family, physical form, lifespan, sacred learning, conduct, wealth, happiness, and intelligence.
They undergo rebirth;
being turned away and acting contrary [to the law], they perish.
These two are protected by the instruction of the teacher and by punishment. Therefore, the king and the teacher are beyond reproach; they are both beyond reproach.
[GDhS-A 2,3 = GDhS-St XII]

GDhS-A 2,3.1 / GDhS-St 12.1: A Śūdra who, having deceived or struck members of the twice-born with verbal or physical violence, shall have the limb by which he committed the offense cut off. GDhS-A 2,3.2 / GDhS-St 12.2: For approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of his property.
{VAR_St: And the confiscation of all his property} GDhS-A 2,3.3 / GDhS-St 12.3: If he is a protector [of the Veda], there is further corporal punishment.
GDhS-A 2,3.4a / GDhS-St 12.4: Now, if he listens to the Veda, his ears are to be filled with molten tin and lac.
GDhS-A 2,3.4b | GDhS-St 12.5: For reciting [the Veda], the tongue shall be cut off. GDhS-A 2,3.4c | GDhS-St 12.6: For retaining [it], the body shall be destroyed.
GDhS-A 2,3.5 / GDhS-St 12.7: One who seeks equality [with a superior] in sitting, lying down, speech, or on the road, shall be punished.
A Kṣatriya shall pay one hundred [paṇas] for insulting a Brāhmaṇa;
for assault with a staff, double that amount;
a Vaiśya shall pay one hundred and fifty.
But for a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa shall pay fifty;
half of that for a Vaiśya;
nothing for a Śūdra.
As it is for a Brāhmaṇa and a Rājanya, so it is for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
The guilt of theft for a Śūdra is eightfold. For the other castes, the penalty increases twofold for each successive class.
GDhS-A 2,3.14 / GDhS-St 12.17: In the case of an offense committed by one who knows better, the punishment is more severe.
GDhS-A 2,3.15 / GDhS-St 12.18: For taking fruits, green vegetables, grain, or pot-herbs, the fine is five *kṛṣṇalas* if the amount is small.
If cattle cause damage, the fault lies with the owner. However, if they are under the charge of a herdsman, the fault lies with him.
On an unenclosed field situated along a path, the responsibility falls upon both the herdsman and the owner of the field.
Five *māṣas* for a cow;
six for a camel or a donkey; ten for a horse or a buffalo.
In the case of goats and sheep,
two each [are sacrificed].
In the event of the total destruction [of the herd], the fine is one-sixth.

GDhS-A 2.3.24 / GDhS-St 12.27: For the non-performance of prescribed duties and for the practice of prohibited acts, there shall always be the forfeiture of one’s own clothes and food beyond what is required for subsistence.

GDhS-A 2.3.25 / GDhS-St 12.28: For the sake of cows and sacrificial fires, one may take grass, fuel, and the flowers of herbs and trees as if they were one's own; likewise, one may take the fruits of trees that are not enclosed by a fence.
Interest on a loan is lawful at the rate of five *māṣas* per month for every twenty [units of currency].
Some say it should not exceed one year’s interest.
When the loan remains outstanding for a long time, the principal becomes doubled.
Interest on a pledge that has been used does not increase.
Interest on [a debt] from one who intends to give it away, and from one who is imprisoned, also does not increase. Interest is of the type that increases by cycles of time.
[Interest] may be stipulated, corporeal, or consist of the use of a pledge;
and [interest on] cattle, wool, fields, and grain shall not exceed fivefold.
Property belonging to one who is not an idiot or a minor, if enjoyed by others for ten years while [the owner] is present, belongs to the enjoyer.
Nor with one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), an ascetic (*pravrajita*), or royal officers (*rājapuruṣa*).
[Variant: *rājanya*]

36. Cattle, land, and women shall not be subject to excessive enjoyment [as security]. 37. Those who inherit the estate shall discharge the debt. 38. Surety-money, trade-duties, fines for liquor, gambling, and judicial penalties shall not devolve upon the sons.

They shall not be liable to punishment for their sons. Deposits, pledges, borrowed items, purchased goods, and advances that have been lost through no fault of the person involved are not to be considered blameworthy in any respect.
GDhS-A 2,3.40 / GDhS-St 12.43: A thief, with disheveled hair and carrying a club, shall go to the king confessing his deed.
GDhS-A 2,3.41 / GDhS-St 12.44: He is purified by either execution or release. GDhS-A 2,3.42 / GDhS-St 12.45: By not killing him, the king becomes guilty of the same offense.

GDhS-A 2,3.43 / GDhS-St 12.46: There is no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa. GDhS-A 2,3.44 / GDhS-St 12.47: [The punishments are] deprivation of specific functions, public proclamation of the offense, banishment, and branding. GDhS-A 2,3.45 / GDhS-St 12.48: If he does not engage in [the forbidden act], he must perform penance (prāyaścitta).
One who acts intentionally like a thief is equal to a thief;
so too is a receiver [of a gift] when it is joined with unrighteousness.
The application of punishment depends on the knowledge of the person's capacity, the nature of the offense, and the circumstances.
Or rather, there may be acquittal based on the statement of a consensus of those learned in the Veda; [this is repeated for emphasis].

GDhS-A 2,4.1 / GDhS-St 13.1: When there is a conflict of testimony, the determination of the truth is based on the witnesses. GDhS-A 2,4.2 / GDhS-St 13.2: There should be many witnesses who are blameless in their own duties, trustworthy, and who feel neither affection nor animosity toward either party before the king.

Even Śūdras [may be questioned]. But a Brāhmaṇa, if he is not bound [by a vow] and has not been summoned by the words of a non-Brāhmaṇa, shall not be detained. Those who are not assembled together and have not been questioned shall not give testimony.
If they do not speak, or if they speak otherwise than the truth, they shall be at fault. (Even if unasked, they are at fault for failing to speak.)
Heaven results from speaking the truth; in the opposite case, hell.
Even those who are not bound [by oath] must speak [the truth].
There is no binding [oath] for the sake of causing pain.
And [there is guilt] in the case of what is spoken by one who is negligent.
There is guilt for the witnesses, the members of the court, the king, and the judges when there is an injury to the administration of justice.

GDhS-A 2.4.12 / GDhS-St 13.12: Some say that the act of truth is accomplished by means of an oath. GDhS-A 2.4.13 / GDhS-St 13.13: That [oath] should take place in the assembly of gods, kings, or Brahmins, for those who are not Brahmins.
GDhS-A 2.4.14 / GDhS-St 13.14: A witness who speaks falsely regarding small cattle destroys ten [generations].
In the case of a cow, a horse, a human, or land, [the fines] increase tenfold respectively; or, in the case of land, the entire property [is forfeited].
In the case of stealing [fire], there is hell.
Water is treated like land.
And the same applies to sexual intercourse.
Regarding honey and clarified butter, [the penance] is as for an animal (GDhS-A 2,4.20 / GDhS-St 13.20).
Regarding clothing, gold, grain, and the Veda, it is as for a cow (GDhS-A 2,4.21 / GDhS-St 13.21).
Regarding vehicles, it is as for a horse (GDhS-A 2,4.22 / GDhS-St 13.22).
GDhS-A 2,4.23 / GDhS-St 13.23: A witness who speaks falsely should be censured and punished.

GDhS-A 2,4.24 / GDhS-St 13.24: There is no fault in speaking untruth when one's livelihood depends upon it. GDhS-A 2,4.25 / GDhS-St 13.25: But not when that livelihood is obtained from a person of more sinful character.
The king, or a judge, or a Brāhmaṇa learned in the scriptures [shall preside]. He shall approach the judge. If there is no immediate appearance of the case, he shall wait for one year.
In cases involving a milch cow, a draft ox, or the procreation of a woman, one must act with haste.
And likewise in cases of emergency.
Among all duties, speaking the truth before the presiding judge is the most important—speaking the truth, indeed.
GDhS-A 2,5.1 / GDhS-St 14.1:
Impurity on account of a death (śāva-āśauca) lasts for ten nights for the sapinda relatives, except for those who are officiating priests, consecrated for a sacrifice, or lifelong students.
GDhS-A 2,5.2 / GDhS-St 14.2: For a Kṣatriya, it lasts eleven nights.
GDhS-A 2,5.4a | GDhS-St 14.3: For a Vaiśya, it is twelve nights.
GDhS-A 2,5.4b | GDhS-St 14.4: Some say it is half a month. GDhS-A 2,5.4 / GDhS-St 14.5: For a Śūdra, it is one month.
If that [impurity] should recur within [the period], they shall be purified by the remainder [of the period]. If it occurs during the remainder of the night, they are purified after two days;
if at dawn, after three days.

GDhS-A 2,5.8 / GDhS-St 14.9: For those killed by cows or Brahmins, [the impurity lasts] as long as the sight [of the corpse]. GDhS-A 2,5.9 / GDhS-St 14.10: And for those killed through the king’s wrath.
GDhS-A 2,5.10 / GDhS-St 14.11: In battle.
If they desire [death] by means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling from a precipice,
the cessation of the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) occurs at the seventh or the fifth generation.
The same applies in the case of birth.
GDhS-A 2,5.14a | GDhS-St 14.15: That [impurity] belongs to the mother and father.
GDhS-A 2,5.14b | GDhS-St 14.16: Or it belongs to the mother alone.
GDhS-A 2,5.15 / GDhS-St 14.17: In the case of a miscarriage, the impurity lasts for as many nights as there were months of gestation.
Or for three days.
Having heard [of the death] after the tenth day, [the impurity lasts] for a "bird-day" (two days with the intervening night).
This applies to one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, to a relative by birth, and to a fellow student.
GDhS-A 2,5.19 / GDhS-St 14.21: For one day [in the case of] a fellow student (sabrahmacārin). GDhS-A 2,5.20 / GDhS-St 14.22: And likewise for a learned brahmin (śrotriya) who has arrived.
GDhS-A 2,5.21 / GDhS-St 14.23: Upon touching a corpse, the period of impurity (āśauca) lasts ten nights, provided it was done intentionally.
The [rules] for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra have been stated. Or, [the penance is] that of the menstrual flow; and also that of the two preceding [castes].
Or [the impurity lasts] for three days.
The same applies in the case of the teacher, his son, a woman, a person for whom one officiates at a sacrifice, and a pupil.
If a person of a lower caste should touch one of a higher caste, or a person of a higher caste should touch one of a lower caste, the period of impurity in that case is as prescribed for a corpse.
Upon touching an outcaste (patita),
a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth (sūtikā), a menstruating woman (udakyā), a corpse, or one who has touched any of these, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on.
And [the same penance applies] for following a corpse (GDhS-A 2,5.29 / GDhS-St 14.31);
and for [following] a dog (GDhS-A 2,5.30 / GDhS-St 14.32);
some say [it applies] when one is struck by it (GDhS-A 2,5.31 / GDhS-St 14.32).
The offering of water for one who has undergone the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) is performed by the sapinda relatives;
so too for their wives.
Some [teachers] say that this applies only to those who have been given away [in marriage].
All [the students] shall sleep and sit on the ground and observe celibacy;
they shall not perform ritual purification.

GDhS-A 2,5.37 / GDhS-St 14.39: They shall not eat meat until the offering has been made. GDhS-A 2,5.38 / GDhS-St 14.40: The water-libation ceremony is performed on the first, third, seventh, and ninth days.
(Variant reading: third, fifth...)
And there is the discarding of garments.
But at the end [of the period], for those of the lowest castes.

The period of impurity for the parents begins from the eruption of the teeth (GDhS-A 2,5.41 / GDhS-St 14.43). For infants, those residing in a foreign land, renunciants, and non-sapiṇḍas, purification is immediate (sadyaḥ śauca) (GDhS-A 2,5.42 / GDhS-St 14.44).
And for kings, it is so because of the obstruction of their duties (GDhS-A 2,5.43 / GDhS-St 14.45).
And for a Brāhmaṇa, it is for the purpose of not interrupting his private Vedic study (svādhyāya).
[GDhS-A 2,6 = GDhS-St XV]
Now follows the Śrāddha rite. One should offer it to the ancestors on the new moon day, or during the latter half of the month beginning from the fifth day.
GDhS-A 2,6.4 / GDhS-St 15.4: Or [the sacrifice may be performed] on every [day], according to one's faith.
GDhS-A 2,6.5 / GDhS-St 15.5: Or there is a restriction regarding the time [only] when the materials, the place, and the Brahmins are present.
One should strive for excellence in the preparation of food and the rules regarding its qualities according to one's ability.
{VAR_St: -vidhinānnasya}
He should feed at least nine guests, an odd number;
or as many as his means permit; or he may invite those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and endowed with eloquence, beauty, youth, and virtuous character.
The first gift should be given to the young men;
some say it should be as [one would give] to one's father;
and one should not perform the duties of a friend with him.

In the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍas*, the mother’s *sapiṇḍas*, and the pupils shall offer [the funeral oblation]. In their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) shall do so.

By the offering of sesame, beans, rice, barley, and water, the ancestors are gratified for one month. By the flesh of fish, the deer, the *ruru* antelope, the hare, the tortoise, the boar, and the sheep, they are gratified for years. By cow’s milk, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and other dairy products, they are gratified for twelve years. By the flesh of the *vārdhrīṇasa* (a type of ox), by *kālaśāka* greens, and by the flesh of the goat, the red deer, and the rhinoceros, when mixed with honey, the gratification is eternal.

One should not feed a thief, a eunuch, an outcast, an atheist, one who lives as such, a slayer of a hero, the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried, one who officiates at sacrifices for women, a village priest, a shepherd, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, a drunkard, a spy, a false witness, a juggler, and a paramour.
[The husband of] a woman with a paramour [is also forbidden].
And [the son belongs] to him to whom he belongs.

(GDhS 2.6.17) One should avoid those who eat from a broken vessel (*kuṇḍāśin*), those who sell *soma*, arsonists, poisoners, those who have violated their vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), servants of a multitude, those who approach women who should not be approached, those who are violent, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him (*parivitti*), a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), one for whom the *paryādhāna* rite has been performed, one who performs the *paryādhāna* rite for another, one who has abandoned himself, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one with white leprosy, the son of a remarried woman, a gambler, one defeated at dice, a servant, a dealer in counterfeit goods, the husband of a *śūdra* woman, one who has renounced the sacred fires (*nirākṛti*), one suffering from consumption (*kilāsin*), a usurer, a merchant, one who lives by manual crafts, and those whose character is devoted to gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. (GDhS 2.6.18)
Those who have been divided from their father against his will. (GDhS-A 2.6.19 / GDhS-St 15.19) [Variant:
*cākāmena*]
Some [teachers] say that one may feed even disciples and those of the same lineage (sagotra).
One should feed more than three [guests],
provided they possess virtuous qualities.

One who performs a *śrāddha* on the same day as the act, having approached a Śūdra woman, causes his ancestors to dwell for a month in her excrement. Therefore, he should remain celibate (*brahmacārī*) on that day.
If one looks upon a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or an outcast (*patita*), [the food] becomes defiled. Therefore, one should give [the food] in an enclosed place.
Or he may scatter sesame seeds;
or a *paṅktipāvana* (one who sanctifies the company at a meal) may pacify [the defilement].

A *paṅktipāvana* is one who knows the six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), who sings the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, who has performed the three *Nāciketa* fire-altars, who knows the three *Madhu* verses, who knows the three *Suparṇa* verses, who maintains the five fires, who is a *snātaka*, who knows both the Mantras and the Brāhmaṇas, who knows the Dharma, and who is a descendant of a lineage where the gift of a daughter in marriage (*brahmadeya*) was never refused.
The same applies to the oblations (*havir*).
At a *śrāddha*, one should feed each of those beginning with the weak (*durbāla*) individually.
And likewise in the case of a *śrāddha* where food has not been prepared; and so it is in this manner and that.
[GDhS-A 2,7 = GDhS-St XVI]
Having performed the *upākaraṇa* ceremony at the beginning of the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon day of Proṣṭhapada, he should study the Vedas for four and a half months,
or for five months during the southern course of the sun.

A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), having had his hair shaved, shall not eat meat. Or, this restriction may last for two months. He shall not study while the wind carries dust during the day.
[One should not study] at night when [the sound reaches] the ear; (GDhS-A 2,7.7 / GDhS-St 16.7) when there is the sound of arrows, kettledrums, clay drums, or cries from a pit;
(GDhS-A 2,7.8 / GDhS-St 16.8) when there is the simultaneous howling of dogs, jackals, and donkeys.
[One should not eat] when there is a red glow, a rainbow, or mist (GDhS-A 2.7.9; GDhS-St 16.9). [Nor should one eat] when clouds appear outside the rainy season (GDhS-A 2.7.10; GDhS-St 16.10).
[One becomes impure] when one has urinated or evacuated [the bowels].
At night, [one becomes impure] in the waters of the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
And while it is raining;
some [hold that this applies] when there is a continuous stream through the gaps in the roof;
during the serving of food by the teacher.
And [one must not study] when there is light from the two luminaries (the sun and the moon).

One who is afraid, one standing in a vehicle, one lying down, or one with feet raised [should not study]. [One must not study] in a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, on a high road, or during periods of impurity.

[The Veda should not be recited] in the presence of a foul odor, a corpse, or within earshot of a *cāṇḍāla*, a *śūdra*, or one whose name should not be uttered; nor when there is belching after having eaten;
nor as long as the sound of the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* formulas or the *Sāman* chants continues.
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, eclipses, and meteors have no fixed time [for impurity];
likewise thunder, rain, and lightning when the sacred fires have been kindled;
and during the day in the rainy season.
In the case of lightning during the night, [the suspension of study lasts] until the latter part of the night. When it occurs during the first third [of the night], the entire [night is affected].

According to some, [the study of the Veda must be interrupted] when a meteor falls or when lightning flashes (GDhS-A 2.7.27 / GDhS-St 16.27). When there is thunder in the afternoon (GDhS-A 2.7.28 / GDhS-St 16.28), or even at twilight (GDhS-A 2.7.29 / GDhS-St 16.29).

GDhS-A 2,7.30 / GDhS-St 16.30: The entire night [is a time for study] until midnight. GDhS-A 2,7.31 / GDhS-St 16.31: And the day [is a time for study] as long as there is light. GDhS-A 2,7.32 / GDhS-St 16.32: Also when the king resides within one's territory has died.
And having returned from a journey, [one should fast] together with each other.

In the case of a confused crowd, a fire being set, the completion of the Veda, vomiting, a *śrāddha*, a human sacrifice (*manuṣyayajña*), and eating [at such an occasion], one must fast for a day and night.
And on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*).
Or for two days. The full moon days of Kārttika, Phālguna, and Āṣāḍha [are the times for the Śrāddha]. The three Aṣṭakās [require] a period of three nights.

Some say [the suspension of study lasts] for the last [day and night]. Or rather, it lasts for the period surrounding the rainy season. All [authorities agree that study is suspended] when rain, lightning, and thunder occur together.
[One should not study] when it is raining;
[nor] after a meal during a festival.
And for one who has studied [the Veda], there is [a suspension of study] for four muhūrtas at night.
Some say this applies constantly in a city.
Even mental [recitation] is forbidden when one is impure.
For those who have performed a *śrāddha*, the impurity lasts until the same time the next day (GDhS-A 2.7.47;
GDhS-St 16.47). This applies even when there is contact with one who has performed a *śrāddha* using uncooked food (GDhS-A 2.7.48; GDhS-St 16.48).
And those [penances] which they prescribe for each specific branch of knowledge.

A Brāhmaṇa may eat the food of twice-born men who are praiseworthy in their own duties; he may also accept gifts from them. Fuel, water, fodder, roots, fruits, honey, that which is offered for fear, a bed, a seat, a dwelling, a vehicle, milk, curd, a vessel made of *dhānā* (grains), *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu* grain, a garland, earth, and vegetables are not to be refused by anyone.
Even when supporting one's father, gods, teachers, and dependents, there is another [means of livelihood]. If there is no other means of subsistence except from a Śūdra.

The keepers of cattle, cultivators of fields, family friends, those who cause work to be done, and personal attendants—these are those whose food may be eaten. A merchant who is not an artisan [is also one whose food may be eaten].
[However, the food of] these [others] is always forbidden.
[Food] contaminated by hair or insects; [food] defiled by a woman in her menses, by a black bird, or by the foot of such a bird; [food] looked upon by a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan).
{VAR_St: bhrūṇaghnā prekṣitam} [GDhS-St 17.12; see GDhS-A 2.8.13] GDhS-A 2.8.12 / GDhS-St 17.13:
That which is defiled in its inner disposition.
That which has been smelled by a cow;
that which is sour but not curd;
that which has been cooked again.
Stale food, except for vegetables, condiments, oils, meat, and honey;

[the food] of those who have renounced the world, of prostitutes, of the accused, of those of unknown origin, of stick-bearers, of carpenters, of misers, of prison-wardens, of physicians, of hunters, of those who live by arrows, of those who eat the leavings of others, and of those who hate their own group.
[Gifts] from those unworthy of the company (apaṅktya) [are forbidden],
except for a Durvāla. Food [given] in vain, [food accompanied by] sipping water, and [food] interrupted by rising [from one's seat] are [forbidden].
GDhS-A 2,8.20 / GDhS-St 17.20: From food that is either equal or unequal [in quality], one may eat that which is either superior or inferior, provided it is offered with honor.
GDhS-A 2,8.21 / GDhS-St 17.21: And likewise, that which is not honored.
GDhS-A 2,8.22 / GDhS-St 17.22: And the milk of a cow during the ten-day period of impurity following birth.
And [the milk] of goats and buffaloes [is forbidden].
The milk of sheep is always unfit for drinking, as are that of camels, of one-hoofed animals, and of those that flow [milk] constantly, of those that have recently given birth, and of those in heat.
And [the meat] of a cow that has lost its calf; (GDhS 2.8.27) the five-clawed animals, excluding the porcupine, the hare, the śvāvidh, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise;
(GDhS 2.8.28) those with teeth in both jaws, the keśī, the hairless animal, the one-hoofed animal, the kalaviṅka, the plava, the cakravāka, and the haṃsa.
Crows, herons, vultures, hawks, aquatic birds, those with red feet or red beaks, domestic cocks, and pigs;
as well as milch-cows and oxen.
Meat from an animal that has not been offered in sacrifice, meat that has turned sour, and meat not intended for consumption;
sprouts,
garlic, onions, and exudations [from trees].
The red ones are the *vraścana* trees. (Variant:
...and [the others]).

The *nicudāru*, crane (*baka*), heron (*balākā*), parrot (*śuka*), water-fowl (*madgu*), lapwing (*tiṭṭibha*), *māndhāla*, and nocturnal animals are not to be eaten. Those that peck (*pratuda*), scratch (*viṣkira*), and web-footed (*jālapāda*) birds are to be eaten.
Fish that are not prepared [as food] may be eaten;
and those that are to be killed for the sake of dharma may also be eaten.
One should consume meat from an animal killed by a predator, or meat whose defects have not been seen, after sprinkling it with water, provided it has been commended by word; one should consume it.
[GDhS-A 2,9 = GDhS-St XVIII]
In matters of dharma, a woman is not independent.
She must not transgress against her husband. She must be restrained in speech, sight, and action.
A man without a wife who desires offspring may take a brother's widow. Once authorized by her husband, she should not let her fertile season pass.
She may obtain offspring from one among those related through funeral offerings (*piṇḍa*), lineage (*gotra*), or *ṛṣi* ancestry, or even from one related solely through the womb.
"Some say [the son belongs] not to the husband.
"Not beyond the second [marriage].
"The offspring belongs to the biological father."
By agreement, [the inheritance belongs] to another;
and while [the father] is still living, [it belongs] to the son born on the wife's field.
GDhS-A 2,9.12 / GDhS-St 18.12: From another [man], it belongs to him (the offspring).
GDhS-A 2,9.13 / GDhS-St 18.13: Or from two [men].
GDhS-A 2,9.14 / GDhS-St 18.14: But because of protection, it belongs to the husband alone.

If her husband is heard from, she must go to him; {if he has disappeared, there is a six-year penance while he is still heard from}. But if he has gone forth as an ascetic, there is an end to the obligation because of its cessation.

GDhS-A 2,9.17 / GDhS-St 18.17: For a Brāhmaṇa, [the period of waiting] is twelve years in connection with the acquisition of knowledge. GDhS-A 2,9.18 / GDhS-St 18.18: The same applies to a younger brother regarding an elder brother, in matters of taking a wife or establishing the sacred fires. GDhS-A 2,9.19 / GDhS-St 18.19: Some say it is six years.
After three menstrual periods have passed, a maiden may, having discarded her paternal ornaments, unite herself with one who is blameless. Marriage may take place before the onset of menstruation.
GDhS-A 2,9.22 / GDhS-St 18.22: One who does not give [the gift] is at fault.
GDhS-A 2,9.23 / GDhS-St 18.23: Some say [he is at fault] prior to the handing over of the garment.
{VAR_St: vāsaḥ}
GDhS-A 2,9.24 / GDhS-St 18.24: One may take property from a Śūdra for the purpose of accomplishing a marriage or for the sake of maintaining religious duties.
GDhS-A 2,9.25 / GDhS-St 18.25: Even in other cases, one may take from a Śūdra who possesses many cattle but performs no religious rites.
GDhS-A 2,9.26 / GDhS-St 18.26: Or from one who owns a hundred cows but has not established the sacred fires.
And [one should not eat] from one who owns a thousand cows if he does not drink Soma; (GDhS-A 2,9.28) nor on the seventh day if it has not been set aside for accumulation;
(GDhS-A 2,9.29) even [from those] whose ritual duties have not been neglected.

If questioned by the king, he should speak [the truth]. For the king must support him if he is endowed with learning and good character. If there is an obstruction to the administration of dharma, there is sin in failing to report it.
The fault of non-performance; the fault is indeed a fault.
The duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) and the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) have been declared.

GDhS-A 3.1.2 / GDhS-St 19.2: Now, indeed, this person becomes tainted by a blameworthy act, such as officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be officiated, eating what is unfit to be eaten, speaking what is censurable, failing to perform prescribed duties, and indulging in forbidden practices.
GDhS-A 3.1.3 / GDhS-St 19.3: Regarding this, they deliberate whether one should perform an expiation or should not perform it.
"One should not perform [it]," so they say;
"for action is never exhausted.
"One should perform it," says another.
It is known from tradition: "Having sacrificed with the *punaḥstoma*, they return to the *savana*. And:
"Having sacrificed with the *vrātyastomas*, he overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin who sacrifices with the *aśvamedha*."
And [it is said]: "One should cause him who is being falsely accused to sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut. And:
"The means of atonement for that are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts."

The Upaniṣads, the Vedānta, the Saṃhitās of all the Vedic meters, the Madhu-hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājana and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Bṛhat and Rathantara, the Puruṣagati, the Mahānāmnīs, the Mahāvairāja, the Mahādivākīrtya, any one of the Jyeṣṭhasāmans, the Bahiṣpavamāna, the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānī verses, and the Sāvitrī— these are the purifying (pāvamāna) texts.

GDhS-A 3.1.13 / GDhS-St 19.13: A milk-vow, eating vegetables, eating fruits, barley-gruel in a handful (*prasṛtayāvaka*), the consumption of gold, the consumption of clarified butter, and the drinking of Soma—these are purifying substances.
GDhS-A 3.1.14 / GDhS-St 19.14: All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords (*tīrtha*), the dwellings of seers (*ṛṣi*), and the grounds of cow-pens—these are purifying places.
3.15. Celibacy, speaking the truth, touching water at the [three] libations, wearing wet clothes, sleeping on the ground, and fasting—these are the austerities.
3.16. Gold, a cow, a garment, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given.

{VAR_St: thus these should be given} GDhS-A 3,1.17 / GDhS-St 19.17: A year, six months, four, three, two, or one [month]; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, or a day and night—these are the durations of time.
{VAR_St: three, two, or one}
GDhS-A 3.1.18 / GDhS-St 19.18: In the absence of a specific injunction, these very [penances] may be performed as alternatives.

GDhS-A 3.1.19 / GDhS-St 19.19: For heavy sins, heavy [penances] are prescribed; for light sins, light [penances]. GDhS-A 3.1.20 / GDhS-St 19.20: The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal expiation (sarvaprāyaścitta).
{The Universal Atonement} GDhS-A 3.2.1 / GDhS-St 20.1:

One should abandon a father who is a regicide, a priest for Śūdras, a priest for those performing rites for Śūdras, a corrupter of the Vedas, a killer of an embryo, or one who dwells together with Antyāvasāyins or with an Antyāvasāyinī woman.
{VAR_St: -antāvasāyibhiḥ; he may cohabit with an antāvasāyinī} GDhS-A 3.2.2 / GDhS-St 20.2:
Having assembled his teachers of learning and his blood relations, they shall perform for him all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libations. {VAR_St:
funeral rites}
And they should overturn his vessel.

A slave or a laborer, having brought an impure vessel from the refuse heap and filled it with water from a female slave’s jar, should, facing south, overturn it while pronouncing the name [of the deceased], saying: "I render so-and-so devoid of water. {VAR_St:
facing south, he should overturn it with his foot; ... saying "so-and-so"}
All of them, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin) and with their topknots loosened, should touch that [animal].
Those who are teachers of knowledge and those related by birth should look on.
Having touched water, they enter the village.

After that, having conversed with such a person, he should remain for one night reciting the Sāvitrī if it was done unintentionally; {VAR_St: after that} if it was done intentionally, he should remain for three nights.

GDhS-A 3.2.10 / GDhS-St 20.10: But he who is purified by a penance—once he is purified, they should fill a vessel made of gold with water from a most sacred pool or from flowing rivers, and then have him touch those waters.

GDhS-A 3.2.11 / GDhS-St 20.11: Then they should give that vessel to him; having accepted it, he should mutter: "Peaceful is the sky, peaceful is the earth, peaceful and auspicious is the intermediate space; I take that which is the radiant light."

{VAR_St: rocanas tam iha gṛh-} GDhS-A 3,2.12a | GDhS-St 20.12: With these *yajus* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *taratsamandī* verses, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, he should offer clarified butter (*ājya*). GDhS-A 3,2.12b | GDhS-St 20.13a: He should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa.
Or a cow [should be given] (GDhS-A 3,2.13 / GDhS-St 20.13b);
and [it should be given] to the teacher (GDhS-A 3,2.14 / GDhS-St 20.14);
but he for whom the penance ends with death shall be purified upon dying (GDhS-A 3,2.15 / GDhS-St 20.15).
{VAR_St: prāyaścittaṃ mṛtaḥ} GDhS-A 3,2.16 / GDhS-St 20.16: They shall perform for him all the funeral rites, beginning with the water libations.
GDhS-A 3,2.17 / GDhS-St 20.17: This very same rite of peace-water (śāntyudaka) applies to all minor offenses (upapātaka).
Regarding the minor offenses (upapātaka):

those who kill a Brahmin, drink liquor, violate the bed of their teacher, or have sexual relations with a mother, a father, or a female relative; thieves; atheists; those who habitually perform censurable acts; and those who abandon their parents or those who abandon a person who has not been outcasted—these are outcasted (patita).

And those who associate with such as these— namely, the slayers of a Brahmin, drinkers of spirituous liquor, and those related to them— as well as those who associate with others who have committed mortal sins (pātaka), shall perform penance for one year while living together with them.
GDhS-A 3,3.4 / GDhS-St 21.4: Falling away from the duties of the twice-born is degradation. GDhS-A 3,3.5 / GDhS-St 21.5: Likewise, there is a lack of success in the hereafter.
Some [call that] hell. Three [of the first four sins] are not to be specified, according to Manu.
GDhS-A 3,3.8 / GDhS-St 21.8: Some say that a woman does not fall [from her caste] by having intercourse with anyone other than her guru.
GDhS-A 3,3.9 / GDhS-St 21.9: A woman falls [from her caste] by causing an abortion or by serving a man of a lower caste.
Giving false testimony,
malicious talebearing that reaches the king, and making a false accusation against one's teacher are equal to mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*).

GDhS-A 3,3.11 / GDhS-St 21.11: Among those unworthy of the company at a meal (*apaṅktya*), up to the one who has lost his sacred fires (*durbāla*), the killer of a cow, the slayer of a Brahmin, one who performs that [act] alone, the student who has broken his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), and one whose *sāvitrī* initiation has lapsed—these are secondary sins (*upapātaka*).

GDhS-A 3,3.12 / GDhS-St 21.12: Through teaching [the Veda] out of ignorance, and through serving an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or a teacher (*ācārya*) who has committed a cause for loss of caste (*patanīya*), these two [the teacher and the priest] are to be abandoned.

GDhS-A 3.3.13 / GDhS-St 21.13: One falls [from caste] by teaching [the Veda] to anyone other than those [who are eligible], except in the case of relinquishing [one's own status]. GDhS-A 3.3.14 / GDhS-St 21.14: And some say that the one who accepts [such a gift] also falls.
GDhS-A 3,3.15 / GDhS-St 21.15: There must never be a lack of maintenance for one's mother and father. GDhS-A 3,3.16 / GDhS-St 21.16: But they shall not divide the inheritance.
GDhS-A 3,3.17 / GDhS-St 21.17: The guilt incurred by falsely accusing a Brāhmaṇa is equal to that [of the crime].
Twice [the penance is performed] for an innocent person;
and also when one who is capable fails to rescue another from the injury of a weak person.
Threatening a Brahmin while enraged leads to the loss of heaven for a hundred years;
in the case of striking him, [the loss lasts] for a thousand years.
Upon seeing blood, he should remain there until it has flowed out, and then he should collect dust from that spot.
GDhS-A 3,4.1 / GDhS-St 22.1: An expiation [is prescribed]. GDhS-A 3,4.2 / GDhS-St 22.2: The slayer of a Brahmin shall cast himself three times into a fire from which the chaff has been removed.
GDhS-A 3,4.3 / GDhS-St 22.3: Or he may become a target for those bearing weapons in a battle.
Or, carrying a skull-topped staff and a begging bowl in his hand, he shall enter a village for alms for twelve years as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), proclaiming his deed.
He should step aside from the path upon seeing an Ārya. By alternating between standing and sitting and touching water at the three daily libations (*savana*), he shall be purified.

Or, in the case of a Brahmin, [the rule applies] when life is at stake or on account of that [life-threatening cause]. (GDhS-A 3,4.7 / GDhS-St 22.7) When there is a loss of property, [the rule applies] after three [days] have elapsed.
(GDhS-A 3,4.8 / GDhS-St 22.8) {VAR_St: -caye vā}
Or at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*);
or even at another sacrifice, provided it concludes with the *agniṣṭut*;
or if he has been released [from the sin] upon the killing of a Brahmin, even if he did not actually kill him.
The same applies to the killing of an *ātreyī*. And also when the fetus is not yet known [to be female].
For killing a Kṣatriya, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give one thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh;
for killing a Vaiśya, however, one shall observe it for three years and give one hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh.
In the case of a Śūdra, he shall give a cow and a bull as the eleventh for one year;
the same applies in the case of a woman who is not an Ātreyī.
And for killing a cow, [the penance is] as prescribed for a Vaiśya. For killing a frog, a mongoose, a crow, a *bimba*, a *daha*, a rat, or a dog, it is likewise.
Having killed a thousand vertebrate animals; having killed boneless animals and having carried a load of oxen; or alternatively, one should give something for each individual vertebrate animal.
For a eunuch, a load of straw and a māṣa of lead;
for a boar, a jar of ghee.
For a snake, an iron rod;
for a woman of the Brahmin class who is unchaste, a blue [rod].
(Note: *jīla* according to the St variant).
GDhS-A 3,4.27 / GDhS-St 22.27: For violating a Vaiśya woman, [the penance lasts] for some time.

GDhS-A 3,4.28 / GDhS-St 22.28: In cases of killing, or in the loss of a bed, food, or wealth, the years [of penance] are distinct [for each]. GDhS-A 3,4.29 / GDhS-St 22.29: For adultery with the wife of another, [the penance lasts] two years.
GDhS-A 3,4.30 / GDhS-St 22.30: Three [days] for one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).
GDhS-A 3,4.31 / GDhS-St 22.31: And upon obtaining wealth, there is the abandonment [of the penance].
GDhS-A 3,4.32 / GDhS-St 22.32: Or he should cause it to go to its proper place.
GDhS-A 3,4.33 / GDhS-St 22.33: If one employs forbidden mantras, he shall perform the Sahasravāka penance.

GDhS-A 3,4.34 / GDhS-St 22.34: The same applies to those who have extinguished the sacred fires, those who have been expelled from their caste, and those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka).
GDhS-A 3,4.35 / GDhS-St 22.35: A woman who has been unfaithful, even if she is guarded, shall receive a portion of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
In the case of non-human females—
with the exception of cows— for intercourse with a woman, there shall be an oblation of clarified butter performed with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras.

GDhS-A 3,5.1 / GDhS-St 23.1: For a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk *surā*, they should pour hot *surā* into his mouth; when he is dead, he shall be purified. GDhS-A 3,5.2 / GDhS-St 23.2: If he drinks it unintentionally, he must consume hot milk, hot clarified butter, hot water, or hot air for three days each; that is the *kṛcchra* penance, after which he undergoes the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
GDhS-A 3,5.3 / GDhS-St 23.3: And the same applies to the consumption of urine, feces, or semen.
[One must fast] for a part of the body [if touched] by beasts of prey, camels, or donkeys;
and also [for a part of the body if touched] by a domestic cock or a pig.
If one smells the odor of liquor, one who has drunk liquor must perform breath-suppressions (prāṇāyāma) and consume clarified butter (ghṛta).
And for one bitten by the aforementioned [serpents], [the same penance applies].
The violator of the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
Or he shall embrace a glowing iron image of a woman.
Or, having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he should walk straight toward the southwest until his body collapses.
Or, having torn them out... [he should do as above].
One who has died shall be purified [by the same rites as for a relative].

[Sexual intercourse] with the wives of a friend, a uterine brother, one of the same lineage (*gotra*), or a pupil, or with a daughter-in-law, or with a cow, is equal to violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*).
Some say he should be thrown to the scavengers. The king shall have a woman who has had intercourse with a man of lower caste devoured by dogs in public.
One should have a male executed;
or, as has been stated [elsewhere].
