One who has committed the *avakīrṇin* offense should sacrifice a donkey to Nirṛti at a crossroads.
Having put on its skin with the hair turned upward and wearing red garments, he should go about for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his deed.
With his hair tied upward and carrying a red vessel, he shall subsist on alms.
He becomes purified after one year.

In the event of seminal emission during a state of fear, illness, or sleep, there shall be for seven nights the kindling of fire, wandering for alms, and the offering of clarified butter or fuel-sticks with the two *retaḥsic* verses.
A student of sacred knowledge who is overtaken by sunrise or sunset while away from home shall remain standing for the day without eating, or for the night, reciting the Sāvitrī verse.
Upon seeing something impure, he should look at the sun after performing a breath-control exercise (prāṇāyāma).

GDhS-A 3,5.23 / GDhS-St 23.23: For eating what is unfit to be eaten, or for consuming impure substances, one must become free of excrement [by fasting until that state is reached]. GDhS-A 3,5.24 / GDhS-St 23.24: Or there shall be fasting for at least three nights. GDhS-A 3,5.25 / GDhS-St 23.25: Or, for seven nights, he may subsist on fruits that have fallen of their own accord, provided he does not overstep [the prescribed limit].
For consuming [forbidden food] prior to the five-toed animals, there shall be vomiting and the consumption of clarified butter.
For verbal abuse, falsehood, and violence, the highest penance is a three-night fast.
GDhS-A 3,5.28 / GDhS-St 23.28: Or, upon speaking a falsehood, there is an oblation with the Vāruṇī and Mānavī verses.
GDhS-A 3,5.29 / GDhS-St 23.29: Some say there is no fault in untruthfulness in cases of marriage, sexual intercourse, jesting, or when one's life is at stake.
But indeed, one must not [speak untruth] regarding matters concerning one's teacher.
Even by merely thinking it in his mind, one who speaks an untruth to his teacher regarding even minor matters destroys seven generations before him and seven after him.
(As for why: "seven...")
For sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste (antyāvasāyinī),
the penance is a Kṛcchra for one year;
if it was unintentional, it is twelve nights.
In approaching a woman in her courses,
there shall be a three-night penance.
GDhS-A 3,6.1 / GDhS-St 24.1: Secret penance is for one whose fault has not been made public.

GDhS-A 3,6.2 / GDhS-St 24.2: One who desires to accept what should not be accepted, or who has already accepted it, should mutter the four verses beginning with *taratsamandī* while standing in water.
GDhS-A 3,6.3 / GDhS-St 24.3: One desiring to eat what is unfit to be eaten should scatter [grain] over the earth.
GDhS-A 3,6.4 / GDhS-St 24.4: Some [teachers] say that for one who has sexual intercourse during the period between menstrual seasons, purification occurs by touching water.
GDhS-A 3,6.5 / GDhS-St 24.5: [The same applies] regarding women; some [say this].

GDhS-A 3,6.6 / GDhS-St 24.6: Or, observing a vow of milk for ten nights, a second [period] on ghee, and a third on water; eating only one meal during the day and so forth, with his clothes moistened by water; [offering as oblations] hair, nails, skin, flesh, blood, sinew, bone, and marrow, with the formula "I offer myself into the mouth of Death"—this at the end of all [these acts] is the expiation for the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*). GDhS-St 24.7: Now, another [expiation].
The rule has been stated.
One should offer oblations with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* and with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* verses, using clarified butter, while reciting the verse "O Agni, do thou carry us across" (*Ṛgveda* 1.189.2).

Or else, while remaining under that very same vow, one who is exhausted by breath-suppressions (*prāṇāyāma*) for the [sins of] killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing, and violating the Guru’s bed, should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn; this expiation is equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
Or, by repeating the Sāvitrī mantra one thousand times, he purifies himself right here in this world. Or,
by repeating the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, he is liberated from all sins.
He is released, he is released.
Regarding this they say: "In how many ways does the *avakīrṇin* enter?"

“[He addresses] the Maruts with his breath, Indra with his strength, Bṛhaspati with his sacred luster, and Agni with all the rest. Having kindled the fire at night on the new moon day, he offers expiatory oblations of clarified butter.

He offers two oblations with the formulas: "I am one who has spilled his seed through desire; I have spilled my seed; to the one who desires desire, svāhā! I am one who has been oppressed by desire; I have been oppressed; to the one who desires desire, svāhā! Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, sprinkled water around it, and performed the rite for the sacrificial site, he stands up and worships three times with the verse:
"May they sprinkle me together... (or: "May they sprinkle me").
"These three worlds—for the sake of conquering these worlds and for the sake of attaining them.

Regarding this very ritual act, some maintain that if one should become as if impure, he should offer oblations in this manner and recite the consecratory formulas in this manner; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is the boon (*vara*), because there is no specific distinction [regarding the penance].
He who, being impure, should thus address [the mantra]:

"In cases of dishonesty, calumny, practicing forbidden conduct, or consuming forbidden food; having discharged semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening; and in performing a blameworthy act even if done intentionally—one should touch water with verses addressed to the Waters (*abliṅga*), or with verses addressed to Varuṇa (*vāruṇī*), or with other purificatory texts."
In the event of an offense committed through forbidden speech or thought, one should recite the *vyāhṛtis* ending with the five *satyas*.
In all cases, one should sip water while reciting: "May the Day and the Sun purify me" in the morning, and "May the Night and Varuṇa purify me" in the evening.
Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks, having offered with the mantra "devakṛtasya... (Gṛhyasūtra 3.7.10), he is liberated from all sin.
(GDhS-St 25.10) [He is] liberated.
[Eight].
Now, therefore, we shall explain the *kṛcchra* penances. (Alternatively:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the three *kṛcchra* penances.)

Having eaten sacrificial food for breakfast, he shall not eat for three nights. Then, for another three days, he shall eat only at night. Then, for another three days, he shall not beg for anything at all.
Then, he should fast for another three days. One who desires speed should stand during the day and sit during the night. He should speak the truth.
One should not converse with those who are non-Aryans. One should always employ the Raurava and Yaudhājaya [Sāmans].

At each *savana*, there is the touching of water; one should purify oneself with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which contain the word *pavitra*, and with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ.
Then follows the water libation (*udakatarpaṇa*).

Homage to Ahamāya, Mohamāya, Maṃhamāya, Dhanvate, Tāpasāya, and Punarvasave; homage! Homage to Mauñjyāya, Urvyāya, Vasuvindāya, and Sārvavindāya; homage! Homage to Pārāya, Supārāya, Mahāpārāya, and Vārayiṣṇave; homage! Homage to Rudrāya, Paśupataye, Mahate Devāya, Tryambakāya, Ekacarāya, Adhipataye, Harāya, Śarvāya, Īśānāya, Ugrāya, Vajriṇe, Ghṛṇine, and Kapardine; homage! Homage to Sūryāya and Ādityāya; homage! Homage to Nīlagrīvāya and Śitikaṇṭhāya; homage! Homage to Kṛṣṇāya and Piṅgalāya; homage! Homage to Jyeṣṭhāya, Vṛddhāya, Indrāya, Harikeśāya, and Ūrdhvaretase; homage! Homage to Satyāya, Pāvakāya, Pāvakavarṇāya, Kāmāya, and Kāmarūpiṇe; homage! Homage to Dīptāya and Dīptarūpiṇe; homage! Homage to Tīkṣṇāya and Tīkṣṇarūpiṇe; homage! Homage to Saumyāya, Supuruṣāya, Mahāpuruṣāya, Madhyamapuruṣāya, Uttamapuruṣāya, and Brahmacāriṇe; homage! Homage to Candralalāṭāya and Kṛttivāsase; homage!

"Salutation to the one who is free from delusion, who shakes off [evil], who is beyond the waves [of existence], the winner of all, the one who brings across, to Hari, the eldest, the most excellent, the ancient, the one clothed in space—salutation!
(GDhS-A 3,8.13 / GDhS-St 26.13). This alone is the worship of the Sun. These same [verses] are the oblations of clarified butter. (GDhS-A 3,8.14 / GDhS-St 26.14)
At the end of twelve nights, having cooked a sacrificial oblation (*caru*), he should offer it to these deities:
"To Agni, svāhā! To Soma, svāhā! To Agni and Soma, to Indra and Agni, to Indra, to the Viśve Devas, to Brahmā, to Prajāpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Thereafter follows the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas.
By this very [rule], the *atikṛcchra* is explained. (GDhS-A 3,8.18 / GDhS-St 26.18) He should eat as much as he can take up in a single mouthful.
(GDhS-A 3,8.19 / GDhS-St 26.19) Subsisting on water for the third [period] is the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. (GDhS-A 3,8.20 / GDhS-St 26.20)
Having performed it for the first time, he becomes pure, cleansed, and fit for ritual action.

Having performed it for the second time, he is released from whatever sin he commits other than the great mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*). Having performed it for the third time, he is released from all sin.
{VAR_St: he destroys all evil} GDhS-A 3,8.24 / GDhS-St 26.24: Now, having performed these three *kṛcchra* penances, one becomes bathed in all the Vedas; one becomes known by all the gods.
GDhS-A 3,8.25 / GDhS-St 26.25: And so too for him who knows this.
And he who knows thus.
Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa.
The rule for that has been stated in the Kṛcchra penance. He shall undergo shaving and observe the vow. (Alternatively: he shall observe the vow after shaving.)
On the day when the full moon has dawned, he should observe the fast.

With the verses "Āpyāyasva" (RV 1.91.17), "Saṃ te payāṃsi" (RV 1.91.18), and "Navo-navo" (RV 10.85.19), he should perform the libation, the offering of clarified butter, the consecration of the oblation, and the worship of the moon. He should offer oblations with the four verses beginning with "Yad devā devaheḍanam."
{VAR_St: ghee with four [verses]}.
At the end, [he offers oblations] with fuel-sticks while reciting "devakṛtasya" and so forth.

With the formulas "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," "tapas," "satyam," "yaśas," "śrīs," "ūrk," "iḍā," "ojas," "tejas," "varcas," "puruṣas," "dharma," and "śivas," he performs the consecration of each morsel mentally, verse by verse.
{VAR_St: the person of splendor} GDhS-A 3.9.9 / GDhS-St 27.9:
Or [he may offer] all [the portions] with "Homage! Svāhā!
GDhS-A 3.9.10 / GDhS-St 27.10: The size of a mouthful is such that it does not distort the mouth.

Caru, alms-food, barley-meal, grain-particles, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits, and water—these are the sacrificial foods, each subsequent one being more highly commended than the preceding.
Having eaten fifteen morsels on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the number by one each day.
Having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the number by one each day.
According to some, it is the reverse;
thus is the Cāndrāyaṇa month.
Having thus attained this, one becomes free from evil and free from sin; he destroys all transgression.

Having reached the second [birth], he purifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, himself as the twenty-first, and his lineage. Having reached the year-long [observance], he attains co-residence (*salokatā*) with the moon.
After the father's death, the sons shall divide the inheritance.
When her menstrual flow has ceased and the mother wishes it,
[the father may divide the estate]; or he may give everything to the eldest son and support the others like a father.
But upon partition, there is an increase in merit.
(GDhS-A 3.10.4 / GDhS-St 28.4) The twentieth part belongs to the eldest: a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked on both sides, and a bull.
(GDhS-A 3.10.5 / GDhS-St 28.5) If there are many, the middlemost son receives those that are one-eyed, lame, hornless, or tailless. (GDhS-A 3.10.6 / GDhS-St 28.6)
A goat, an iron [implement], a house, a vehicle, and a quadruped— each of these belongs to the youngest [brother]. If there are many, [the same applies to each].
If they are equal, the rest [of the property] is shared equally; or the first-born may take two shares.
GDhS-St 28.10: Each one [of the others] receives one [item]. GDhS-A 3.10.9 / GDhS-St 28.11: Or, each one obtains one desirable object of wealth, with each preceding person receiving first.
{VAR_St: labheta}
Ten [animals] for domestic animals;
{VAR_St: ten hundred} not [ten] of one-hoofed or two-footed creatures.
An extra bull is for the eldest son;
sixteen cows and a bull are for the son born of the eldest wife;
the younger brothers share equally with the son born of the eldest wife.
Or rather, there may be a specific division of shares according to each mother within their own respective group.

A man who has no other sons shall set aside a daughter as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) after performing sacrifices to Agni and Prajāpati, having made an agreement that "this offspring is for my sake."

According to some, she is designated as an *aputrīkā* (appointed daughter) by the mere intention [of the father]. Because of the uncertainty regarding that [status], one should not marry a girl who has no brothers.
The sons born of the same *piṇḍa*, *gotra*, and *ṛṣi* ancestors shall divide the inheritance of a man who dies without offspring, or [the inheritance] of a woman who has no offspring;
or he may seek to obtain [another] seed.
GDhS-A 3,10.21 / GDhS-St 28.23: In Devaravatī, that which is born of another [man] has no share.
GDhS-A 3,10.22 / GDhS-St 28.24: The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and not established in life.
GDhS-A 3,10.23 / GDhS-St 28.25: The bride-price of a sister belongs to the uterine brothers after the mother's death.
And some [teachers] say that it should be performed first.
The division of the inheritance of deceased persons who were not reunited belongs to the eldest brother. When one who was reunited has died, the reunited brother is the heir to the estate.
A son born after partition inherits only his father's share.
A learned son may, at his pleasure, refuse to give to those who are unlearned property that he has acquired by himself.
Those who are unlearned shall divide it equally.

GDhS-A 3.10.30 / GDhS-St 28.32: The legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*dattaka*), the son made (*kṛtrima*), the son secretly born (*gūḍhotpanna*), and the son cast off (*apaviddha*) are the heirs to the estate (*rikthabhāj*).

GDhS-A 3.10.31 / GDhS-St 28.33: The son of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), the son received with the bride (*sahoḍha*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), the son given himself (*svayaṃdatta*), and the son bought (*krīta*) are entitled to a share of the lineage (*gotrabhāj*).
GDhS-A 3.10.32 / GDhS-St 28.34: In the absence of the sons beginning with the legitimate son of the body, these [latter] receive one-fourth of a share.
GDhS-A 3.10.33 / GDhS-St 28.35: The eldest son of a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya wife, if endowed with good qualities, is entitled to an equal share.
GDhS-A 3.10.34 / GDhS-St 28.36: The other [shares] are reduced by the portion due to the eldest.
GDhS-A 3.10.35 / GDhS-St 28.37: In the case of a combination of sons by a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya wife, it is the same as in the case of the sons by a Brāhmaṇa wife.

If [the son] is from a Kṣatriya woman... Even a son of a Śūdra woman, if he is obedient and there are no other offspring, shall receive a means of subsistence according to the rule for a pupil (antevāsin).
GDhS-A 3,10.38 / GDhS-St 28.40: According to some, even the son of a wife of equal caste (savarṇā) does not receive [the inheritance] if he has behaved improperly.

GDhS-A 3,10.39 / GDhS-St 28.41: The learned Brāhmaṇas (śrotriyāḥ) shall divide the estate of a Brāhmaṇa who dies without offspring. GDhS-A 3,10.40 / GDhS-St 28.42: In the case of others, the king [shall take it].
The idiot and the eunuch are to be maintained.
The offspring of an idiot is entitled to a share.
In the case of women born of inverse castes (*pratiloma*), they are treated like the sons of a *śūdra*.
There is no division regarding water, security, and prepared food (GDhS-A 3.10.44; GDhS-St 28.46). Nor is there division among women who are united [in marriage] (GDhS-A 3.10.45;

GDhS-St 28.47). When the matter is unknown, that which is praised by at least ten learned men who are conversant with the *ūha*, free from greed, and disciplined, should be performed (GDhS-A 3.10.46; GDhS-St 28.48).

Four who have mastered the four Vedas, three persons from among the [first] three stages of life (āśrama) who are experts in their respective duties (*dharma*), and [one] who knows the highest [truth]— these ten or more constitute what is called an assembly (*pariṣad*). (GDhS 3.10.47)

But in the absence of these, a *śrotriya* who knows the Veda and is distinguished [in learning] shall decide in case of disagreement; for he says: Since this man is incapable of [exerting] injury or favor toward living beings, the knower of *dharma*, through his specialized knowledge and his devoted application, attains the heavenly world.
"Thus is dharma, [this is] dharma. —
*Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra* 3.10.51.

[Abhandlungen für die Kunde des Morgenlandes, 16]. Leipzig, 1922. [K] Edited by Umesh Chandra Pandeya: *The Baudhāyana-Dharmasūtra* with the ‘Vivaraṇa’ Commentary by Śrī Govinda Svāmī and Critical Notes by M. M. A. Chinnaswāmī Śāstrī. [The Kashi Sanskrit Series, 104]. Varanasi, 1972.
Now begins the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.
Dharma has been taught according to each Veda.
We shall now explain that [Dharma] in accordance with it.
The second [source of dharma] is that which is based on tradition (smārta).
The third is the tradition of the learned (śiṣṭāgama).

The learned (śiṣṭas) are indeed those who are free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only as much grain as fits in a jar, lacking greed, and abandoned by hypocrisy, arrogance, avarice, delusion, and anger.

"Those whose Veda, along with its supplements, has been acquired through righteous means, who are learned in the inference thereof, and for whom the Śruti is the direct cause [of their knowledge], are the *śiṣṭas*. (BDhS 1.1.1.6) "In the absence of such persons, an assembly (*pariṣad*) consisting of at least ten members [is authoritative]. (BDhS 1.1.1.7)
Moreover, they cite this: "One learned in the four Vedas, one who can interpret alternatives, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), one who recites the Dharma,
and three Brahmins established in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*)— this is an assembly (*parṣad*) consisting of at least ten members."
There should be five, or three, or even one who is blameless;
for he alone is the expounder of Dharma, and not others, however many there may be.
Just as an elephant made of wood, and just as a deer made of leather, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied; these three are merely bearers of names.
Whatever those deluded by darkness, fools who do not know the Dharma, may say—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon the speakers.
The course of Dharma, which has many doors, is subtle and difficult to follow;
therefore, in a matter of doubt, it should not be declared by even one who is highly learned.
The twice-born, mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wielding the sword of the Vedas—
whatever they may declare, even in jest, that is remembered as the supreme Dharma.
Just as water situated upon a stone may be dried up by the wind and the sun,
even so whatever sin resides in the agent is completely dissolved like water.
Having carefully examined the body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and the nature of the act with his intellect, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe the penances.

"Among those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by birth—even if they have gathered in their thousands—the status of a *pariṣad* (an assembly qualified to judge dharma) does not exist. Thus it is said.
There is a fivefold divergence of practice among those to the south and likewise among those to the north.
We shall now explain those [rites] which are performed on the south side.

BDhS 1.1.2.3: For example, eating together with one who has not been initiated, eating with a woman, eating food that has been kept overnight, and sexual intercourse with the daughter of a maternal uncle or a paternal aunt.
Now, to the north, there are the sale of wool, the drinking of *sīdhu* liquor, trade with people from both sides of the sea, the profession of arms, and sea voyages.
If one performs the one [duty] at the time for the other, one becomes defiled by performing the one at the time for the other.
In each such case, the authority of the local custom alone shall prevail.
"This is false," says Gautama.
One should not respect even both [the Veda and the Smṛti] if one perceives a contradiction with the Smṛti of the learned (śiṣṭa).

BDhS 1.1.2.9: That region which lies east of Ādarśa, west of Kanakhala, south of the Himavat, and north of the Pāriyātra mountains is Āryāvarta. Whatever custom prevails therein is authoritative. [K: from Kālakavana] BDhS 1.1.2.10: Some say it is the land between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers.
Moreover, in this regard, the followers of the Bhāllavi school cite this verse:
"To the west lies the Sindhu, the divider; to the east is the rising of the sun.
As far as the dark [waters] flow, so far indeed extends the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus it is said.
The Avantis, the Aṅgas and Magadhas, the Surāṣṭras, the people of the Deccan,
the Upāvṛts, and the Sindhu-Sauvīras— these are of mixed origin.
Having gone to the Āraṭṭas, Kāraskaras, Puṇḍras, Sauvīras, Vaṅgas, Kaliṅgas, and Prānūnas, one should perform the Punastoma sacrifice or the Sarvapṛṣṭhā.
Moreover, they also cite this:

Therefore, for whatever night a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) does not bring firewood, he dwells having cut away a portion of his own life-span. Therefore, a student of sacred knowledge should bring firewood, thinking: "Lest I dwell having cut away a portion of my life-span."

He who enters upon the student life (brahmacarya) enters upon a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra). When a Brāhmaṇa enters upon the life of a student (*brahmacarya*), he enters the beings divided into four parts: one part into the fire, one part into death, and one part into the teacher; his fourth part remains within himself.
When he places a fuel-stick (*samidh*) into the fire, he thereby ransoms that very part of himself which is in the fire; having consecrated it, he takes it into himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he makes himself poor, becomes shameless, begs for alms, and practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which was in Death; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.
Then, when he obeys the word of the teacher (*ācārya*), he thereby ransoms that foot of his which was in the Teacher; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he studies his private recitation (*svādhyāya*), he thereby ransoms that very foot of his which resides within himself; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters into him.
