Or, having washed that spot, touched it with fire, washed it again, and washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A Brahmin who has been bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean,
becomes purified by performing one hundred *prāṇāyāmas* and consuming clarified butter."
"Or, having bathed with water from the horns of cows mixed with gold and silver, or with nine new jars [of water], one becomes pure immediately. Thus it is said.
Domestic animals are not to be eaten.
Carnivorous birds [are also forbidden].
Likewise, [the meat of] a cock and a pig.
Except for goats and sheep.
The porcupine, the iguana, the hare, the hedgehog, the tortoise, and the rhinoceros—these five five-toed animals are edible, with the exception of the rhinoceros.
Likewise, the five cloven-hoofed animals—the ṛśya, hariṇa, pṛṣata, mahiṣa, and varāha—with the exception of the kuluṅga.
Among birds, five types of scratchers (viṣkira) are permitted—namely the partridge, the pigeon, the grey partridge, the vārdhrāṇasa, and the peacock—with the exception of the vāraṇa and the vāraṇava.
The fish are the Sahasradaṃṣṭra, the Cilicima, the Varmi, the Bṛhacchiras, the Maśaka, the Rohita, and the Rājīva.
The milk of a cow that has not yet passed ten days since calving, nor of one in heat, is unfit for drinking.
And [the same applies] to two cows, one of which has lost its calf and the other whose calf is elsewhere.
Woolen cloth, camel’s milk, and the milk of one-hoofed animals are not to be drunk.
For drinking water that should not be drunk, one must perform the *kṛcchra* penance, except in the case of cow's milk.
In the case of cow-products, however, there is a fast for three nights.
One must avoid stale vegetables, vegetable broth, meat, clarified butter, parched grains boiled in milk, molasses, curd, honey, and flour-meal.
Likewise, fermented liquids and molasses that have not yet solidified [are forbidden].

Having performed the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Āṣāḍha, they should perform the concluding ceremony (*utsarga*) on the full moon day of Taiṣya or Māgha. They should perform the concluding ceremony.
The gods delight in a pure sacrifice.
For the gods desire purity and are themselves pure.
Regarding this, he recites the following:

"O Maruts, pure is the oblation for you who are pure; I present the pure sacrifice to the pure ones. Through the *ṛta* (cosmic order), those who are devoted to *ṛta* have come—the pure-born, the pure, the purifiers. (*Ṛgveda* 7.56.12)
Among garments, that which is unwashed is pure.
Therefore, whatever is connected with a sacrifice, all of that one should perform using unwashed garments.
The wife, the sacrificer, and the officiating priests shall put on garments that have been washed, aired, and unworn.
Thus it is after the commencement [of the rite].
The same applies to long Soma sacrifices and sacrificial sessions (sattras).
And according to the traditional recitation.

Just as in the case of the *iṣṭi*, animal, and *soma* sacrifices performed for malevolent purposes (*abhicāra*), the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should proceed wearing red turbans and red garments; and [the ritual is performed] with the *Ṛgveda* hymns "citravāsasaḥ" and "citrāsaṅgā vṛṣākapiḥ."
At the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna), the garments should be made of linen; in their absence, they may be made of cotton or wool.
For those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, purification is by means of earth and water through washing.
The rules regarding linen, silk, and bark garments are the same as those for clothing.
The rules regarding black antelope skins are the same as those for bark garments.
One should not wear a garment that has been put on over another, nor one that is elevated above the body, nor one that has not been washed, nor an upper garment.
One should not employ for the gods water that has been stirred up or that has been used by humans.
In the case of compact ground, the remedy for defilement is smearing it with cow-dung.
The plowing of a porous field.
Having taken pure material from a moist place, it serves as a covering.
The earth is purified by four means: by the treading upon it by cows, by digging, by burning, and by being rained upon.
And from the fifth smearing and the sixth time.
Grass placed on unprepared ground should be washed.
For things that have been defiled out of sight, sprinkling with water is the purification.
The same applies to small fuel-sticks.
In the case of contact with large pieces of wood, one should wash [the object] and leave it to dry.
But for many [objects], sprinkling is prescribed.
For wooden vessels that have come into contact with food remnants, the purification is by scraping.
For those things defiled by the remnants of food or by stains, there shall be planing.
The discarding of those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, shall take place.
This is so except where there is a specific injunction to the contrary.

Just as in these cases—the Agnihotra, the remnant of the *gharma*, the *dadhigharma*, the *kuṇḍapāyinya* sacrifice, the *utsarginām ayana*, the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*, the *aiḍādadha*, the *catuścakra*, and the *brahmaudana* offerings—in all of these, there is purification with water using *darbha* grass. (BDhS 1.6.13.30) In all instances of consuming *soma*, the purification is performed with water alone at the *mārjālīya* shed. (BDhS 1.6.13.31)
The discarding of those [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, shall take place.
Earthen vessels that have come into contact with food-leavings should be submerged in water.
For those [utensils] defiled by contact with food-leavings or stains, there shall be reburning.
The discarding of [objects] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, shall take place.
For metallic vessels that have been scrubbed as previously described, the purification is by washing.
The materials for wiping are cow dung, earth, and ashes.
The re-consecration of vessels defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and similar substances must be performed.
Or, one may remain immersed in cow urine for seven nights, or likewise in a great river.
This same rule applies to objects made of stone.
The cleaning of gourds, bilva-vessels, and reed-pipes is performed with cow-hair.
For enclosures made of reeds, bamboo, *śara* grass, or *kuśa* grass, purification is by means of cow-dung and water, as prescribed.
In the case of damage to grains, they should be washed and dried.
But for many [objects], sprinkling is prescribed.
The offering of rice grains.
The same applies to prepared sacrificial offerings.

In the case of large objects defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, one should remove that portion [of the object] and the food from the person; then, sprinkling [the remainder] with this *anuvāka* beginning with "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ" is prescribed.
In the case of honey, water, and products of milk, there is no requirement for purification when they are transferred from one vessel to another.
In this same manner, one should place oil and clarified butter into water that has been touched by food-leavings and then consume them.
If impure matter is placed into the fire, one should consign the fire into the kindling woods, churn out a new fire, and perform the Pavamāneṣṭi.

In cases of differences regarding purity, place, mantras, repetition, purpose, substances, preparation, and time, each preceding factor is more important than the one following it; each preceding factor is more important.
The sacrificial ground is characterized by movement from left to right.
Likewise, there is liberation.
In rites for the ancestors, the procedure is the reverse.
One should wash what has been struck by a foot.
Having touched a limb or the water-pitcher, he should touch water.
The same applies to acts of cutting, splitting, digging, throwing away, and to rites dedicated to the ancestors (pitr), the rākṣasas, the nairṛtas, the raudras, and to malevolent incantations.
One should not protect oneself by means of a sacrificial implement accompanied by a mantra.
The internal components of the sacrifice [are as follows].
The officiating priests are outsiders.
The wife and the sacrificer are the two most closely related to the officiating priests.

From the limbs of the sacrifice comes the clarified butter; from the clarified butter, the sacrificial offerings; from the offerings, the animal victim; from the animal victim, Soma; and from Soma, the sacred fires.
The officiating priests shall not turn back from the sacrificial ground according to their respective duties.
If he faces the east, he should turn around toward his right shoulder.
Facing west, he [should offer] with the left hand.
The space between the *cātvāla* pit and the *utkara* heap is the *tīrtha* of the sacrifice.
In the absence of a sacrificial pit (cātvāla), the Āhavanīya fire and the rubbish-heap (utkara) [are established].
Then the performers—the sacrificer and his wife—should enter [the sacrificial hall].
When it has not been completed.
When the ritual has concluded, the movement [of the priests] takes place from the region of the *utkara* heap.
One should not place upon the fire a piece of wood or a fuel-stick that has not been sprinkled with water, nor one that is unbroken, nor one that is damp.
The Brahman and the sacrificer enter by the front of the Āhavanīya fire.
"Behind the Āhavanīya fire," say some.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire is the station of the Brahman priest; behind that is the station of the sacrificer.
The northern buttock [of the altar] is to the north of the Hotṛ's [station].
The utkara is the [site] of the Āgnīdhra.
Behind the Gārhapatya fire is the place for the wife.
At each of those times, he spreads out darbha grass at that very moment.
And for each person, a vessel of water should be kept ready for the purpose of sipping.
Endowed with the vow, he should be consecrated.
One should not speak of another's sin, one should not become angry, one should not weep, and one should not look at urine or feces.
Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights. O Consecration, do not abandon me!"

BDhS 1.7.15.32: Now, if it rains upon him, he should recite: "O flowing waters, bestow strength; bestow vigor; bestow power. Do not destroy my consecration, nor my austerity. BDhS 1.8.16.1: There are four social classes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among them, according to the sequence of the castes, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives.
A Kṣatriya has three wives.
For a Vaiśya, there are two.
A Śūdra [should have] one [wife].
Among those wives, sons born of women of the same caste or of the next lower caste are of the same caste as their fathers.
From women one degree or two degrees lower [than the father], the Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, and Niṣāda are born.
From women in the reverse order of castes, there are the Āyogava, Māgadha, Vaiṇa, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, and Caṇḍāla.
From an Ambaṣṭha man and a woman of the first caste, there is the Śvapāka.
From an Ugra, on the second day, a Vaiṇa is born.
From a Niṣāda and a woman of the third caste, a Pulkasa is born.
In the case of the opposite, it is a cock.
A son born of a Niṣāda father and a Niṣāda mother, up to the fifth generation, removes the status of a Śūdra.
One should initiate him; one should cause him to sacrifice at the sixth [stage].

The seventh, whose seed is unaltered, is the "equal-seeded" (*samabīja*); these are their names, which fall in sequence. One should initiate that sixth [son], and one should cause him to sacrifice; thus the seventh becomes unaltered. Those whom a man who does not observe his vows begets through similarity among the three castes—the wise call them *vrātyas*, fallen from the *sāvitrī*.
The wise call these *vrātyas*.
The Rathakāra, Ambaṣṭha, Sūta, Ugra, Māgadha, Āyogava, Vaiṇa, Kṣattṛ, Pulkasa, Kukkuṭa, Vaidehaka, Caṇḍāla, Śvapāka, and others [are such].
Among them, those born from women of the same caste as their fathers are of the same caste (*savarṇa*).
From a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Brāhmaṇa; from a Vaiśya mother, an Ambaṣṭha; and from a Śūdra mother, a Niṣāda.
"Some say he is a *pāraśava*."
From a Kṣatriya on a Vaiśya woman is born a Kṣatriya; on a Śūdra woman, an Ugra.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is born a Rathakāra.
From a Śūdra, on a Vaiśya woman, a Māgadha is born; on a Kṣatriya woman, a Kṣattṛ; and on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Caṇḍāla.
From a Vaiśya on a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; on a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Vaidehaka. From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta.
In that regard, when there is a union of the first two [classes], an Ambaṣṭha is born as one who follows the natural order (anuloma).
[K: In this case] BDhS 1.9.17.10: When there is a union of the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka, it is one who follows the inverse order (pratiloma).
One born from an Ugra father and a Kṣatriya mother is a Śvapāka.
From a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhā mother is born a Vaiṇa.
From a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother, a Pulkasa is born.
From a Śūdra, on a Niṣādī woman, a cock is born.
The wise call those born from the intermixture of castes *vrātyas*; the wise call them *vrātyas*.
The king, who receives a sixth part [of the produce], shall protect his subjects.

Brahman indeed placed its own majesty within the Brāhmaṇas—endowed with the acts of studying, teaching, sacrificing for oneself, sacrificing for others, giving, and receiving—for the protection of the Vedas.
In the *kṣatra*, strength is joined with study, sacrifice, giving, weapons, the treasury, and the protection of beings for the prosperity of the *kṣatra*.
For a Vaiśya, it is the occupation connected with the study of the Vedas, performing sacrifices, giving gifts, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, for the sake of increasing his wealth.
Among Śūdras, [the duty] of the former [classes] is service.
"For the cups were indeed created," so it is said.
He should appoint as domestic priest one who is capable of bearing the burden in every respect.
One should abide by his instruction.
In battle, he shall not retreat.
One should not strike with hollow-pointed arrows nor with poisoned ones.
One should not fight with those who are frightened, intoxicated, insane, or deranged; nor with those whose armor is missing, nor with women, children, the elderly, or Brahmins.
Except in the case of an *ātatāyin* (one who intends to kill).
Moreover, they also cite this:

"If one kills an assailant who has come to attack, even if that assailant is a teacher born of a noble family, he does not become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*); rather, it is the fury that meets the fury. Thus [it is said].
The maritime toll shall be ten paṇas per hundred, after deducting a preferential fee for the goods.
In the case of others as well, one should determine a righteous share in accordance with their relative worth, provided it does not cause injury.
After retaining for one year property whose owner is unknown, the king shall take it from a non-Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa is indeed not to be killed for any offenses whatsoever.

For a Brāhmaṇa who has committed the murder of a Brāhmaṇa, sexual intercourse with the wife of a Guru, theft of gold, or the drinking of liquor, the punishment is banishment from the realm after branding his forehead with red-hot iron with the marks of a female organ, a vulva, a jackal, or a tavern-sign.
In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment for Kṣatriyas and others is death and the confiscation of all their property.
In the case of killing those who are equal to or inferior to them, he shall prescribe appropriate punishments according to their respective strength.
Upon killing a Kṣatriya, one should release a thousand cows with an additional bull to the king for the purpose of avenging the enmity.
For a Vaiśya, one hundred; for a Śūdra, ten, and in this case, an additional bull.
The killing of a woman and the killing of a cow are explained by the [penance for] the killing of a Śūdra, except in the case of killing an Ātreyī, a milch cow, or a bull.
In the case of killing a milch cow or an ox, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance at the end [of the period].
The killing of an Ātreyī woman is explained by the [penance for] the killing of a Kṣatriya.

For killing a swan, a vulture, a peacock, a ruddy goose, a peacock-pheasant, a crow, an owl, a frog, a *ḍiḍḍika*, a *derikā*, a dog, a mongoose, a mongoose-cat, or similar creatures, the penance is the same as for a Śūdra.
For the sake of maintaining social order, a witness should give testimony exactly as it was seen or heard.
One quarter of the unrighteousness falls upon the perpetrator; one quarter goes to the witness;
one quarter reaches all the members of the court; and one quarter falls upon the king.
The king becomes free from sin, and the members of the court are released;
the guilt falls upon the perpetrator where the one deserving of blame is indeed censured.
And having thus designated a witness, the discerning judge should question him with diligence.
On whatever night you were born, and on whatever night you shall die— the good deeds that may have been performed by you during the interval between these two,
all of that shall go to the king if you speak untruth.
A witness who speaks falsely regarding testimony kills three fathers and three grandfathers, as well as seven generations of those already born and those yet to be born.
In the case of a lie for the sake of gold, one destroys three ancestors;
in the case of a lie regarding small cattle, one destroys five; and in the case of a lie regarding a cow, one destroys ten.
A witness who speaks falsely in testimony kills a hundred horses through untruth regarding a horse, a thousand men through untruth regarding a man,
and everything through untruth regarding land.

The four castes, provided they have sons, may be witnesses, except for those who are Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), royalty (*rājanya*), renunciants (*pravrajita*), eunuchs (*mānuṣya*), and the low-born (*hīna*).
In the Smṛti, the understanding is primarily based on tradition.
Otherwise than this, he becomes liable to be impaled on a stake.
"One should drink heated milk for twelve nights, or one should offer oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras; or one should offer oblations with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras."
There are eight forms of marriage.
Having ascertained his learning and character, [the gift] is given to a student who requests it; that is the *brāhma* [gift].
Having clothed and adorned her, [he says], "Let this woman practice dharma together with you"; such is the Prājāpatya rite.

Having offered the first oblation of parched grain, the gift together with two cows is the *ārṣa* form. [K: Having offered the first oblation of parched grain and having given a pair of cows to the one who provides the maiden, the taking of her hand is the *ārṣa* form.
When the sacrificial fees are being led forth, the gift to the officiating priest within the sacrificial enclosure is the *daiva* form.

The Āsura [form] consists of gratifying [the bridegroom] with wealth. The Gāndharva [form] is the mutual union of one who desires her with one who desires him. The Rākṣasa [form] results from abduction by force.
One may approach a woman while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged; this is the Paiśāca rite.
Of these, the first four belong to the Brāhmaṇa; among them, each preceding one is superior to the following.
Among the subsequent ones, each succeeding one is more sinful than the preceding.
Even here, the sixth and seventh [stages] follow the duties of the Kṣatriya, because the Kṣatriya depends upon them.
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the fifth and eighth [nights] are [the times for initiation].
For Vaiśyas and Śūdras have wives who are not restricted [to a single husband].
Because they are authorized for agriculture and service.
Some praise even the Gāndharva form of marriage, because it is characterized by mutual affection among all its participants.
It is known from tradition: "As is the marriage, so are the offspring."

Moreover, they cite this: "It is known that the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman sanctifies ten ancestors, ten descendants, and himself—ten on account of the *ārṣa* rite, ten on account of the *daiva* rite, and ten on account of the *prājāpatya* rite. Only for such sons does the capacity to master the Veda likewise exist.
A woman who has been purchased with wealth is not ordained as a wife (*patnī*).
She is neither for the *daiva* nor for the *pitrya* rites; Kāśyapa declared her to be a slave-girl (*dāsī*).
Those who, deluded by greed, bestow their own daughter for a bride-price are sellers of themselves; they are sinful men who commit a great transgression.
They fall into a terrible hell and destroy the family unto the seventh generation;
furthermore, all matters concerning going and coming are prescribed by way of a toll.

On the full moon day, the eighth day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon day, during a fire-omen, an earthquake, at a cemetery, upon the death of a local ruler or a learned *śrotriya*, and when setting out on a journey together with such persons, there shall be no study for a day and a night.

In the case of a wind carrying a foul odor, in mist, and during the sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, weeping, or the chanting of Sāman hymns, [the recitation must be suspended] for as long as those conditions persist.
When there is a simultaneous occurrence of thunder, rain, and lightning, there shall be a suspension of study for three days, except during the rainy season.
Even during the rainy season, [the study] is suspended except for the time of rain; and during the days and nights [of the new moon], it is suspended for that duration.
And after accepting a gift from or eating at a funeral rite for the ancestors, one must fast for the remainder of that day.
At meals, [one may eat] until satiety.
For the Brāhmaṇa has his hand as his mouth.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"What is eaten and what is accepted as a gift are indistinguishable," so says the Śruti.
When the father has passed away, [the impurity lasts for] three nights.

There are indeed two kinds of seed for a learned *brāhmaṇa* of good repute: one is above the navel, and the other is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of it he procreates when he initiates *brāhmaṇas*, when he teaches them, when he officiates at their sacrifices, and when he performs what is virtuous; all these constitute his offspring. Now, that which is below the navel—by means of it he has offspring born of his own loins (*aurasī*). Therefore, they do not say of a learned man of good repute who is childless, "He is sonless."
Therefore, a Brahmin has two names, two faces, two seed-sources, and two births.
And upon hearing or seeing a Śūdra who is unworthy of receiving gifts (apapātra), one must remain in that state for as long as that time lasts.
One should not study at night when jackals howl, until one falls asleep.
One should not study during the day and night, at the two twilights, or on the days of the lunar phases.
He shall not eat meat, nor shall he approach a woman.
For it is known that on the lunar festival days (parvan), the Rākṣasas and Piśācas become prone to transgression.
On account of other extraordinary portents and calamities, there shall be no study for a day and a night, except when one's mind is otherwise engaged.
Even in the case of mental [birth or death], there is a suspension of study upon birth and death.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The eighth day destroys the teacher; the fourteenth day destroys the pupil;
the fifteenth day destroys knowledge. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] on these sacred days (*parvan*)."
Therefore, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] on the festival days (parvan).
Now, therefore, follow the rules for expiation.
A killer of an embryo [shall perform penance] for twelve years.

Carrying a skull-bowl and a staff topped with a skull, clothed in the skin of a donkey, and making his dwelling in the forest, he should construct a hut in a cremation ground using a corpse’s head as a banner; there he should reside. Wandering for alms at seven houses while proclaiming his own deed, he should sustain his life by that means; if he obtains nothing, he should fast.
He should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha, the Gosava, or the Agniṣṭut.
Or he may purify himself at the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"By killing a Brahmin unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to the Dharma;
for that act committed without prior intent, the seers prescribe an expiation."
For one who kills intentionally, no atonement is found.
"Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; in the case of actually striking, the *atikṛcchra*;
and upon the flow of blood, both the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
Therefore, one should never threaten, nor should one cause blood to flow. (BDhS 2.1.1.7)
For a Kṣatriya, it is nine years.
A Vaiśya has three wives.
For a Śūdra, [the period of impurity lasts] one year.
And [the same applies] to a woman.
The *ātreyī* is treated like a *brāhmaṇī*.
One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall lie upon a heated iron bed.
Or he should embrace a glowing iron image.

Alternatively, having cut off the male organ together with the testicles and placed it in his joined palms, he should walk toward the intermediate direction between the south and the west until he collapses.
A thief, having disheveled his hair and taken a club made of *saidhraka* wood, should go to the king on his shoulder, saying, "Kill me with this. With that [club], the king should strike him.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Taking a club upon his shoulder, a thief should go before the king, saying:
'O King, remembering the duty of a Kṣatriya, punish me with this!'"
"Whether he is punished or released, the thief is freed from his guilt;
but by failing to punish him, the king incurs the guilt of the thief. (BDhS 2.1.1.17–3)
Having drunk *surā*, one should burn the body with hot [liquor].
If one drinks [forbidden liquor] unintentionally, one should perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for a year and undergo a second initiation.
And there is no lapse of the rules regarding shaving and vows, because they have already been performed previously.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Having unintentionally drunk *vāruṇī* liquor, or having consumed urine or feces,
a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya deserves to undergo the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*)."
If one drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for keeping *surā*,
he should subsist for six days on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
If one should die while commissioned by his teacher, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
This same [penance applies] to one who has not been consecrated.
For a religious student (brahmacārin), the performance of funeral rites for anyone other than his mother, father, or teacher results in the suspension of his vow.
If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remains of his teacher's food for the sake of medicine.
One may treat with whatever [medicine] one desires.
When he should become ill, he should rise and worship the sun with this verse: "The swan dwelling in purity...
[BDhS 2.1.1.28]. Having discharged semen during the day, he should drink water that reaches his heart three times with the *retasyā* verses. [BDhS 2.1.1.29]
A student who approaches a woman is an *avakīrṇin*.
He should sacrifice a donkey as the animal victim.

The animal victim and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belong to Nirṛti; they have the Rakṣases as their deity, or Yama as their deity. It is known from tradition that the portion for the sacrificer (prāśitra) is taken from the penis, and that they proceed with the ritual using the portions (avadāna) in the water.

Alternatively, on the night of the new moon, having kindled the fire and performed the ritual services pertaining to the *dārvihoma*, he offers two oblations of clarified butter: "O Kāma, I am one who has spilled his seed; I am one who has spilled his seed. To Kāma, to desire, svāhā! O Kāma, I am one who has been deceived by desire; I am one who has been deceived by desire. To Kāma, to desire, svāhā! [K: dārvihomikīm]

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence and turned slightly away from the fire, he should address the fire [or stand before it]: "May the Maruts sprinkle me; may Indra, may Bṛhaspati, and may this Agni sprinkle me with long life and strength; make me possessed of long life."

BDhS 2.1.1.36: Then his relatives, in an assembly, should pour out a vessel of water, saying, "I, being such-and-such, [am released]. Having performed the penance, when he has begun by consuming water, milk, ghee, honey, and salt, the Brāhmaṇas should ask him, "Has it been performed by you? He replies, "Om. They should then perform for him the *savanīya* sacrifice which completes the penance. BDhS 2.1.1.37: If he should unintentionally approach a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), he should maintain her like a mother.

BDhS 2.1.1.38: If she has given birth, he shall perform a quarter of the Kṛcchra penance for one year and offer oblations with these two verses: "Whatever deficiency has occurred in my self," and "Agni has given back my sight. BDhS 2.1.1.39ab: The younger brother who marries before his elder, the elder brother who is so superseded, and the woman who marries him— BDhS 2.1.1.39cd: All of them go to hell, as do the giver of the girl and the officiating priest, making five.

"The one who has been superseded by a younger brother, the one who has superseded, the giver [of the girl], and also the officiating priest—these are purified by a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance; a woman is purified in three nights. Thus it is said.
Now, the acts causing loss of caste (patanīya).
2.1.2.2 Traveling by sea.
The misappropriation of a Brahmin’s property entrusted to one's care.
Falsehood regarding land.
Dealing in all kinds of merchandise.
Service to Śūdras.
Born from a Śūdra woman.
And [the same applies to] being the offspring of such a person.
Having performed any one of these, they should eat at the fourth mealtime with their food restricted; they should enter the water for bathing according to the ritual sequence of the *savanas*;
and by alternating between standing and sitting, they remove that evil within three years.
"The sin that a Brāhmaṇa incurs by associating with one of black complexion for a single night, he destroys by subsisting on water at every fourth mealtime for three years. Thus it is said.
Now, the minor offenses (upapātaka).

BDhS 2.1.2.13: Having approached a woman who should not be approached, the wife of a teacher, the female friend of a teacher, one who has lost her caste, or an outcast; practicing medicine, officiating at sacrifices for a village, subsisting by the stage, being a teacher of acting, tending cattle and buffaloes, and whatever else is of a similar nature, as well as defiling a maiden.
But their means of subsistence shall be the mode of life of an outcast for two years.
Now, the causes of impurity.

Gambling, performing malevolent magic, living by gleaning for one who has not maintained the sacred fires, the practice of begging for one who has returned home from his teacher’s house, his continued residence in the teacher’s house beyond four months, teaching him [the Vedas], and the pointing out of the lunar mansions.

The expiation for these, however, consists of twelve months, twelve half-months, twelve periods of twelve days, twelve periods of six days, twelve periods of three days, twelve days, six days, three days, one day and night, or one day, according to the repetition of the act.

Now, those who have fallen [from their caste], having gathered together, should practice the duties of those who sacrifice for one another, teach one another, and intermarry with one another. Having produced sons, they should say to them: "Depart from us; in this way you will attain the status of the Āryas."
Moreover, one does not fall [to a lower state] as long as one's sense organs remain intact.
This is to be understood by means of this: even one who is deficient in a limb may produce a son who possesses all limbs.
Hārīta says that this is false.
Women have the same status as a curd-pot. For when one churns impure milk that has been poured into a curd-pot, the learned do not employ that [curd] for religious rites.
In this way, there is no contact with that impure semen which is emitted.
For those born from impure semen who desire it, there is an expiation.
A third part of the [penance] for those who have committed mortal sins (patanīya) is the share for women.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than eating, anointing, or giving as a gift, he becomes a worm in a dog's excrement and sinks there together with his ancestors. Thus it is said.
He who sells sesame seeds sells his ancestors; he who sells rice grains sells his vital breaths; and he who, for the sake of profit, gives away his daughter in marriage sells his shares of merit.

BDhS 2.1.2.28: Grass and wood that have not been processed may be sold. [K: grass and wood] BDhS 2.1.2.29–1: Moreover, they also cite this: BDhS 2.1.2.29–2ab: Single-hoofed animals, and stone extracted from salt mines.
"O Brāhmaṇa, this is your merchandise: a thread dyed with safflower. Thus [it is said].

Or, excluding the most heinous sins (pātaka), one should pour clarified butter over a tawny, reddish-brown cow with thick hair, scatter black sesame seeds upon it, and give her to a learned Brahmin (anūcāna).
Or, one may perform the *kūśmāṇḍa* rites for twelve days.
"By this, one is released from whatever sin has been committed prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā)."
In the case of falsely accusing another of a mortal sin (pātaka), one must perform a Kṛcchra penance.
BDhS 2.1.2.34: That curse falls upon the one who utters it.
BDhS 2.1.2.35: One becomes an outcast by associating with an outcast for a year through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or sexual intercourse, but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food.
The penance for consuming impure substances is the *naiṣpurīṣya* rite; that is accomplished within seven nights.
Water, milk, clarified butter, and air—each for three days respectively; this is the *satapta-kṛcchra* when performed with these substances while they are hot.

BDhS 2.1.2.38: Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, eating only what is unasked for three days, and fasting for the final three days—this is the *kṛcchra* penance. [K: Eating in the evening for three days, eating what is unasked for another three days, and not eating at all for the final three days is the *parāka*. BDhS 2.1.2.39: The three four-night periods consisting of morning meals, evening meals, unasked food, and fasting constitute this *kṛcchra* penance for women, children, and the elderly.
He should eat as much as he might take up once; as before, that is the *atikṛcchra*.
Subsisting on water is the third; that is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance.
In the Kṛcchra penance, there is bathing in water at the three sessions of the day.
Sleeping on the ground.
Wearing a single garment, and the shaving of the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails.
This same [rite] applies to a woman as well, with the exception of shaving the hair; with the exception of shaving the hair.

One who constantly uses water for purification, constantly wears the sacred thread, constantly engages in Vedic study, avoids the food of a *vṛṣala*, approaches his wife only during her season, and offers oblations according to the rules— such a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"The Vedic revelation states: 'Manu divided his inheritance among his sons.'"
[The inheritance] shall be divided equally among all, because there is no distinction [between them].
Or the eldest may extract the best portion or the most excellent form.
"Therefore, they exclude the eldest son from his share of the wealth," so says the Śruti.
Or the eldest may set aside one share from ten.
The others shall divide [the estate] equally.
The division of the inheritance takes place with the father's consent while the father is still living.
Among the four castes, cows, horses, goats, and sheep constitute the senior share.
In the case of a son born of wives of different castes, one should divide the inheritance into ten parts and distribute them respectively as four, three, two, and one.
But when a legitimate son of the body (aurasa) has been born, those of the same caste (savarṇa) shall receive a third share.
Between the son of a wife of the same caste and the son of a wife of the next lower caste, if the son of the next lower caste is virtuous, he shall take the share of the eldest.
For one who possesses good qualities becomes the supporter of the others.
One should know that the son begotten by oneself upon a wife of equal caste who has been consecrated is the *aurasa* (legitimate) son.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"From limb by limb you are produced; from the heart you are born."
"Thou art indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! [K omits].
Regarding the daughter born after a formal agreement, there is the son of the appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), distinct from the other types of sons' sons (*dauhitra*).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā) should designate his mother in the first rice-ball offering, his father in the second, and his paternal grandfather in the third. Thus it is said.

He who is begotten on a widow, or on a man who is impotent or diseased, by another with her consent upon his own wife, is a *kṣetraja* son. He has two fathers and belongs to two gotras; he partakes of the funeral offerings (*svadhā*) and the inheritance of both.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"For one who has two fathers, there should be the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas) for both; and with each individual rice-ball, the names of both should be mentioned.
There should thus be three rice-balls for six ancestors; by acting in this way, one does not go astray."
One who is given by both parents or by either one, and is taken up for the sake of offspring, is a *datta* (given) son.
One whom she herself makes her own, being of similar status and with mutual desire, is the *kṛtrima* (adopted son).
22. One born secretly in the house and recognized at the end is a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born). 23.
One who is abandoned by both parents or by either one, and is then taken up for the sake of offspring, is an *apaviddha* (cast-off).
If one should approach a woman who has not been consecrated by marriage and has not been given away in marriage, the son born of her is a *kānīna*.
If a woman who is already pregnant is married—whether that pregnancy was known or unknown—the son born of her is a *sahoḍha*.
One who is purchased from the hands of his mother and father, or from either one of them, and is taken for the sake of offspring, is a "purchased" (krīta) son.
If a woman, having abandoned a eunuch or an outcast husband, takes another husband, the son born of her as a remarried woman (paunarbhavī) is called a paunarbhava.
One who, being deprived of both mother and father, gives himself away is a self-given son (svayaṃdatta).
One born from a Śūdra woman by a man of the foremost of the twice-born castes is a Niṣāda.
From lust, the Pāraśava is born; these are the sons.
Moreover, they also cite this: "The son of the body,
the son of an appointed daughter, the son begotten on the wife, the son given, the son made, the son born in secret, and the son cast off— these are declared to be the sharers of the inheritance."

The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a pregnant bride, the bought son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Niṣāda son— these they declare to be sharers of the family name.
"Of these, the first alone [is the most important]," says Aupajaṅghani.
"O progenitor of women, I am envious of you now, but not formerly,
because they declared in the abode of Yama that one should address the son as belonging to the progenitor."
"The progenitor of the seed leads the son away after death to the abode of Yama;
therefore, let men guard their own wives, fearing the seed of others. "Guard this lineage with vigilance; let not the seeds of others be sown in your field."
"In the life hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; he who knows this in vain weaves this thread.

[BDhS 2.2.3.36] For those [sons] who have not yet attained legal capacity, they shall deposit their shares along with the increments [of interest], well-guarded, until they reach the age of legal capacity.
They shall support those whose legal capacity has expired with food and clothing.
And those who are blind, mentally dull, eunuchs, addicted to vices, diseased, and so forth.
Those who do not perform their duties.
Except for those born of outcasts.
There is no social interaction with those who have fallen [from their caste].
But even if his mother has fallen [from her caste], he should support her without speaking to her.
The daughters shall inherit their mother’s personal ornaments, as well as her traditional inheritance, or other property.
A woman possesses no independence.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood; the husband protects her in youth."
"But in old age, a son shall not allow a woman independence.
Thus [it is said]. For the Śruti declares: "Women are considered to be without sensory power and without inheritance."
Striving for the welfare of their husband, they shall conquer the heavenly world.
In the event of a transgression, the Kṛcchra penance is required.
In the case of a Śūdra, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
In the case of those born in the inverse order from Vaiśyas and others, one should perform the Kṛcchra, Atikṛcchra, and other such penances.
For men of the Brahmin and other castes, the period of studentship lasts for one year.
One should burn a Śūdra with a fire of straw mats.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
For a non-Brāhmaṇa, corporal punishment shall be the penalty in the case of adultery.
For all social classes alike, a wife is more worthy of protection than wealth.
But there is no execution for those who are performers' wives, nor for those on the stage;
for they cause these men to mingle and even lead them astray when they are well-guarded.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their sins.
Soma gave them purity; Gandharva, eloquent speech;
and Agni, the capacity to consume all things; therefore, women are free from blemish.
One should abandon a woman who bears no offspring by the tenth year, and one who bears only daughters by the twelfth.
One whose children have died [should wait] for fifteen years, but one who speaks unpleasantly [may be superseded] immediately.
For one year, the widow of the deceased shall avoid honey, meat, liquor, and salt; she shall sleep on the ground.
"For six months," says Maudgalya.
From this point forward, a woman without a son may, with the permission of her elders, procreate a son through her husband's brother.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"A barren cow, one that has already borne a son, one that is without menses, and one whose offspring has passed away—such a cow should not be employed against her will, for no fruit is found in her. Thus it is said.
A maternal uncle’s sister, a father’s sister, a sister, a sister’s daughter, a daughter-in-law, a maternal aunt, and a friend’s wife—these are women who must not be approached for sexual intercourse.
For approaching women who should not be approached, the penance is the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa.
By this, sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Moreover, they cite this:

"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached a Caṇḍālī woman, or having eaten [with her], or having accepted a gift [from her]—if he does so unknowingly, the learned Brāhmaṇa falls from his status; but if he does so knowingly, he becomes equal [to her]."

"Having unintentionally approached the wife of a father, a teacher, or a king, one becomes a violator of the Guru’s bed; for that, the atonement previously mentioned applies. (BDhS 2.2.4.15) "If he is unable to subsist by teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or receiving gifts, he may live according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, because it is the next in order. (BDhS 2.2.4.16)
"Not so," says Gautama; "for the duty of the Kṣatriya is exceedingly fierce for a Brāhmaṇa."
Moreover, they also cite this:
"For the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, or even in the case of a confusion of castes,
a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms out of regard for dharma."
The mode of life of a Vaiśya should be adopted [by a Kṣatriya] because it is the one immediately following his own.
Before the morning meal, he should be a laborer.
[He should perform the rite] with two goats whose nostrils are unperforated and which have their testicles intact, without striking them with a goad, repeatedly encouraging them by shouting aloud.
The fire begins with the wife; in that fire, the performance of rites takes place prior to the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya).

BDhS 2.2.4.23: From the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya) onwards, these [rites] become perpetual: namely, the establishment of the fires, the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa, the animal sacrifice at the solstices (both the northern and southern courses), the Cāturmāsya sacrifices at the beginning of each season, the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ offering, and the Jyotiṣṭoma in spring; thus [is] the attainment of security.
Moreover, they cite this example:
"Neither by one habituated to sleeping during the day, nor by one who eats all kinds of food,
can it be possible to go to heaven— unless perhaps by one who has fallen after having ascended."
One should avoid wretchedness, deceit, and crookedness.
Furthermore, in this regard, they cite a verse from the dialogue between Uśanas and Vṛṣaparvan’s two daughters:
“You are indeed the daughter of one who praises, begs, and accepts; But I am the son of one who is praised, gives, and does not accept.”
"For one who gives and for one who does not accept," so it is said.
2.3.5.1 Ascetic practice consists of immersion in water.
2.3.5.2 Having gratified the deities, one should perform the libation for the ancestors.
He pours out water at the bathing-place with the verse, "Carrying strength...
(BDhS 2.3.5.3). Furthermore, they also cite this:
(BDhS 2.3.5.4-2ab) "In flowing waters that are not obstructed, the three twice-born castes [may perform their rites]."
Having risen in the morning, they should perform the libations for the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
They should not perform them when the waters are obstructed; in that case, the builder of the embankment shall share in the merit.
Therefore, one should avoid embankments and wells made by others.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"Or, having drawn out three lumps of earth, one should perform [the rite] in times of distress, but not always;
however, when [water sources] are blocked, one should likewise take three lumps of earth from a well and three jars of water."

BDhS 2.3.5.8: Having accepted what is forbidden to be accepted, or having failed to officiate at a sacrifice for one for whom it is forbidden to officiate, or having eaten the food of one whose food is forbidden to be eaten, one should recite the *taratsamandīya* hymn.
BDhS 2.3.5.9–1: Furthermore, they also cite this:
BDhS 2.3.5.9–2ab: Those who cause confusion among their teachers, and those who cause confusion among their pupils;
"Those whose food is mixed with mantras enter into long-lasting darkness. Thus [it is said].
Now follow the observances of a Snātaka.

In the evening and in the morning, having offered the Vaiśvadeva oblation with whatever food is fit for consumption, he should honor Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have arrived as guests according to his ability.
If he is unable [to give] to many, he should give to one who possesses good qualities.
Or he may be one who has arrived first.
If a Śūdra has arrived, he should employ him in labor.
Or one should give the first portion to a learned scholar of the Vedas.

A distribution of food is ordained for those who are permanent dependents, provided it does not interfere with the needs of others. However, one must never eat without having first given them something.
Moreover, in this regard, they cite two verses from the *Anngīta*:
"He who, out of delusion, eats well-prepared food without first offering it to the ancestors, the gods, his servants, guests, and his circle of friends—him I devour; for I am his death."
Having offered the *agnihotra* oblation and performed the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, he who— having honored his guests and his dependents,
being contented, pure, and full of faith— eats what remains of my food, for him it becomes nectar (*amṛta*), and he, in turn, nourishes me.

BDhS 2.3.5.19: A distribution of wealth according to one's ability should be made to those who are not merely nominal Brahmins but are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them—specifically when they are seeking the teacher’s fee, when they are settling in a new home, when they are destitute for the sake of medicine or livelihood, when they are about to perform a sacrifice, when they are engaged in Vedic study, when they are traveling on a journey, or when they are competing in a universal contest (vaiśvajita)—provided they are begging outside the sacrificial altar.
In the case of the other [guests], cooked food [is offered].

Having thoroughly washed his hands and feet and sipped water for purification, he should take the food brought to him in a clean, enclosed place; having cast away desire, anger, malice, greed, and delusion, he should eat with all his fingers, making no sound.
One should not throw the remainder of the rice-balls into the vessel.
If one consumes food mixed with meat, fish, or sesame seeds, one should touch water and then touch fire.
And one should bathe after the sun has set.
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*.
One should not eat food held in the lap.
One should not eat while seated on a chair.
He should carry a bamboo staff and two golden earrings.
One should avoid washing one foot with the other and stepping upon it.
One should not wear a garland outside [the body].
One should not look at the sun at either sunrise or sunset.
One should not point out a rainbow to another, saying, "It is Indra’s bow."
If he should say "maṇidhanus," one should simply say "maṇidhanus."
One should not pass between the gate-tower and the bolt-bar of a city gate.
One should not pass between the two swing-boards.
And one should not walk over a rope tied to a calf's neck.
One should not step upon ashes, bones, hair, chaff, potsherds, or bath-water.
One should not point out to another a cow that is suckling.
One should not say of a non-cow, "She is a cow."
If he should say, "A cow that will become [a milch-cow]," one should simply say, "A cow that will become."
One should not utter words that are sour, harsh, or rough.
One should not travel alone on a road.
Not with outcasts, nor with a woman, nor with a Śūdra.
One should not go out at evening.
One should not bathe naked.
One should not bathe at night.
One should not cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One should not look into a well.
One should not look into a pit.
One should not sit down in such a place where another might make one rise up.
The way must be yielded to a Brāhmaṇa, to a cow, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elderly person, to one afflicted by disease, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.

A righteous person should strive to dwell in a village that has abundant firewood, water, fodder, fuel, *kuśa* grass, and garlands; one from which people can easily exit, which is crowded with wealthy folk, prosperous with industrious people, abounding in noble persons, and inaccessible to barbarians.
If a Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a Śūdra woman dwells for twelve years in a village where water is available only from a well, he incurs the same status as a Śūdra.

With his body covered by the dust of the city, and his eyes and face filled with that same dust, even one who dwells in the city with a well-restrained self will not attain perfection; such a thing is impossible.
The dust raised by chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious;
however, the dust of a broom, dogs, goats, sheep, donkeys, and clothing is not recommended.
One should honor those worthy of honor.
The seers, the learned, the king, the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, and the officiating priest—
these are declared by the scriptures to be worthy of the *arghya* offering according to the division of time.
Sages, learned men, and kings who have arrived at the commencement of a rite are to be honored as the bridegroom and the officiating priest;
likewise, one’s maternal uncle and father-in-law are to be honored whenever they arrive within the course of a year. Thus it is said.
In the fire-sanctuary, in the midst of cows, in the presence of Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should expose the right arm.
In these five activities, an upper garment must be worn:
during Vedic study, the voiding of excrement, giving gifts, eating, and sipping water for purification.

Offering oblations, eating, giving, presenting offerings, and receiving gifts—these, as well as the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), should not be performed with the knees outside [the hands]; so it is recorded in the tradition.
"Beings are supported by food; 'food is life,' so says the Śruti.
Therefore, food must be given, for food is the supreme oblation."
"Sin is pacified by the oblation; the oblation is pacified by food;
food attains peace through the sacrificial fee—such is the Vedic revelation (śruti). "It attains peace—such is our revelation. [K omits]
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the performance of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), whether he is impure and has bathed, or pure and has not bathed, he should wash his feet and hands, sip water (ācamana), and sprinkle himself with water using mantras containing the word "surabhi," the *abliṅga* verses, the *vāruṇī* verses, the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *vyāhṛtis*, and other purificatory texts; thus he becomes pure.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Immersion in water is prescribed as bathing for all social classes;
however, sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras is specifically distinguished for the twice-born. Thus it is said.
And at the commencement of all ritual acts, before the time for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), one becomes pure by sprinkling oneself with this very collection of purifiers.
Moreover, they also cite this: Sitting on *darbha* grass, holding *darbha* blades, with hands wet with water and facing westward, one should repeat the *Sāvitrī* mantra a thousand times.
Or alternatively, one may perform it a hundred times with each breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Or, mentally, ten times, with the seven vyāhṛtis and the praṇava at both ends.
And when exhausted by three breath-restraints, one should [recite] the Brahmahṛdaya.
With two verses addressed to Varuṇa—namely, "This [oblation] to me, O Varuṇa" and "That I implore of thee"—he worships the night.
In this very same manner, in the morning, he stands facing the east.
With two verses addressed to Mitra—one beginning "Of Mitra, the supporter of the people," and the other "Mitra impels the people"—he worships the day.
One may begin even the preceding day if it is well-prepared, and complete it after the sun has risen.
Having begun before sunset, one may even perform the western [oblation] well after [sunset].
And at the two twilights, through their conjunction, there is the continuity of day and night.
Moreover, there are two verses sung by Prajāpati on this subject:
"Those Brahmins who do not perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā) before the morning has come, nor after the evening has passed— how can they be considered true Brahmins?"

"Those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the evening and the morning—let the righteous king, at his discretion, employ them in the labor of Śūdras. Thus [it is said].
In that regard, if the evening [meal] is omitted, there is fasting for the night; if the morning [meal] is omitted, there is fasting for the day.
One obtains the fruit of standing and sitting.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Whatever sin has been committed with the organ of generation, or whatever has been done with the feet,
or whatever has been done with the arms, with the mind, or even with speech."
Having performed the evening twilight worship, one is thereby liberated from that [debt].
And he is joined with the night as well, and Varuṇa does not seize him.
In this very same way, having performed the morning worship, one is liberated from the evil committed during the night.
By day he is united with Mitra; Mitra protects him, and Āditya leads him up to the heavenly world.

In this very manner, worshipping day after day at the junctions of day and night, purified by the Veda, become one with the Veda, and following the sacred scriptures, the Brahmin conquers the world of Brahman; so it is known. He conquers the world of Brahman; so it is known.
Then, having washed his hands and taken hold of his water-pot and a lump of earth, he goes to a bathing place and washes his feet three times and himself three times.
Now, some indeed say: "A cemetery, water, a temple, a cow-pen, and wherever there are Brahmins—one must not enter these places without having washed one's feet."
Then he approaches the water, reciting:
"I take refuge in Varuṇa, whose horns are of gold;
grant me a ford when I entreat you, [for] that which has been eaten by me from the unrighteous and the acceptance of gifts from the wicked."

"Whatever evil has been committed by me through thought, speech, or action—may Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, and Savitṛ purify that again and again. Then, with joined palms, he takes water, saying: "May the waters and the plants be friendly to us."
He sprinkles that water toward the direction in which he has an enemy, saying: "May ill-fated enemies befall him who hates us and whom we hate."
Then, having touched water, he turns the water three times clockwise, saying: "Whatever in the waters is cruel, whatever is impure, whatever is unpeaceful—let that depart.
Having submerged himself in the water and emerged, [he performs this].
For one who is in water, no purification is prescribed, nor the washing of clothes, nor the ritual touching of water.
If they should be besieged, he worships with this: "Homage to Agni accompanied by the waters; homage to Indra; homage to Varuṇa; homage to Vāruṇī; homage to the waters."
Having emerged from the water and sipped water, one who has already sipped should sip again, reciting:
"May the waters purify the earth; may the purified earth purify me. May Brahmaṇaspati purify; may the purified Veda purify me.

Whatever is impure from remnants, whatever is unfit to be eaten, or whatever evil deed I have committed—may the waters purify all that in me, and [purify] the acceptance of gifts from the wicked, svāhā!"

Having prepared two strainers (*pavitre*), he purifies himself with water using the three verses beginning with "O Waters, you are indeed the source of bliss" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*), the four verses beginning with "Golden-colored, pure, and purifying" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), and the verse beginning with "The self-purifying one, born of light" (*pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*). Having purified himself with this section (*anuvāka*), having gone into the water, he should hold his breath three times while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Then, having emerged, wrung out his garment, and put on unwashed clothes that have been washed and aired, he should sip water (*ācamana*), sit upon *darbha* grass holding *darbha* blades, and facing eastward, repeat the *Sāvitrī* mantra a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times, at least ten times.
Then he worships the sun with the verses: "Up from the darkness," "Up that one," "The bright," "That eye established by the gods," and "He who has risen."
Moreover, they also cite this: "The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*—these five constitute the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), which purify a Brāhmaṇa from sin day after day."
Purified by these five Brahmayajñas, he thereafter satiates the deities.

Om! Agni, Prajāpati, Soma, Rudra, Aditi, Bṛhaspati, and the Sarpas—these deities of the eastern doors, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas, I satiate. Om! And I satiate the Vasus.

*Oṃ,* I satiate the deities of the southern gate—Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga, Savitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, and Agni—together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. *Oṃ,* I satiate the Rudras.

*Oṃ,* I satiate the deities of the western gate—Mitra, Indra, the Great Pitṛs, the Waters, the Viśvedevas, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu—together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. *Oṃ,* I satiate the Ādityas.

Oṃ, I satiate the Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pūṣan, the two Aśvins, and Yama—these deities who have their gates facing north, together with the constellations, the planets, the days and nights, and the muhūrtas. Oṃ, I satiate the Viśvedevas. Oṃ, and I satiate the Sādhyas.

Now, [the rule for] the *nivīta* [mode of wearing the sacred thread].

Om, I satiate all the classes of divine beings. Om, I satiate all living beings. Thus [he says]. [K: ... I satiate the Atharvāṅgirasa...]

BDhS 2.5.10.1 Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī): "Oṃ, I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the great-grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers' fathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers' grandfathers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Oṃ, I satiate the maternal grandfathers' grandmothers with *svadhā* and obeisance."

Om, I satiate the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of the teachers with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the gurus with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of the gurus with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the friends with *svadhā* and obeisance. Om, I satiate the wives of the friends with *svadhā* and obeisance. He pours out water at every sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
"Carrying strength, nectar, clarified butter, milk, sweet drink, and flowing liquor—you are the *svadhā* offerings; satisfy my ancestors! Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! Thus [he says].
One should not perform rites dedicated to the gods while wearing only a single garment or while one's clothing is wet.
"And those connected with the ancestors," so say some; "and those connected with the ancestors," so say some.

Now, these are the five great sacrifices (mahāyajñas); they are indeed the great sacrificial sessions (mahāsattras): the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, the sacrifice to men, and the sacrifice to Brahman.
Day after day, he should offer oblations with the word "svāhā" until at least a piece of wood is used; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to the gods.
Day by day, he should offer the *svadhā* oblation, at least as much as a vessel of water; in this way, he completes the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*).
Day after day he should pay homage [to the elements] up to the flowers; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña).
Day by day he should give food to Brāhmaṇas, even down to roots, fruits, and vegetables; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña).
Day by day he should perform the private recitation of the Veda up to the syllable *oṃ*; in this way, he completes this sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*).

The private recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, speech is the *juhū* ladle, the mind is the *upabhṛt*, the eye is the *dhruvā*, intelligence is the *sruva* spoon, truth is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world is the conclusion. Indeed, as much of the heavenly world as one wins by giving away this earth filled with wealth, so much of a world does he win—and even more, an inexhaustible one—who, knowing this, studies his private recitation; he conquers repeated death. Therefore, the private recitation must be studied; for thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Moreover, they also cite this: "Anointed with oil, well-fed, and lying on a comfortable bed, whatever sacrifice he studies, by that very sacrifice it is as if he has performed the offering."
Regarding this very dharma, some say that it has a fourfold division because it is not directly perceived; those who speak of "the four" are proponents of ritual action (*karmavāda*).

[This applies] to the sacrifices involving oblations (iṣṭi), animal sacrifices (pāśuka), Soma sacrifices (saumika), and wood-offerings (dārvihoma). Regarding this, the following verse declares: "The four paths leading to the gods, which extend between heaven and earth—"
"O all you gods, grant him here among us who shall bring about for them freedom from decay and freedom from defeat. Thus [it is said].
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
A student of sacred knowledge shall serve his teacher until death.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) follows the conduct prescribed by the Vaikhānasa scriptures.

The Vaikhānasa, dwelling in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity, touching water at the three libations, having established the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, eating no village food, and worshipping the gods, ancestors, spirits, humans, and ṛṣis, shall entertain all guests; he may even consume honey, provided it is not from a prohibited source. He must not stand upon land tilled by the plough, nor enter a village. Wearing matted hair and clothed in bark or skins, he shall not eat more than once a year.
A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), having abandoned his kinsmen and remaining without possessions, should go forth according to the prescribed rule;
having gone to the forest.
He should have his hair shorn except for a tuft.
He should possess only a loincloth for clothing. During the rainy season, he should remain in one place.
Wearing saffron-colored garments.
He should beg for alms when the pestle has been laid aside, when the embers have been extinguished, and when the activity of the cooking ladles has ceased.
One who does not bear malice toward living beings through the restraints of speech, mind, and action.
One should carry a purifier for the sake of purification.
When performing water-related rites, one should do so with water that has been drawn up and strained.
Having cast aside Vedic rites, saying, "We shall cling to the middle state, being cut off from both sides," they [live].
But the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life (āśrama), because the others do not lead to procreation.
Regarding this, they cite an example: "There was indeed an Asura named Kapila, the son of Prahlāda. Competing with the gods, he created these divisions. A wise man should not respect them."
"Because they are not seen. Regarding the phrase "those four," this is a statement concerning ritual action (*karmavāda*), referring to the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, *saumika*, and *dārvīhoma* sacrifices.
Regarding this, the following verse is recited:

"This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa: he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. His very self is the knower of the path; having known that, he is not tainted by evil action. (BDhS 2.10.17.7)
He should say:
"By that splendor kindled by which the sun shines, the father becomes possessed of his son, from womb to womb.
One who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One, the Self who experiences all, in the hereafter. Thus.

"Those who move neither hither nor thither, who are not true Brāhmaṇas, nor performers of the Soma-pressing; having resorted to evil speech, they weave a web like that of a spider for the sake of non-procreation. Thus it is said.

"O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality. For a Brāhmaṇa, being born, is indeed born with three debts: through studentship to the sages, through sacrifice to the gods, and through offspring to the ancestors. Thus, there are innumerable statements concerning the connection with these debts. The triple Veda, studentship, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—these are the seven sacrificial fires. Those who perform these sacrifices are not overcome by death. One should offer these seven sacrifices throughout one's life. By performing them according to one's ability, one attains immortality; for it is said that immortality is attained through progeny. Therefore, one should diligently strive for offspring. One should never say, "I have no son. For it is said: "He who says, 'I have no son,' slays his ancestors. Therefore, one should always desire offspring. It is further stated: "Through offspring, O Agni, may I attain immortality. "Those who perform these acts—by being with them, one becomes dust and is destroyed while praising something else.
Thus [it is said]. "He is destroyed while praising something else.
Now, we shall explain the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*) of the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* types of self-sacrificers.

At the conclusion of all necessary duties, having sat down facing the east in a place that has been swept and smeared with cow-dung, and having offered reverence to the elements being brought forth with the words "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ," he should restrain his speech.

Having sprinkled water clockwise around the placed food with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, and not releasing it with his left hand, he first drinks water with the mantra, "Thou art the underlayer of immortality. Then, with the food, he offers the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*): "Seated in the *prāṇa*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me auspiciously, for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the *prāṇa*! "Seated in the *apāna*, I offer immortality; may thou enter me auspiciously, for the sake of non-burning. *Svāhā* to the *apāna*! "Seated in the *vyāna*, I offer immortality..."

"May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the vyāna! Seated in the udāna, I offer the oblation of immortality. May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the udāna! Seated in the samāna, I offer the oblation of immortality. May Śiva enter me for the sake of non-burning! Svāhā to the samāna! Having offered these five oblations of food to the vital breaths (prāṇa), he should thereafter consume his meal in silence while meditating on Prajāpati with his mind; he must not utter speech in the interval.
BDhS 2.7.12.5: If he should release speech in the interval, he should mutter "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar oṃ" and then eat again. BDhS 2.7.12.6:

Upon seeing skin, hair, nails, insects, or mouse-droppings, he should remove that portion of the food, sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, sprinkle it again with water, and then consume what remains, provided it has been commended by word.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"Seated, facing the east, with speech controlled, one should eat food without disparaging it; without letting any [food] fall, and being focused on that, having eaten, one should touch fire. Thus [it is said].
One should not bite with the teeth any food, cakes, bulbs, roots, fruits, or meat. One should not eat until completely satiated.

"Thou art the covering of immortality," [he says]. Having drunk water from above and sipped [water] for purification, he touches the region of his heart, saying: "Thou art the knot of the vital breaths; may Rudra, the destroyer, enter me; through this food, cause me to swell."
Having sipped water again, he pours the remaining water over his right big toe [with the mantra]:
"The Person the size of a thumb resides within the thumb;
the Lord of the entire world, the Master, the consumer of all, is pleased. (BDhS 2.7.12.11-2ab, 3cd)

With his hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*) with these five verses: "Entering into faith (*śraddhā*), may the immortal oblation enter into the out-breath (*prāṇa*); nourish the out-breath with food. Entering into faith, may the immortal oblation enter into the in-breath (*apāna*); nourish the out-breath with food. Entering into faith, may the immortal oblation enter into the diffused breath (*vyāna*); nourish the out-breath with food. Entering into faith, may the immortal oblation enter into the up-breath (*udāna*); nourish the out-breath with food. Entering into faith, may the immortal oblation enter into the equalizing breath (*samāna*); nourish the out-breath with food. [The K version omits: "Entering into faith... in the in-breath... in the equalizing breath... nourish with food."]
"May my self be in Brahman for the sake of immortality," [thus he addresses himself].
And one should unite the self with the syllable.
Among those who perform all types of sacrifices, the one who sacrifices to the Self is distinguished as superior.
Moreover, they also cite this:
For just as cotton from the *iṣīkā* reed, when cast into a fire, is consumed by flame,
even so all the sins of one who sacrifices to the Self are burnt away.
"He who eats alone becomes the sole possessor of sin; the thoughtless man obtains food in vain. (BDhS 2.7.13.2)
In this very manner, he should offer oblations every day, both evening and morning.
Or, in the evening, with water.
Moreover, they also cite this:
First, one should feed the guests; immediately thereafter, those who are pregnant;
likewise, children, the elderly, the destitute, and especially the sick.
But he who eats before giving to these [deities] according to the rule, while eating he does not realize it; he does not eat, rather he is eaten.

"Restraining his speech, he should eat the remains (vighasa) after [satisfying] the ancestors, the deities, his dependents, as well as his mother, father, and teacher; thus is dharma ordained. |||
