Moreover, they also cite this:
"An ascetic (*muni*) should eat eight morsels; one dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyavāsin*), sixteen;
a householder (*gṛhastha*), thirty-two; and for a student (*brahmacārin*), there is no limit."
"The one who has maintained the sacred fires, the ox, and the student—these three succeed only while eating;
there is no success for them while fasting. Thus it is said.
Whether he be a householder or a student, if one practices austerity while fasting,
he becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has violated his vow) through the neglect of the *prāṇāgnihotra*.
Except in the case of expiation; for expiation, that same rule applies.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who never eats anything between his morning meal and likewise his evening meal, is always one who observes a fast."
"One should mutter the mantras of the Prāṇāgnihotra when food is withheld;
just as one mutters the mantras of the Tretāgnihotra when sacrificial materials are unavailable. Thus it is said.
Acting in this manner, one is fit for becoming Brahman; "one is fit for becoming Brahman. The ancestral rite (pitrya) bestows long life, leads to heaven, brings fame, and provides nourishment.

One who knows the *trimadhu*, one who knows the *triṇāciketa*, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who knows the *śīrṣaka*, one who knows the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, and a *snātaka*—these are the purifiers of the company (*paṅktipāvanas*).
In his absence, one who knows the secret [teachings].
"The Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants—this is the greatness of the Śrāddha. Therefore, one who knows this should feed even a sapinda relative."

One should cause him to hear, slowly and with focused intent, the *sāmans* that destroy demons, the *yajus* formulas containing the word *svadhā*, the honey-verses (*madhvṛc*), and the purificatory texts (*pavitra*).

On the previous day, or indeed at dawn on that very day, he should invite an odd number—at least three—of those who possess good conduct, are learned in the Vedas, are pure, and are well-versed in the mantras, provided they are not related to him by birth, lineage, or Vedic school; having invited them, he seats them facing either east or north upon seats prepared with Darbha grass.

Then, having caused them to receive water mixed with sesame seeds and having adorned them with perfumes and garlands, he says, "I shall perform the fire-oblation. Being permitted, he kindles the fire, strews grass around it, performs the *agnimukha* rite, and offers three oblations of food alone, saying: "To Soma, who is drunk by the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the ancestors, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! "To Agni Kavyavāhana, the maker of good offerings, *svadhā*! Adoration! *Svāhā*! [K: having performed [the oblations] of clarified butter alone].
Having sprinkled the food with the remainder of that [ghee], he should offer these same three oblations of the food [or: three oblations].
He should give a morsel to the birds.
"For it is known from sacred tradition that the ancestors move about in the likeness of birds."
Then he touches the other [parts] with his hand together with the thumb.

"O you who are equal to the earth, Agni is your witness; the *ṛc*s are your greatness for the non-neglect of what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman. I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among the ancestors there in yonder world. [K: equal to the earth for him]

"Vāyu is the listener for you who are equal to the intermediate space; the Yajus-formulas are your greatness for the non-neglect of what has been given. The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid. I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among my grandfathers in that world yonder."

"May the Sun be the witness of that which is equal to heaven; may the *sāmans* be the illuminators of those [offerings]; for the non-neglect of what has been given, the earth is your vessel and the sky is your lid. I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the learned Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish among my great-grandfathers in yonder world, in that world. Now, indeed, it is said: "BDhS 2.8.15.1" [The text continues: "Then, indeed, it comes to pass..."
One should sprinkle that food with the remnants from the offering into the fire;
for that which is given without the thumb does not indeed gratify the ancestors.
When food is offered to the ancestors, released from both hands,
the evil-minded Asuras wait in the interval;
the Yātudhānas and Piśācas plunder that sacrificial offering.
For by the gift of sesame seeds, those who are without heirs [attain heaven], and likewise the Asuras in the realm of Krodhavaśa.
Whatever recitations, burnt offerings, or acceptances of gifts one performs while wearing saffron robes—

that oblation, whether among the offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*), does not reach the deities. And whatever is given without the thumb, or whatever is accepted [in that manner], [is likewise ineffective].
"And he who sips water while standing does not prosper by that act. Thus it is said.
In all cases, water is to be offered at the beginning and at the end.
From the *jaya* oblation onwards, it is to be performed according to the prescribed rule.
The remainder has been explained in the section on the Aṣṭakā oblation.
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each of the two; even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large company.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it.
"His ancestors are in front, his grandfathers on the left, and his great-grandfathers on the right; behind them are those who seek the rice-balls. Thus it is said.
The instruction for one desiring offspring.
"The designation is based on the cause of procreation," so said the two Aśvins.
Endowed with long life and austerity, devoted to the private study of the Vedas and sacrifice, he should,
with his senses subdued, diligently procreate offspring within his own respective caste (or lineage).
From birth, a Brāhmaṇa incurs three debts;
by discharging them, he becomes self-possessed and liberated from doubt regarding dharma.
Having honored the sages through the private recitation of the Vedas, Indra with Soma,
and his ancestors with offspring, he becomes free from debt and rejoices in heaven.
"Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality;
and then, through a great-grandson, one ascends to the very heavens. Thus it is said.

And it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts—to the sages by means of the life of studentship (brahmacarya), to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of progeny. Thus the Veda demonstrates this connection with debts.
By procreating a virtuous son, one delivers oneself.
A man who obtains a virtuous son delivers seven descendants, seven ancestors, and six others, himself being the seventh, from sin and fear.
Therefore, having produced a lineage of offspring, one obtains the fruit.
Therefore, one should strive to produce offspring.
By means of the application of medicinal herbs and mantras.
The instruction regarding that [subject] is taught by means of a similarity in verbal expression.
"Because it bears fruit for all social classes. Regarding "because it bears fruit":
[Deutero-Baudhāyana] BDhS 2.10.17.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
According to some, he goes forth as a wandering mendicant while remaining a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) for that very reason.
Now, [the following applies] to those of the Śālīna and Yāyāvara classes who are childless.
Or, being incapacitated, he may establish his subjects in their own duties.
After seventy years, they prescribe renunciation.
Or for a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) at the cessation of ritual duties.

"This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa: he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. His very self is the knower of the path; having known it, he is not tainted by evil action. (BDhS 2.10.17.7) [cf.
BDhS 2.6.11.30] "It leads to non-rebirth, therefore it is eternal" (BDhS 2.10.17.8).
Because it causes him to go to greatness, it is called "Mahiman" (the Greatness).
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved off, he prepares [the following items].
The staffs, the sling, the water-strainer, the water-pot, and the bowl.

Having taken this [mixture] to the edge of the village or to the boundary of the village, or to the fire-hall, he should consume the *trivṛt* consisting of clarified butter, milk, and curds, and then fast.
Or water.

"Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyam*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*. [One should recite it] foot by foot, then hemistich by hemistich, and then the whole verse both separately and together."
"Having led himself from one stage of life (āśrama) to another stage of life, he becomes purified by Brahman; so it is known.
Furthermore, they also cite:
"Having gone from stage to stage, having offered oblations, and having conquered his senses..."
"Exhausted by begging and making offerings, he subsequently becomes a mendicant. Thus it is said.
This very mendicant leads to infinity.

Before sunset, having kindled the *gārhapatya* fire, brought the *anvāhāryapacana* fire, and drawn out the flaming *āhavanīya* fire, he melts clarified butter over the *gārhapatya*, purifies it, takes four portions into the *sruva* ladle, and offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the *āhavanīya* which has a fuel-stick placed upon it, saying: "Oṃ Svāhā!"
"This is known as the Brahmānvādhāna."

Then, when the evening *agnihotra* has been offered, having spread grass-blades to the north of the *gārhapatya* fire and placed the vessels upon them in pairs with their openings facing downwards, and having spread *darbha* grass in the *brahmāyatana* to the south of the *āhavanīya* fire and placed a black antelope skin over it, he remains awake for that night.

A Brāhmaṇa who, knowing this, fasts on the night of Brahmā (the Brahmarātri), consigns his sacred fires within himself, and dies, overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. Then, having risen during the Muhūrta of Brahmā, he performs the morning Agnihotra at the very proper time.
Then, having strewn the *pṛṣṭhyā* line and having carried forward the waters, he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara. That sacrifice concludes in the well-known manner.

In the Āhavanīya fire, he throws the Agnihotra vessels that are neither made of clay nor made of stone, with the formula: "Become for us of one mind. In the Gārhapatya fire, he throws the two kindling sticks (araṇī) with the formula: "Be of one mind toward us."
He internalizes the fires within himself. With the mantra, "That body of yours, O Agni, which is fit for sacrifice," he smells each [fire] three times.
Then, standing within the sacrificial altar, having recited three times in a low voice—"Om, bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ; renounced by me, renounced by me, renounced by me"—he recites it three times aloud.
"For the gods are indeed threefold in truth," so it is known from scripture.
Saying, "Fearlessness to all beings from me," he pours out a full handful of water.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted freedom from fear to all beings—no fear arises for him from any being, even in this world. Thus it is said.
He remains restrained in speech.
With the words, "O friend, protect me," he takes up the staff.
With the words, "That which is on the further shore of the dust," he grasps the sling.
With the mantra, "By that purifier with which the gods... he takes up the water-purifier.
With the mantra, "By which the gods rose upward through the light," he takes up the water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
With the seven vyāhṛtis, he takes up the vessel.

Having taken up his staff, sling, water-strainer, water-pot, and bowl, he goes to where there is water; having bathed, sipped water, and purified himself with verses containing the word *surabhi*, with those containing the word *adbhyaḥ* (the *ābliṅga* verses), with those addressed to Varuṇa, with those beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and with the *pāvamānī* verses, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having emerged from the water, wrung out his garment, put on another clean garment, and sipped water, he says: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ. Taking the water-strainer, he offers libations: "Oṃ bhūḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ suvaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ mahaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ janaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ tapaḥ, I satisfy; Oṃ satyaṃ, I satisfy."
Having offered a handful of water to the ancestors as he would to the gods, [he says]: "Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ suvaḥ svadhā; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar mahar namaḥ.
Then, with the two verses "ud u tyam" and "citram," he worships the sun.

"Om" is Brahman. Indeed, this light that shines is Brahman; this light that shines is the Veda; this light that shines is that which is to be known. In this very way, he satisfies his own self; he pays homage to his own self. The self is Brahman; the self is the light. One should recite the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, or a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times.

BDhS 2.10.17.42: Having taken the water-purifier with the words "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ," he takes up water. BDhS 2.10.17.43: From this point forward, he shall not sip water that has not been drawn out, nor that which is unstrained, nor that which is unpurified. BDhS 2.10.17.44: And from this point forward, he shall not wear white clothing.
He may carry either a single staff or three staffs.
Now, these are the observances: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and the avoidance of sexual intercourse; indeed, renunciation alone.
There are exactly five subsidiary vows: freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and purity of food.
Now, regarding the practice of begging for alms: he should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas who follow the *śālīna* and *yāyāvara* modes of life, after the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has been completed.
One should cause [the guest] to pronounce the word "bhavat" first.
One should wait for as long as it takes to milk a cow.

Now, having returned from the practice of begging for alms, he should wash his hands and feet in a clean place and offer them to the Sun with the hymns "ud u tyam" and "citram. He offers them to Brahman with the hymn "brahma jajñānam."

It is known from scripture: "From the time of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires belong to the sacrificer alone. His out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the *gārhapatya* fire; his in-breath (*apāna*) is the *anvāhāryapacana*; his diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the *āhavanīya*; and his upward and equalizing breaths (*udāna* and *samāna*) are the *sabhya* and *āvasathya* fires. These five fires are indeed situated within the self; he offers oblations into the self itself."
It is known that this very sacrifice of the self, centered on the self and established in the self, leads the self to security.
Having first distributed [the food] with compassion among all living beings, he should touch the remainder with water and eat it like medicine.

Having consumed [the remainder] and sipped water, he worships the sun with the *jyotiṣmatī* verses, beginning with "ud vayaṃ tamasas pari. Having murmured the mantra, "May speech be in my mouth; may breath be in my nostrils," he should eat only as much food as is necessary for the maintenance of life—food that is unasked for, not prepared in advance, and obtained by chance. Thus it is said.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"An ascetic (muni) should eat eight morsels; one living in the forest, sixteen;
a householder, thirty-two; and for a student (brahmacārin), there is no limit."

"Alms may be sought from all castes, or food from a single meal at the houses of twice-born men; or else, alms may be sought from all castes, but not food from a single meal at the houses of twice-born men. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding that which the teachers declare to be the *upaniṣad*, they cite this:

for one who is engaged in the vows of standing, silence, the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*), bathing at the three libations, touching water, and observing the fasts on the fourth, sixth, and eighth lunar days, there is also the practice of subsisting on grains, oil-cakes, barley-gruel, curd, and milk.

In that regard, being engaged in silence, he should converse with those learned in the three Vedas, with teachers, sages, or others belonging to the various stages of life who are deeply versed in scripture, keeping his teeth joined to his teeth, facing inward, and speaking only as much as is necessary. It is known from tradition: "He should not speak with women, nor where there is a lapse [of discipline]. (BDhS 2.10.18.16) He should practice one of the following: standing, silence, or the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*). He should not bring these three together simultaneously. (BDhS 2.10.18.17)
It is known from tradition that wherever one has gone, one should observe the vows to the same extent as before, so that there is no loss of the vow even in times of distress.

For one who is engaged in the vows at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times, characterized by standing, silence, the *vīrāsana* posture, bathing at the three daily libations (*savana*), and ritual sipping (*upasparśana*): water, roots, clarified butter, milk, sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine—these eight do not destroy the vow.
He should mutter the mantras of the Agnihotra sacrifice both in the evening and in the morning.
Having performed the evening twilight worship with the *vāruṇī* verses and the morning twilight worship with the *maitrī* verses;

being without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without protection, the sage should seek a village only for the sake of alms, and should cease his Vedic recitation. Thus it is said.

And it is known from scripture: "The *ṛc*s are limited, the *sāmans* are limited, and the *yajus* formulas are limited; but for this Brahman, there is no end. One should explain that to the one who responds; that is the response (*pratigara*)."
In this very manner, until the liberation from the body, he remains at the root of a tree as one who has renounced the Vedas.
The Veda is a tree; its root is the syllable Om (praṇava). The Veda has the syllable Om as its essence.
"Prajāpati said: 'Meditating upon the *praṇava*, one who possesses the *praṇava* becomes fit for union with Brahman.
One should wash the vessel of Brahman with the seven *vyāhṛtis*; one should wash it."
Now, concerning those who desire to follow the dharma of the *śālīna*, *yāyāvara*, and *cakracara* [householders], and who subsist by means of nine modes of livelihood:
Because they proceed according to those [rules], it is called their "mode of conduct" (vṛtti).
Because it takes its refuge in the house (śālā), it is called *śālīna*.
The state of being a Yāyāvara arises from the fact that one travels by means of an excellent mode of livelihood.
Because they move in succession, they are called *cakracaras*.
We shall explain them in detail.

BDhS 3.1.7: The Ṣaṇṇivartanī, Kauddālī, Dhruvā, Saṃprakṣālanī, Samūhā, Phālanī, Śiloñchā, Kāpotā, and Siddhecchā—these are the nine. BDhS 3.1.8: Or there is yet another tenth mode of livelihood among these very ones. BDhS 3.1.9: Up to the ninth mode of livelihood.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he prepares the following items.
BDhS 3.1.11: A black antelope skin, a water-pot, a staff, a shoulder-bag, and a *kutapa* blanket.
BDhS 3.1.12: Having performed the *traidhātavīya* sacrifice, he shall set forth, or having performed the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice.

BDhS 3.1.13: Then, in the morning when the sun has risen, having kindled the fires according to the sūtra, having melted the clarified butter over the *gārhapatya* fire and purified it, having heated the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons and wiped them, and having taken four portions of butter into the *sruk*, he offers the oblation to Vāstoṣpati in the *āhavanīya* fire. BDhS 3.1.14: Having recited the invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), "O Vāstoṣpati, recognize us," he makes the offering with the offering verse (*yājyā*), "O Vāstoṣpati, with your auspicious assembly..."
Some say that everyone who has established the sacred fires [is subject to this].
"According to some, he is a Yāyāvara."
Having departed, he stays at the edge of the village or at the boundary of the village; there he builds a hut or a monastery, or enters one already built.

BDhS 3.1.18: One should employ the black antelope skin and other items that have been prepared for their respective purposes according to the specific requirement of each. BDhS 3.1.19: The maintenance of the sacred fires is well known; the performance of the New and Full Moon sacrifices is well known; the regular practice of the five great sacrifices is well known; and the threshing of produced grain is a visible necessity.
Having prepared them, he cooks them either with the formula, "I offer what is pleasing to the Viśvedevas," or silently.
For him, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and accepting gifts are discontinued, as are other sacrificial rites.
And that which is seen as fit for the sacrificial oblation is also prescribed for the commencement of the vow.

BDhS 3.1.23: That is to say, [food] mixed with clarified butter, mixed with curd, not prepared with alkaline salt, without meat, and not stale. BDhS 3.1.24: He observes celibacy, or he approaches his wife during her season.
At every change of the moon (parvan), one should shave the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails, and observe the rules of purification.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"It is heard that purity is of two kinds, which has been practiced by the cultured (śiṣṭas):
external purity, which is free from stains and odors; and internal purity, which is non-injurious."
"The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by non-violence; and the mind is purified by truth. Thus it is said.
Regarding this which has been said: "the sixfold turning-back."
He makes exactly six furrows that are free from injury; he sets aside a portion for the owner, or takes it with the owner's permission.
BDhS 3.2.3: Before his morning meal, he should be a ploughman, not piercing the nostrils of the oxen nor their testicles, and driving them repeatedly with a goad while encouraging them by shouting.

BDhS 3.2.4: By this method, he performs six turns of the plough; thus it is called *ṣaṇṇivartinī*. BDhS 3.2.5: Regarding the *kauddālī*: near water, he digs with a spade, or a ploughshare, or a sharp piece of wood; he sows seeds and produces bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and medicinal herbs.
One who works with a spade is called a *kauddālī*.

Moving with the *dhruvā* [ladle], he wraps his head with a white cloth, saying: "For prosperity, I wrap your head. He takes up a black antelope skin with the formula: "Thou art Brahman-splendor; for Brahman-splendor, thee! He takes up the strainer with formulas not containing the word *bhṛṅga*. He takes up the water-pot with the formula: "Thou art strength; for strength, thee! He takes up the carrying-pole with the formula: "Thou art grain; for nourishment, thee! He takes up the staff with the formula: "Friend, protect me!"
Then, having gone outside and muttered the *vyāhṛtis*, he mutters the consecration of the quarters:
"May Earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the stars, and the quarters;
may Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—may these deities protect me on the path. Thus.
Having muttered the *mānastokīya* hymn and entered the village, he shows himself at every door with his load; thus they call him a *saṃdarśin*.
When there is no means of subsistence from one source after another, because one continues to live by that very [means] in a constant manner, it is proclaimed as "dhruvā" (the constant).

"Saṃprakṣālanī" means: the throwing away of herbs that have grown; there is no setting aside or hoarding. Having thoroughly washed the vessels, one turns them upside down; thus it is called "saṃprakṣālanī."

Regarding the term *samūha*: it refers to one who, in places where there is no prohibition—whether on roads, in fields, or in any open space where medicinal herbs are found—gathers them together by means of this "gathering" (*samūhana*) and subsists upon them; thus he is called a *samūha*.

BDhS 3.2.13: "Phālanī" means non-injury; this is what is being stated here. She desires husked rice grains or seeds from virtuous people. Because she "causes to grow" (phālayati), she is called *phālanī*. [K: *pālanī*... because she protects (*pālayati*), she is called *pālanī*]. BDhS 3.2.14: "Śiloñcha. In places where grain is not forbidden—on paths, in fields, or in open spaces where herbs are found—she gathers a single ear of grain from each such place and subsists on those gleanings from time to time; thus she is called *śiloñchā*. [K: *śiloñcheti*... *śiloñchā*]

Regarding the *kāpotī* [gleaning]: in unobstructed places, on paths, in fields, or in any open space where herbs are found, one should gather a single herb at each spot with the fingers by means of pinching; because it is done like a pigeon (*kapota*), it is called *kāpotī*.

"Desiring what is prepared" (siddhecchā): one who, exhausted by his means of livelihood, or due to old age or the depletion of his bodily constituents, desires food that has already been prepared by others; thus it is called "desiring what is prepared."

BDhS 3.2.17: For him, there exists the internal installation (*ātmasamāropaṇa*); his conduct is like that of a renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*), with the exception of the sacred grass ring (*pavitraka*) and the saffron-colored garment (*kāṣāyavāsa*).

BDhS 3.2.18: Or else, "wild" (*vānyā*) refers to trees, shrubs, creepers, herbs, and grasses such as *śyāmāka*, wild sesame (*jartila*), and so forth; he subsists on these wild things, thus he is called "one who lives on the wild" (*vānyā*). BDhS 3.2.19-1: Now they also cite this example:
Moving about together with wild animals, dwelling with them alone,
and a mode of life identical to theirs— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
"The characteristic of heaven is perceptible. (BDhS 3.2.19–3;
BDhS 3.3.22) Now, there are two kinds of forest-dwellers (vānaprastha). (BDhS 3.3.1) [K: of the forest-dweller, there are two kinds.]
Those who cook and those who do not cook.

Among them, those who cook for themselves are of five kinds: those who live entirely in the forest, those who remove the husks from grain, those who eat roots and tubers, those who eat fruits, and those who eat vegetables.

In this regard, those known as the "all-forest-dwellers" (sarvāraṇyaka) are of two kinds; they resort to two types of forest: those impregnated by Indra (indrāvasikta) and those impregnated by semen (retovasikta).

In that case, having brought creepers, shrubs, climbing plants, and trees called *indrāvasiktā*, and having cooked them, he should perform the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, give [the food] to guests and those observing vows, and then the others shall eat the remains.

Regarding those [animals] called "impregnated by semen": having brought meat killed by a tiger, a wolf, a hawk, or any other such creature, and having cooked it, one should perform the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, give portions to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then the rest is for consumption as remnants.

Having brought rice grains that have been dehusked—excluding those with their husks—and having cooked them, one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and in the morning, give [the food] to ascetics, guests, and those observing vows, and then consume the remainder as the leftover portion.
The same rule applies even to those who subsist on bulbs, roots, fruits, and vegetables.
There are exactly five types of those who do not cook for themselves: the *unmajjaka*s, the *pravṛttāśin*s, the *mukhenādāyin*s, the water-drinkers, and the air-eaters.
In that regard, those called "emerging" (unmajjaka) exclude [the use of] iron and stone implements.
Those who eat with their hands have taken up [the food].
Those who eat with their mouths eat what has been taken with the mouth.
Subsisting on water means subsisting exclusively on water.
Subsisting on air and abstaining from food altogether.
Thus, ten initiations (dīkṣās) are prescribed for the Vaikhānasas.
He who, having undertaken his own scripture, observes the staff, silence, and vigilance—
the Vaikhānasas are purified by being without food.
The acceptance of the [Vedic] scriptures is for all Brahmins and Vaikhānasas.
He should not harm gadflies or mosquitoes; he should be like the Himalayas, a true ascetic, established in the forest, contented, and fond of rags, skins, and water.
A forest-dweller, devoted to austerity, should first honor guests who have arrived at his hermitage at the proper time,
as well as the gods, Brahmins, and the sacred fires.
A difficult livelihood that cannot be taken away, shared with wild animals and birds,
procured from people on that very day, and consisting of astringent and bitter foods.
Having adopted this auspicious mode of life, which is avoided by the wicked,
and having taken refuge in dwelling in the forest, a Brāhmaṇa does not come to grief.
Moving about together with wild animals, dwelling among them alone,
and a mode of life identical to theirs— this is the manifest characteristic of heaven.
"Direct perception is the characteristic of heaven.

Now, if a religious student (*brahmacārin*) should act as if contrary to his vow, or eat meat, or have sexual intercourse with a woman—even in times of all kinds of distress—[he must perform penance].

BDhS 3.4.2: Having established the fire within the inner chamber and having strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the oblation to Agni, he then offers the following oblations of clarified butter: "By desire it was done; desire acts; all this belongs to desire alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! By mind it was done; mind acts; all this belongs to mind alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! By passion (rajas) it was done; passion acts; all this belongs to passion alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! By darkness (tamas) it was done; darkness acts; all this belongs to darkness alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! By evil (pāpman) it was done; evil acts; all this belongs to evil alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! By wrath (manyu) it was done; wrath acts; all this belongs to wrath alone—svāhā! To him who causes me to act, svāhā! {cf. BDhS 2.8.14.7}
From the point of victory until the gift of the cow as a boon, [the sacrifice] is completed.
Having covered himself behind the fire with a black antelope skin, with its neck pointing eastward and the hair side up, he dwells there.

BDhS 3.4.5: When dawn has broken, having drawn himself away from the rear half [of the sacrificial ground], gone to a bathing place (*tīrtha*), and bathed according to the established rule, he enters the water and performs sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having performed the established ritual up to the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*), he goes to the house of his teacher. BDhS 3.4.6: One should understand this to be exactly like the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Aghamarṣaṇa, which is the most purifying among purifiers.

Having gone to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and bathed, wearing clean garments, having cleared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the water’s edge, he shall recite the Aghamarṣaṇa as a private Vedic study (svādhyāya), facing the sun, with a garment moistened once and with his hand filled once with water.
One hundred [times] in the morning, one hundred at midday, one hundred in the afternoon, or an unlimited number.
When the stars have risen, he should consume a handful of barley-gruel.

One is released from minor offenses committed either intentionally or unintentionally after seven nights, except for the killing of an embryo, violating the teacher’s bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor, which require twelve nights.
By means of the twenty-one-night rite, one crosses over even those [obstacles] and conquers them as well.

Baudhāyana says that [one who performs this] crosses over everything, conquers everything, obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, becomes as one who has bathed in all sacred fords, becomes one who has fulfilled his vows in all the Vedas, becomes known by all the gods, purifies the assembly of those within sight of the eye, and his ritual acts reach fulfillment.
BDhS 3.6.1 Now, if one should regard oneself as heavy with the weight of one's own committed actions, one should cook a handful of barley-gruel for one's own sake when the stars have risen.
One should not offer oblations into the fire from that [impure substance].
And there is no offering of oblations (bali) in this case.
One should consecrate with mantras the milk while it is uncooked, while it is being cooked, and when it has been cooked.

BDhS 3.6.5-1ab: You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey. BDhS 3.6.5-1cd: You are the cleanser of all sins; you are remembered by the seers as a purifier.
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, barley is water, barley is nectar.
May they purify all my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me—
whether spoken with speech, performed as action, or conceived as a wicked thought in the mind.
O barley grains, purify for me all misfortune and ill-fortune;
O barley grains, purify for me all that has been trodden upon by dogs or pigs, that which has been defiled by the leavings of crows, and my failure to serve my mother and father.
"O barley grains, purify for me all that is joined with mortal sins, the terrible offense against the king, the conduct of children and the aged, and every unrighteousness;
as well as the theft of gold, the neglect of vows, and the officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to offer."

"May the barley grains purify for me all reviling of Brāhmaṇas. May the barley grains purify for me the food of a multitude, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a house of impurity due to a birth or death, the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral rite (navaśrāddha). Thus it is said.

While the food is being cooked, he should perform protection rites with the following: "Homage to Rudra, the lord of beings! May heaven be peaceful! with this *anuvāka*; with the five sections beginning "The gods who sit in front, led by Agni, slayers of demons"; and with the two verses beginning "Mā nas toke" and "Brahmā devānām. (BDhS 3.6.7) When it is cooked, he should eat it quickly, having poured it into a vessel while remaining pure.

"O gods born of the mind, yoked by the mind, highly skillful, with Dakṣa as father—may they protect us, may they favor us; homage to them, svāhā to them! Thus one should offer the oblation into oneself.
One who desires intelligence should observe this for three nights.
Having drunk it for six nights, the evildoer becomes pure.
Having drunk [the decoction] for seven nights, one purifies oneself from killing an embryo, violating the teacher’s bed, stealing gold, and drinking liquor.
Having drunk it for eleven nights, one casts off even the sin committed by one's ancestors.

"Or else, having drunk barley-gruel made from grains that have emerged from a cow for twenty-one nights, one beholds the hosts, beholds the lord of the hosts, beholds knowledge, and beholds the lord of knowledge—thus said the venerable Baudhāyana."
BDhS 3.7.1: One who considers himself impure should offer oblations with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras.
BDhS 3.7.2: Just as a thief and just as a killer of an embryo, so does he become who sheds semen outside the womb.
"By this, one is released from whatever sin prior to the killing of a learned Brahmin (bhrūṇahatyā)."
Having discharged semen in a place other than the womb, except during sleep, one who is free from taint or desires purification [should perform penance].

On either the new moon day or the full moon day, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he undertakes the vow according to the rule for a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
For one year, one month, twenty-four days, twelve nights, six, or three.
He shall not eat meat, he shall not approach a woman, he shall not sit on elevated ground, and he shall loathe untruth.
Subsisting on milk is the first rule; or, consuming barley-gruel, he should perform the twelve-night kṛcchra penance or beg for alms.
In the case of those [who are qualified] for that [offering], a Kṣatriya should offer gruel (yavāgū) and a Vaiśya should offer curdled milk (āmikṣā).

In the forenoon, having established the fire according to the ritual rules for the *pākayajña* and having strewn grass around it, he performs the *agnimukha* rite and then offers oblations of clarified butter with these three sections: "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed," "When playing at dice, whatever debt I have incurred," and "Bestowing long life upon you from every side. He should offer the clarified butter verse by verse.

Having offered four spoonfuls with the verses, "In the lion, in the tiger, or in the viper," and having offered the four "returning" oblations with the verses, "O Agni, returning," "O Agni Aṅgiras," "With strength again," and "Together with wealth," he stands in the world of the sacrificer with fuel-sticks in hand and worships with the twelve-verse hymn beginning, "We announce to Vaiśvānara.
Whatever sin has ever been committed by me through mind or speech—
"Be gracious to me from all that; for you know the truth as it truly is, svāhā! Having offered the fuel-stick (*samidh*), he gives a boon.
From the *jaya* oblation onwards, the rite is established until the giving of the cow as a boon.
Only one person shall attend to the fire.

Now, regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*): "Whatever offense against the gods we have committed, whatever debt I incurred while not gambling—bestowing long life upon you from every side. With these words, he offers full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having offered the Agnihotra and being about to begin it, he offers with the *daśahotr* formula; having offered the New and Full Moon sacrifices and being about to begin them, he offers with the *caturhotṛ* formula; having offered the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and being about to begin them, he offers with the *pañcahotṛ* formula; having offered at the animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), he offers with the *ṣaḍḍhotṛ* formula; having offered at the Soma sacrifice, he offers with the *saptahotr* formula.
And it is known from scripture: "One should offer oblations with these at the beginning of ritual acts; purified, one attains the worlds of the gods"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. So says the Brāhmaṇa.
BDhS 3.8.1 Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
BDhS 3.8.2 One should fast on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, or else having merely shaved his beard and wearing unwashed clothes, he should enter the dwelling while speaking the truth.
In that [case], his fire is either once brought forward or produced by friction from the two kindling woods.
A student, a friend, or one who prepares the instructions should be present for the consecration.
BDhS 3.8.6: And the sacrificial food fit for oblation is that which is to be used for undertaking the vow.
BDhS 3.8.7: Having kindled the fire, having strewn grass around it, and having performed the rites beginning with the offering to Agni, he makes an offering from the cooked food.

BDhS 3.8.8: [The offering] for Agni is on the lunar day (tithi) which corresponds to the constellation together with its presiding deity; on this occasion, one says, "The cow has lowed. The fifth belongs to the Moon, the sixth to Heaven and Earth, the seventh to Day and Night, the eighth to Rudra, the ninth to Sūrya, the tenth to Varuṇa, the eleventh to Indra, and the twelfth to the Viśvedevas.
Now they recite other [verses]: "And from the quarters together with their deities, and from the wide intermediate space together with its deity."

Having offered the oblation for Svistakrt with the verse, "Being born, he becomes ever new," he then draws out this remnant of the sacrificial food into a bronze vessel or a wooden cup, pours over it condiments made of sacrificial grains, and eats fifteen mouthfuls of ordinary food.

With "For breath, thee," he offers the first; with "For out-breath, thee," the second; with "For diffused breath, thee," the third; with "For up-breath, thee," the fourth; with "For equalizing breath, thee," the fifth. When there are four [oblations], he offers two first. When there are three, he offers two first. When there are two, he offers three first. One [remaining oblation] is offered with all [the formulas].

"O Nigrābhyās," he says. Having drunk water, he then offers oblations of clarified butter: "May my prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna be purified; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil, svāhā! Speech and mind! Head and hands! Skin, hide, and flesh! Sound, touch, form, earth, water, and fire!

May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified; may I become light..."

"May I become free from passion and free from evil, svāhā!"—with these seven sections (anuvākas) [or, according to K: with these seven sections beginning with "consisting of food" and "consisting of vital breath"], the rite is completed starting from the Jaya-oblation up to the bestowing of the boon of a cow.
He worships the sun with verses addressed to Sūrya and the moon with verses addressed to Candra.
Reciting "O Agni, do thou watch well," he murmurs as he lies down to sleep.
Having awakened, he recites: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows."
One should not converse with women or Śūdras, nor should one look at urine or excrement.

Having seen something impure, he mutters: "The mind is unbound, the eye is poor; the Sun is the best of lights; O consecration, do not abandon me. [K adds: Now, if it rains upon him, he says: "Wetting [the earth], bestow strength. BDhS 3.8.19:
On the first day of the second fortnight, there are fourteen mouthfuls.
In this manner, by decreasing one [meal] each day, [the fast continues] until the new moon day.
On the new moon day, no morsel [of food] is prescribed.
Now, on the first day of the bright fortnight, one [oblation]; on the second, two.
In this manner, by increasing by one [day] each, [the sequence continues] until the full moon day.
On the full moon day, he offers an oblation of cooked rice to Agni, to whichever lunar day it may be, and to the constellations together with their presiding deities.
Having offered oblations to the constellations prior to Śroṇā and Abhijit, together with their presiding deities, one should give a cow to the Brāhmaṇas.
This same Cāndrāyaṇa penance is called "ant-centered" (pipīlikāmadhya) when performed in the regular order; it is called "barley-centered" (yavamadhya) when performed in the reverse order.
Having performed either one of these, the doer of evil becomes purified from all sins.
"For every desire, for every desire, this is to be brought forth"—so they say.
Whatever desire one desires, that one obtains by means of this [rite].

By this means, the seers purified themselves in ancient times and accomplished their tasks. This [rite] is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to the birth of sons and grandsons, beneficial for cattle, bestowing long life, leading to heaven, bringing fame, and fulfilling all desires.
He attains the splendor of the stars and union with, or residence in the same world as, the sun and the moon—whosoever studies this, whosoever studies this.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the recitation of the entire Veda while fasting.
He should wear clean garments or garments made of bark.
He should desire sacrificial food, water, or fruits.

Having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung, having sprinkled it with water, having drawn the ritual marks upon it, and having sprinkled it again with water, he should kindle the fire, strew grass around it, and offer oblations to these deities: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Prajāpati, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, to the Self-existent One, to the Ṛg-verses, to the Yajus-formulas, to the Sāman-chants, to the Atharvan-hymns, to Faith, to Wisdom, to Intelligence, to Prosperity, to Modesty, to Savitṛ, to Sāvitrī, to the Lord of the Assembly, and to Anumati. (He should recite these names and not pause in the middle.)
Having offered the oblation, he should begin with the beginning of the Veda and recite it continuously.

He should not speak in between, nor should he pause in between. If, however, he should speak in between or pause in between, he should restrain his breath three times and begin again from the very point where he left off.

BDhS 3.9.8: In the event of a lack of comprehension, he should study that [text] for as long as it takes until he knows it—whether from the perspective of the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, or the *Sāmaveda*. BDhS 3.9.9:
He should then study its *Brāhmaṇa*, its *Chāndas* (phonetics/metrical rules), and its *Daivata* (deities).

One should study the twelve collections of the Veda. Whatever one has studied during improper times for study, whatever has caused displeasure to the gurus, and whatever improper acts one has committed—one purifies oneself by means of these [recitations]. Thus his sacred knowledge (*brahman*) becomes pure and purified.
From this point forward, there is accumulation.
Having studied another twelve collections of Vedic hymns, one attains through them the world of Uśanas.
Having studied another twelve collections of Vedic hymns, one attains through them the world of Bṛhaspati.
Having studied another twelve collections of the Veda, one attains the world of Prajāpati by means of them.
Fasting, he should study the *Saṃhitā* a thousand times; having become Brahman, free from passion, he becomes Brahman.
One who employs the practice of begging for alms for a year attains divine vision.

For six months subsisting on barley-gruel, for four months subsisting on water and barley-meal, for two months subsisting on fruits, for one month subsisting on water, or for twelve nights not eating at all—one quickly becomes invisible; he purifies his kinsmen—seven descendants and seven ancestors—and he purifies himself as the fifteenth, as well as the row [of diners].
This very [practice] they call "the support of the gods."
By this [knowledge], indeed, the gods attained godhood and the seers attained seerhood.
Indeed, for this very sacrifice, there are exactly three times for its commencement: at the morning libation, at the midday libation, or during the latter part of the night in the sacred precinct.
Prajāpati taught this very [work] to the Seven Seers; the Seven Seers to Mahājajña; and Mahājajña to the Brāhmaṇas. From the Brāhmaṇas [it has come down].
The duty of the social classes and the duty of the stages of life have been declared.

Now, indeed, this person behaves falsely through a blameworthy act; or he officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed; or he accepts a gift from one from whom gifts should not be accepted; or he eats the food of one whose food should not be eaten; or he engages in what should not be practiced.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not perform it?"
"For action is never exhausted. (BDhS 3.10.4)
"One should simply perform [the rite]," so it is said.
It is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punastoma*, they return to the *savana*.
Furthermore, they cite this: "He who sacrifices with the *aśvamedha* crosses over all evil; he crosses over even the murder of a Brahmin."
"One who is being falsely accused should perform the Agniṣṭut sacrifice," it is said.
Its means of expiation are: recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, the *saṃhitās* among all the Vedic meters, the honey-hymns (*madhucchandas*), the *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *Atharvaśiras*, the *Rudras*, the *Puruṣasūkta*, the *Rājana* and *Rauhiṇa* Sāmans, the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*, the *Puruṣagati*, the *Mahānāmnīs*, the *Mahāvairāja*, the *Mahādivākīrtya*, any one of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, the *Bahiṣpavamāna*, the *Kūṣmāṇḍas*, the *Pāvamānīs*, and the *Sāvitrī*—these are the purifiers.

According to the rule for approaching [the teacher], the following are purifying: subsisting on milk, eating vegetables, eating fruits, eating roots, eating a handful of barley-gruel, consuming gold, consuming clarified butter, and drinking Soma.
All mountains, all flowing rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, the dwellings of seers, cow-pens, fields, and threshing-floors—these are the [sacred] places.

Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, touching water at the three libations, service to the teacher, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, wearing a single garment, and fasting—these are the austerities.
Gold, a cow, a garment, a horse, land, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and food—these are the things to be given.
The periods of time are: one year, six months, four, three, two, or one month; twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, a day and night, or a single day. BDhS 3.10.15.
These [rites] should be performed when there is no specific instruction.
In cases of grave sins, the penances shall be grave; in cases of minor sins, they shall be minor.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the expiation for all [sins]. This is the expiation for all [sins]. This is the expiation for all [sins].
We shall now declare the penances, which serve various purposes and are distinct from one another,
both heavy and light according to their respective offenses.
For if something were appropriate here, he would have specified it right there;
likewise, among the heavier [offenses], the [penances] are more frequent, while among the lighter ones, they are fewer.
One should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures.
Whatever sin has been committed through the genitals, or whatever has been done by the feet,
by the arms, the mind, speech, the ear, the skin, the nose, or the eyes— [all that is purified].
BDhS 4.1.4 Or else, in cases of transgression involving the eyes, ears, skin, nose, or mind, one becomes pure by means of three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

BDhS 4.1.5 In the case of eating the food of a Śūdra, sexual intercourse with a woman, or eating [forbidden food] alone—each separately—one should perform seven breath-restraints for each, for a period of seven days.

In the case of eating what is unfit to be eaten, consuming what is unfit to be consumed, drinking what is unfit to be drunk, or eating what is unfit to be eaten; likewise, in the sale of forbidden commodities—with the exception of honey, meat, ghee, oil, alkaline substances, salt, and the food of low-caste persons—and in whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for each of these acts for a period of twelve days.

In cases other than the great sins (pātaka), the sins causing loss of caste (patanīya), and the minor sins (upapātaka), as well as in other instances of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) each day for half a month.

In cases other than those involving mortal sins (pātaka) or acts causing loss of caste (patanīya), and whatever else is of a similar nature, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each of twelve days.
In cases other than those involving mortal sins (pātaka), and for whatever else is similarly prescribed, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each of the twelve half-months.
Now, regarding mortal sins (pātaka), one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each [day] throughout the year.
One should give a maiden who is still naked (pre-menarche) to a virtuous man observing celibacy;
or else, one should not withhold her until she has reached puberty, even if he is deficient in virtues.
He who does not give away a maiden who has reached puberty within three years undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
If he does not beg, this is so;
but if he begs, Manu has declared that for each individual season he incurs the fault of a mortal sin (pātaka).
A woman who has reached puberty should wait for the command of her father for three years;
then, in the fourth year, she should obtain a suitable husband. If no suitable man is available, she may resort even to one deficient in qualities.
If a maiden has been forcibly abducted but not consecrated with the sacred mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for she remains just as a maiden as before.
If her husband should die after she has been given away in marriage, or even after the oblation has been offered, she—
provided she remains a virgin and has returned [to him]—
is entitled to undergo the rite of consecration again according to the *paunarbhava* (remarriage) procedure.
If a man does not approach his wife when she has reached her season for three years,
he undoubtedly incurs a guilt equal to that of killing an embryo.
But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present near him—
his ancestors lie upon that menstrual blood for that entire month.

"He who does not approach his wife during her season, and he who approaches her outside of her season—they both incur an equal fault, as does he who discharges seed in a place other than the womb. (BDhS 4.1.19)
If a wife, by staying in her husband’s house of residence, should cause her fertile season to pass in vain,
he shall proclaim her as a destroyer of the embryo (bhrūṇahni) in the midst of the village and drive her out from the house.
If he does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses— she being self-restrained and faithful to dharma—
it is traditionally taught that for such a transgression of his vow, he must perform one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
Seated with purifying grass in hand, one should practice the daily Veda-recitation, as well as breath-restraints, purificatory formulas, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava.
Always disciplined, one should repeatedly practice breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma);
by doing so, one performs the highest austerity from the tips of the hair to the tips of the nails.
From suppression, wind is born; from wind, fire is born;
from heat, water is produced; thus, it becomes pure internally through these three.
Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
All virtues have their root in yoga; therefore, one should always be disciplined in yoga.
The three Vedas begin with the syllable Om and are established within the syllable Om;
the syllable Om and the Vyāhṛtis are indeed the eternal, primeval Brahman.
For one who is constantly disciplined in the *praṇava*, in the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
and in the three-footed *gāyatrī*, no fear exists anywhere.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath;
that is called prāṇāyāma.

Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava, performed daily for a month, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin. This is the foremost austerity; this is the defining characteristic of dharma.
For the purpose of destroying all defects, this very [practice] is distinguished as superior.
"This very [rule] is further specified as follows."
We shall declare the penances, which serve various purposes and are distinct from one another,
both heavy and light, corresponding to their respective offenses.
For if something were appropriate here, he would have specified it right there;
likewise, among the more serious [offenses] he mentions those that are more frequent, and among the lighter ones, those that are fewer.
One should prescribe the penances according to the rule seen in the scriptures.
But one who is about to receive a gift, or has already received it,
should recite four times the four *ṛc* verses beginning with "taratsamandī."
BDhS 4.2.5ab: But for all those whose food is not to be eaten, if one eats the food of such a person, BDhS 4.2.5cd:
purification from the evil is performed by sprinkling with water while reciting the *taratsamandī* verses of the *Ṛgveda*.
BDhS 4.2.6ab: However, there is another rule regarding the killing of a learned Brahmin (*bhrūṇahatyā*); I shall explain that hereafter.
By which rule they are liberated from all sins whatsoever.
BDhS 4.2.7ab: One should likewise recite breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*), purificatory formulas (*pavitra*), the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *praṇava*.
BDhS 4.2.7cd: Or, subsisting on milk, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn for twelve nights while remaining pure.
BDhS 4.2.8ab: Or, for three nights, one may subsist on air alone, wearing wet clothes, or having bathed, remaining pure.
"Even if one repeatedly practices prohibited customs, by performing the *upasthāna* rite with the *vāruṇī* verses, one is liberated from all sins. Thus [it is said].

Now, having kindled the fire at night on the new moon day, an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken the vow of celibacy) should perform the ritual service pertaining to wood-offerings and offer two oblations of clarified butter, saying: "O Kāma, I have been scattered; I am scattered, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! O Kāma, I have been violated; I am violated, O Kāma! To Kāma, svāhā! [cf. BDhS 2.1.1.34]

Having offered the oblation, with hands joined in reverence (*añjali*), he should worship the fire transversely, saying: "May the Maruts pour into me; may Indra pour into me; may Bṛhaspati pour into me; may this Agni pour into me with life and with strength; make me long-lived" (BDhS 2.1.1.35). The Maruts bestow the vital breaths upon him; Indra bestows strength; Bṛhaspati bestows spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); and Agni bestows everything else. Having become whole in body, he attains a full span of life. He should recite the mantra three times, for it is known that "the gods are true to the triad."
He who considers himself as if unpurified by minor offenses (upapātaka) is liberated from all sin by performing an oblation according to this rule.

Alternatively, after consuming food that is unfit to be eaten or drunk, or eating what is forbidden, or performing a blameworthy act—whether intentionally or unintentionally—or after discharging semen into a Śūdra woman or into a non-vaginal opening, one becomes pure by sipping water while reciting the *ābliṅga* and *vāruṇī* verses.

Moreover, they cite this: "In the case of eating what is not to be eaten, drinking what is not to be drunk, consuming what is forbidden, or performing actions contrary to dharma— even when such acts are committed intentionally— one is purified from those sins that are equal to mortal transgressions, as well as from all other sins."
Or, fasting for three nights and entering the water three times a day,
restraining his vital breaths within himself, he should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times;
Manu has declared that this is equal to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice.
And it is known from scripture:
"The ancient, wide-spread, purifying conduct—by which one who is purified overcomes evil deeds—with that pure and purifying [conduct], being cleansed, may we cross over sin and enmity. Thus.
We shall declare the penances, especially those that have not been specifically mentioned;
how should it be for those who are composed and disciplined when they commit lapses?
In all cases of transgressions, one should sip water while reciting the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and including all of them.
When he sips water for the first time, by that he gratifies the Ṛgveda; when the second time, by that the Yajurveda; when the third time, by that the Sāmaveda.
That which he wipes first, by that [he obtains] the Atharvaveda; that which he wipes second, by that [he obtains] the Itihāsa-Purāṇa.

When he sprinkles his left hand, his feet, his head, his heart, his two nostrils, his two eyes, his two ears, and his navel, he thereby gratifies the plants, the trees, and all the deities. Therefore, by that very act of sipping water (ācamana), he is liberated from all evil.

Or he should offer eight fuel-sticks: "Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the gods, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against men, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against the ancestors, svāhā! Thou art the expiation for the sin committed against oneself, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed by day and by night, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed while sleeping and while waking, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For whatever sin we have committed knowingly and unknowingly, thou art its expiation, svāhā! For every single sin, thou art the expiation, svāhā!"
Having offered these eight oblations, one is liberated from all evil.
Moreover, they also cite:
The *aghamarṣaṇa*, the *devakṛta*, the *śuddhavatīs*,
the *taratsamās*, the *kūśmāṇḍyas*, the *pāvamānyas*, the *virajas*, and the *mṛtyulāṅgala*.
The Durgā verses, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Rudras are the destroyers of great evils.
"These [mantras] are the destroyers of great evils."
We shall declare the penances for those who have been concentrated and disciplined, specifically regarding those not previously mentioned; how should it be in cases of negligence?
"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca"—by reciting this Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Reciting this verse, "The spotted cow has come hither," three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all evil.
Reciting this verse—"Like a snake freed from its skin"—three times while submerged in water, one is released from all evil.
"Haṃsaḥ śuciṣat"—by reciting this verse three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the Sāvitrī verse—first quarter by quarter, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse—three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Alternatively, by reciting the Vyāhṛtis, both individually and collectively, three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.
Or alternatively, by reciting the syllable *praṇava* alone three times while submerged in water, one is liberated from all sin.

BDhS 4.4.9 This treatise on Dharma should not be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year. [K: nor to one who is not devoted, nor to one who is not a son] BDhS 4.4.10 A thousand [cows] as a sacrificial fee, with a bull as the eleventh, or the favor of the teacher; or rather, the favor of the teacher. BDhS 4.5.1ab Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the Sāman, Ṛg, Yajus, and Atharvan [Vedas].
By those rites through which one quickly attains the desires dwelling in the mind.
Having purified one's own body through recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, yantras, and so forth, one should accomplish all rites; otherwise, one does not attain success.
A twice-born man, intending to perform recitations, burnt offerings, sacrifices, or mystical diagrams,
should first have his hair and beard shaved on a day of the bright fortnight, during an auspicious lunar mansion.
He should bathe at the three periods of the day and protect himself from anger and falsehood;
as a student observing the vow of the *havir* sacrifice, he should not converse with women or Śūdras.
While sleeping during the day, he should pay homage to cows, Brahmins, ancestors, and gods;
remaining engaged in recitation, burnt offerings, sacrifices, and the use of mystical diagrams, he should stand during the day and sit at night.
The Prājāpatya Kṛcchra consists of eating only what is obtained by begging during the day for three days, and likewise at night for three days;
then for three days eating only wind (fasting), and for another three days eating only wind (fasting). This is done sequentially for twelve days, with each stage lasting three days.
One day and likewise one night, or subsisting on air when it is unknown; this threefold rite, when performed in reverse order, is called the *bāla-kṛcchra* (the child’s penance).
One should eat a single morsel for three days each, according to the previously mentioned rule;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *atikṛcchra*.
Subsisting on water for these three days and thereafter subsisting on air, this third penance is known as the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; it is exceedingly purifying.
For three days each, one should drink hot milk, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass;
for another three days, one should subsist on air alone—this is called the *taptakṛcchra*.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a one-night fast, is known as the *sāṃtapana* penance.

Taking cow urine with the *gāyatrī* verse, cow dung with the verse beginning "gandhadvārām," milk with the verse "āpyāyasva," curd with the verse "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter with the verse "śukram asi jyotiḥ," and *kuśa*-water with the verse "devasya tvā."
One part of cow urine, half of that of dung, three parts of milk, two of curd,
one of clarified butter, and one of water infused with *kuśa* grass:
thus is the *sāṃtapana* penance, which purifies even a dog-eater.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter— [or cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water infused with *kuśa* grass]—
one whose food consists of these for five nights becomes purified by means of the *pañcagavya*.
When one who is vigilant abstains from food for twelve days,
this penance called Parāka destroys all sins.
The exponents of the Veda declare that when each of these [substances], beginning with cow’s urine, is practiced for twenty-one days,
it constitutes the Mahāsāṃtapana Kṛcchra penance.
"In the bright fortnight, one increases the rice-balls by one each day; then, in the dark fortnight, one decreases them by one.
There are two fasts at the beginning of the two fortnights; that indeed is remembered as the Cāndrāyaṇa."
A Brahmin, composed in mind, should eat four morsels in the morning;
when the sun has set, he should eat four more. This is the Śiśu-Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Alternatively, one may eat eight morsels at midday for one month.
With self-restraint, one should perform the *yaticāndrāyaṇa* using sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
O twice-born, by eating eighty-three morsels (*piṇḍas*) of sacrificial food in any manner whatsoever during a month, one attains the same world as the Moon.
Just as the rising moon destroys the world's fear of darkness,
so too does the twice-born man performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance destroy the fear of sin. He may subsist on grains, oil-cakes, buttermilk, barley-water, or air, or likewise on water.
"Consisting of one, three, five, or seven [verses], this Tulāpuruṣa destroys sin."
Barley gruel consumed for seven nights destroys the sins of embodied beings;
or alternatively, a fast of seven nights achieves this—this has been observed by the wise.
In the months of Pauṣa, Bhādrapada, and Jyeṣṭha, by taking refuge in the rain, the open air, and the sun respectively,
a twice-born man is freed from the three white sins, except for those that cause loss of caste.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass; when combined with barley and fasting water, this is the *brahmakūrca*, which is supremely purifying.
Fasting on the new moon day and eating sesame seeds on the full moon day,
one is liberated from the sins committed during the bright and dark fortnights by means of these seasonal festivals throughout the year.
One who subsists on almsfood becomes purified in one month by [giving it] to those who maintain the sacred fires;
[one becomes purified] in ten or five days by giving it to forest-dwellers of the Yāyāvara type.
One who possesses wealth from a single day is purified by one day's fast;
one who is devoted to the pigeon-like mode of subsistence (kāpotavṛtti) is purified by drinking water for three days.
Having recited the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, or *Sāma* Vedas, or any one of the Vedas,
three times through to completion while fasting, he becomes supremely purifying.
Now, if he hastens to perform it, he should subsist on air during the day;
staying in water at night until dawn, that is equal to a *prājāpatya* penance. Having performed eight thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī* when the sun has risen, [he is purified].
He is released from all sins, provided he has not been a killer of an embryo.
He who gives food, speaks the truth, and abides in compassion toward all beings surpasses all those previously mentioned as purified by the *yantras*.
The Rudra hymn with the *ucchandas* verses, the *gāyatrī* accompanied by the *praṇava*,
and the seven *vyāhṛtis* should be recited as they destroy sin.
The *mṛgāreṣṭi*, the *pavitreṣṭi*, the *trihavis*, and the *pāvamānī* hymns [should also be recited].
Sacrifices accompanied by the Vaiśvānara oblation are destroyers of sin.
And listen now to this other secret being declared:
one is released from all sins, except for the greatest of transgressions.
Performing the purification with purifiers while reciting the Rudraikādaśinī, offering oblations of clarified butter with purifiers, and bestowing gold, cows, and sesame seeds; BDhS 4.6.4cd.
He who eats cooked barley-gruel mixed with cow urine,
dung-liquid, curd, milk, and ghee, is liberated from sin in an instant.
He who has procreated upon a Śūdra woman, and he by whom an unapproachable woman has been violated—
both of them are liberated from that sin after seven nights by this rite.
In the case of consuming semen, urine, or feces, or eating food that should not be eaten,
as well as in the rites of re-consecrating the sacred fires, performing a sacrifice, and for one who has married before his elder brother, this [fasting] is the remedy.
"Even after having committed very many deeds that do not cause loss of caste,
one is released from all sins"— this is the statement of the wise.
The procedure proclaimed here is the authoritative standard for the path of mantra,
by which Bharadvāja and others attained identity with Brahman.
A Brahmin whose heart is serene through the performance of this rite [attains that same state].
He attains those various desires, whatever desires reside in his heart.
"Whatever desires reside in the heart," and so forth.
For that Brahmin who has turned away from evil deeds and is engaged in meritorious deeds,
his ritual actions succeed even without the use of mechanical devices.
Because Brāhmaṇas are upright, whatever they desire in their minds,
that very thing they quickly attain, being purified by their straightforward deeds.

Thus, a wise man should perform these restraints for as long as it takes until his body attains purity of the self. Having purified himself by means of these restraints, he should then fast for three nights.
He should undertake that action by which he desires to attain success.
The *kṣmāpavitra*, the *sahasrākṣa*, the *mṛgāra*, the two *aṃhomuc* groups, the *pāvamānī* verses, the *kūśmāṇḍya* verses, and those verses addressed to Vaiśvānara; BDhS 4.7.5cd.
Offering oblations of rice cooked in ghee three times a day for seven days, observing a vow of silence, eating sacrificial food, and restraining the activities of the senses; BDhS 4.7.6cd.
Having looked into a vessel full of water at a crossroads while reciting "siṃhe me," one is released from all sins, even from a great mortal transgression.
Whatever accumulation of sin has been committed in old age, youth, or childhood,
and even that which was done in previous births through ignorance— from all that one is liberated.
Having fed the twice-born at the conclusion with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, [one is purified].
And having bestowed cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold upon those who have already eaten.
The Brahmin becomes purified in soul, with the fuel of his sins completely consumed;
he thus becomes fit for optional rites as well as for the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires.
He who performs this rite out of excessive greed or through negligence—
Possessed by the sin of another, he perishes like one who has swallowed poison.
Performing this rite for his teacher, his father, his mother, and himself, the learned man shines like the sun; therefore, this rite must be performed for them.
Who, by means of this thousand-eyed purifier,
made Agni, Vāyu, Ravi, Soma, Yama, and the other lords of the gods pure?
Whatever is renowned here as meritorious throughout the three worlds,
that has been accomplished by the Brahmins and others through this purifying rite.
This secret *prājāpatya* [mantra], which destroys sin, was first produced;
thereafter, thousands of purifiers (*pavitra*) have emerged from it.
He who offers oblations for these eight groups— namely, the year, the solstice, the season, the fortnight, and the day—
purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants of his own lineage.

Even while remaining on earth, he is recognized by the immortals dwelling in heaven as one of meritorious deeds; moreover, the doer of merit rejoices like a god in the heavenly world. (BDhS 4.8.7) If a twice-born man is unable to offer these eight groups [of oblations], [he should perform the following]. (BDhS 4.8.8ab)
Even if he offers only one [oblation] with that [mixture], his impurity is thereby destroyed.
He whose sons or disciples offer these eight groups [of oblations] is also liberated from sin, even though he has been hired for the purpose of teaching.

Even by means of those purchased with wealth, one who desires to destroy his own sin must have the oblations offered; for the one who bears the body should not be despondent when he is unable [to perform them himself].
The relinquishing of wealth and even of well-performed deeds is performed; at times, liberation from sinful man is brought about when he is freed from his debts.
Released by this rite from the ocean of all debts of sin,
he considers himself pure and capable of performing ritual acts.
But when one whose self is liberated from the debt of all sins undertakes ritual actions,
those actions reach fulfillment without effort for that person of purified body.
This meritorious *prājāpatya* [text], proclaimed by the seer,
one should constantly teach, retain in memory, or even hear;
such a person is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One who desires to master those mantras should mutter them for twelve days,

consuming rice once at night with ghee, milk, and curd. Likewise, there should be ten oblations of clarified butter during each of the three daily pressings for the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and also the Atharvāṅgirasa.

BDhS 4.8.16–1cd: This shall be the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for these mantras in the accomplishment of ritual acts. BDhS 4.8.16–2: "In the accomplishment of ritual acts for the mantras"—[this applies] due to excessive greed or negligence. One who has desisted from evil deeds, [and whose] Rudra-mantras are well-composed through the Vedic meters. Now, therefore, I shall fully declare; we shall declare the expiations (*prāyaścitta*); we shall declare the expiations; we shall declare the expiations; we shall declare the expiations. Thus ends the fourth book. 4. Thus the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra is completed.
