Text based on the edition:
*Vasiṣṭhadharmaśāstra*, Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series, 23, input by M. Fushimi, checked by F. Enomoto.
Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into dharma for the sake of the supreme good of man.
Having understood [the dharma], one who practices it is righteous.
He becomes most praiseworthy in this world and, after death, attains the heavenly world.
Dharma is that which is prescribed by Śruti and Smṛti.
In the absence of that, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa) is the authority.
The cultured man, moreover, is one whose nature is free from desire.
Dharma is that whose cause is not perceived.
Āryāvarta lies to the east of Ādarśa, to the west of Kālakavana, to the north of Pāriyātra, and to the south of the Himavat.
And [the region] to the north of the Vindhya mountains.
Whatever duties and whatever customs exist in that region, all of them are to be accepted everywhere.
But this does not apply to others who follow the duties of those born in the inverse order of castes.
Some [say] even between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Others say that spiritual luster extends as far as the black antelope roams.
Moreover, the Bhāllavins cite this verse in their Nidāna:
To the west is the Sindhu, the supporter; to the east is the rising of the sun.
As far as the dark one (Kṛṣṇa) hastens, so far indeed extends spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

That which those who have mastered the three Vedas and know the Dharma declare to be Dharma—both in times of prosperity and in times of purification—that indeed is Dharma; there is no doubt in this matter.
Manu declared that, because there is no revealed scripture (śruti) for them, one should follow the laws of regions, the laws of castes, and the laws of families.
One who has been overtaken by the sun rising while he is still unclean, and one who has been overtaken by the sun setting while he is still unclean—
these, they declare, are among the five great sins (mahāpātaka).
Violating the teacher's bed, drinking liquor, killing an embryo, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and associating with outcasts.
Or through the *brāhma* [form of marriage], or through the *yauna* [form of marriage].
Moreover, they also cite this:

"By associating with an outcast for a year—through officiating at his sacrifices, teaching him, or forming a matrimonial alliance—one becomes an outcast; but not through sharing a vehicle, a seat, or the giving of gifts."
"Those who cast away the sacred fires, those who show malice toward their teacher, atheists, those who live as atheists, and those who sell *soma*—these are the minor offenses (*upapātaka*)."
A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives according to the order of the castes; a Rājanya, two; and a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, one each.
Some [teachers] say that one may likewise marry a Śūdra woman, provided it is done without the recitation of mantras.
One should not act in that manner.
For from this results the certain degradation of the family, as well as the loss of heaven after death.
There are six forms of marriage.
The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Gāndharva, Kṣātra, and Mānuṣa [are the forms of marriage].
If she should give herself of her own accord preceded by water, that is the Brāhma marriage.
When the sacrificial ritual has been spread out and the officiating priest is performing his duties, one should give a daughter adorned with ornaments; they call that the Daiva form of marriage.
And the Ārṣa [form of marriage] is performed with a pair of cattle.
If one approaches a willing woman of equal birth who desires him, that is the Gāndharva marriage.
That which they carry off by force, having violently overpowered her, is the Kṣātra marriage.
Having bartered for her, she is a human being purchased with wealth.
Therefore, it is understood here that the purchase [of the bride] consists in giving a hundred [cows] plus an extra chariot to one who has a daughter.
"She who, having been purchased by her husband, then behaves with others"—this is stated in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Knowledge that has been lost may be regained; but when a family line perishes, there is total destruction here.
For even a horse is honored by the designation of its lineage; therefore, one should marry a woman of noble birth."
The three castes shall conduct themselves according to the instruction of the Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa shall proclaim the duties.
And the king shall also issue instructions.
But the king, ruling according to dharma, shall take a sixth part of the wealth.
Except in the case of a Brāhmaṇa.
But it is said that he partakes of a sixth share of his *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works).
The Brāhmaṇa makes the Veda wealthy; the Brāhmaṇa rescues one from calamity; therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is not to be eaten. "Soma is his king," so it is said.
"And that which leads to prosperity after death—thus it is known, thus it is known. (VaDhS 1.46)
There are four social classes: the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
The three castes—the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—are the twice-born.
For them, the first birth is from the mother; the second is at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
Here, the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, while the teacher is called his father.
Because he imparts the Veda, they call the teacher "father."

Moreover, they cite this: "A man has indeed two kinds of seed for a Brāhmaṇa: that which is above the navel and the other which is below it. That which is above the navel—by means of it, offspring is produced when he initiates Brāhmaṇas, when he teaches them, when he officiates at their sacrifices, and when he performs meritorious deeds. Now, that which is below the navel—by means of it, his legitimate offspring is produced here in this world. Therefore, they do not say of a learned man who has studied the Vedas, 'You are childless.'"
Hārīta also cites:
"Indeed, no ritual act whatsoever exists for him prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
for he is equal to a Śūdra in his mode of livelihood until he is born into the Veda."
Except for water-rites, *svadhā* offerings, and those connected with the ancestors.
"Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin, saying: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.
Do not speak of me to one who is censorious, dishonest, or undisciplined, so that I may remain full of power.'"
O Brahmin, teach me to that guardian of the treasure who you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, endowed with the practice of celibacy, and who would never do you any harm in any way whatsoever.

He who pierces one's ears with that which is not false, causing no pain and bestowing immortality—him one should regard as both father and mother; one should never do him any harm on any day whatsoever.

Those Brahmins who, having been instructed, do not respect their teacher in word, thought, or deed— just as they are not worthy of being fed by the teacher, even so does that sacred learning not nourish them.
Just as fire burns dry grass, so does the Veda burn one who questions it without respect; one should not teach the Veda to such a person, for it is impossible to make him show due honor.
VaDhS 2.13: There are six duties for a Brāhmaṇa.
The study and recitation of one's own Veda, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.
A Kṣatriya has three [sacrificial fires].
Study, sacrifice, and giving are [the duties].
And the protection of subjects by means of the sword is his own duty; he should live by that.
These same [rules] apply to the Vaiśya.
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and money-lending.
Service to them is the constant duty and livelihood of a Śūdra.
All [the mourners] must maintain their hair and dress according to the prescribed rule, or else all may have their hair loose except for the topknot.
If they cannot subsist by their own specific duty, they should adopt the next lower mode of livelihood.
But never [should he marry] one who is older.
Adopting the livelihood of a Vaiśya, one who lives by trade [must avoid] stones, salt, gems, whetstones, silk, linen, and skins.
All woven cloth that is dyed red [is impure].
Cooked food, flowers, fruits, roots, fragrances, flavors, water, the juice of medicinal plants, Soma, weapons, poison, meat, milk and its derivatives, iron, tin, lac, and lead.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A Brāhmaṇa falls immediately from his caste by selling meat, lac, or salt; by selling milk, he becomes a Śūdra within three days."
Among village animals, those with solid hooves and those with manes, as well as all wild animals, birds, and fanged creatures [are not to be eaten].
Regarding grains, they say that sesamum seeds [are the most important].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If one performs any act with sesame seeds other than eating, anointing, or giving as a gift,
he becomes a worm and sinks into the excrement of dogs along with his ancestors."
Or, if they so desire, they may themselves cultivate sesame seeds and sell them.
Therefore, from dawn until the morning meal, he should be a ploughman with two oxen yoked by a thong.
In the summer, one should offer water.
"The plough, sharp-pointed, very auspicious, with a handle of *soma*-wood—may it turn up for us cattle, sheep, and a fat, prolific cow, as well as a chariot and a wagon."

VaDhS 2.35: He throws away [the soma-stalks] at a distance, saying, "O you whose stalk is for the Soma-drinker; for the Soma reaches his stalk. He sows [the seeds]: cows, sheep, goats, horses, mules, and camels, as well as a stout, beautiful, auspicious, and excellent young woman.
VaDhS 2.36: For how indeed could one plow with a ploughshare except through the sale of grain?
Flavors are to be exchanged for flavors, whether they are superior or inferior.
But one must never [add] salt to [other] flavors.
Through bartering, sesame seeds, rice, cooked food, knowledge, and human beings may be acquired.
A Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya shall not practice usury.
Furthermore, they also cite this:
"He who, having taken grain at a low price, gives it back at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer and is censured among those who discourse on the Veda."
He weighed the killing of a Brahmin against usury on a scale;
the killer of an embryo remained steady at the end, while the usurer trembled.
Or they may, at their will, give [the property] to one who is more wicked but has neglected his duties.
Gold [is increased] twofold, grain threefold.
By means of grain alone, the [rules regarding] liquids are explained.
And flowers, roots, and fruits.
A fine weighed on a scale shall be eightfold.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One may take interest of two, three, four, five,
and a hundred per month, respectively, according to the order of the social classes."
But a king, by means of his death, destroys the increase of wealth;
yet again, through royal consecration, the root of wealth increases.
Listen to the rate of interest proclaimed by the words of Vasiṣṭha regarding a moneylender:
five māṣas on twenty [kārṣāpaṇas]; thus the dharma is not violated.
"He does not fall away," so it is said.
Those who have not studied the Vedas, those who do not recite them, or those who maintain no sacred fires, become equal in status to Śūdras.
And regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"The twice-born man who, without having studied the Veda, exerts himself in other pursuits,
quickly sinks to the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his progeny."
A Brāhmaṇa does not become [unworthy] by not reciting the Ṛgveda, nor by being a merchant, nor by being an actor;
nor by serving a Śūdra, nor by being a thief, nor by being a physician.
For the king should punish that village where twice-born men wander for alms without observing their vows and without studying the Veda; for such a village provides sustenance for thieves.
Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely on their birth-status do not possess the status of an assembly (*pariṣad*).
Whatever those fools, deluded by darkness and ignorant of dharma, proclaim—
that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it.
Whether they be four or even three who have mastered the Vedas, whatever they declare should be known as Dharma; not so that of thousands of others.
Sacrificial offerings for the gods and the ancestors must always be given to one learned in the Vedas;
for what is given to one unlearned in the Vedas reaches neither the ancestors nor the deities.
If one has a fool in his own house or a man of great learning far away, the gift should be given to the man of great learning; there is no transgression in not giving to the fool.
There is no offense in bypassing a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of Vedic knowledge;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
An elephant made of wood, a deer made of leather,
and a Brahmin who has not studied the Veda— these three are merely bearers of names.
In those kingdoms where ignorant people eat the food of the learned,
they encounter drought or a great danger arises.
VaDhS 3.13: If [the property] is not recognized [as belonging to anyone], [it shall be kept by the king].
VaDhS 3.14: If a Brāhmaṇa should acquire [property while] engaged in the six duties, the king shall not take it away.
VaDhS 3.15: Having slain an assailant, they say that there is no sin whatsoever for the one who takes the life.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The incendiary, the poisoner, one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth,
and the seizer of land or wife— these six are *ātatāyin*s (assassins)."
One may strike down an assailant who approaches with intent to kill, even if he is a master of the Vedāntas; by doing so, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
He who slays an assailant born of a noble family and devoted to Vedic study does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; for it is the wrath of the assailant that meets the wrath of the slayer.

One who has performed the *triṇāciketa* sacrifice, one who maintains the five fires, one who knows the *trisuparṇa*, one who knows the four *medha* sacrifices, a follower of the *Vājasaneyi*, one who knows the six Vedāṅgas, one who continues the lineage of a *brahmadeya* (land granted to a Brahmin), a singer of the *chandoga* hymns, a singer of the *jyeṣṭhasāman*, and one who knows the *mantra* and *brāhmaṇa* texts and studies the *dharma*: these, as well as those whose maternal and paternal lineages for ten generations are known to have been learned *śrotriyas* and who are themselves learned *snātakas*, are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
One who is learned in the four Vedas, one who can deliberate on legal cases, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and a reciter of the Dharma;
these three belonging to the [three] stages of life (*āśrama*) are the principal members, and an assembly (*parṣad*) of at least ten such persons is required.
Having initiated him, he should teach him the entire Veda; such a person is an Ācārya.
But he who teaches a single portion [of the Veda] is an upādhyāya.
And he who [studies] the Vedāṅgas.
In self-defense and in the protection of the social orders, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya may take up arms.
But for a Kṣatriya, that [study] is indeed obligatory, because of his duty to protect [the people].

Having washed his feet and hands up to the wrists, and sitting facing either east or north, he should sip water three times silently using the *brāhma* tīrtha—the line at the base of the thumb—with the water making no sound.
He should wipe [the mouth] twice.
One should touch the cavities of the head with water.
He should pour water on his head and into his left hand.
One should not perform ācamana while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing.
A Brāhmaṇa [should sip water] from water that reaches the heart, which is free of bubbles and froth.
But by [the water] reaching the throat, a Kṣatriya [is purified].
A Vaiśya [is purified] by sipping water.
And likewise, having touched a woman or a Śūdra with [water] that has already been used for bathing.

Even from a wound, those [rays] which are capable of providing satisfaction to a cow [are acceptable]. (VaDhS 3.35) [One should not use water] that is corrupted by color, smell, or taste, nor that which comes from an impure source. (VaDhS 3.36)
Large drops do not make one impure with remnants if they have not touched the limbs.
Having slept, eaten, sneezed, drunk, wept, or bathed, and after rinsing the mouth, one should rinse again; likewise, after putting on a garment.
Having touched the two lips where they are hairless.
There is no impurity from what adheres to the beard.
Regarding things stuck between the teeth, as with the teeth themselves, and whatever may enter the mouth, one becomes pure by simply swallowing it.
Even for one who is causing others to sip water, those drops that have fallen upon his feet do not cause him to become ritually impure; they are considered equal to the ground.
If, while eating, he should touch something impure (ucchiṣṭa),
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the sipping of water (ācamana), and then proceed with the meal again.
Whatever may require examination, one should touch it with water.
Wild animals killed by dogs, fruit fallen by birds, that which has been stepped over by children, and that which has been handled by women; these are pure.
And whatever merchandise is displayed for sale, as well as those defects which are found in the faces of women.
"One is not defiled by mosquitoes or flies that have settled upon it;
and Prajāpati has declared that all water remaining on the ground which satisfies the thirst of cows is pure."
VaDhS 3.48: Purification for the removal of stains and odors consists of water and earth for that which is smeared with impure substances.
For objects made of metal, clay, wood, or cloth, the methods of purification are respectively: cleansing with ashes, burning, scraping, and washing.
The purification of stones and gems is like that of gold.
The purification of conch shells and mother-of-pearl is like that of gems.
The treatment of bones is like that of wood.
The purification of ropes, split bamboo, and leather is like that of cloth.
For those made of fruit, [the purification is] with cow-hair.
For those made of linen, [purification is] with a paste of white mustard seeds.
The ground attains purity according to its specific defect through sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, scraping, sprinkling, and covering, each applied to its appropriate place.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"By digging, by burning, by trampling, and also by being trodden upon by cows..."
The ground is purified by four means, and by a fifth, by smearing it.
A woman is purified by her menstrual flow; a river is purified by its current;
bell-metal is purified by ashes; and an earthen vessel is purified by being fired again.
An earthen vessel that has come into contact with intoxicating liquors, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears,
or blood is not purified even by baking it again.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.
Gold is purified by water alone.
Likewise, silver [is forbidden].
Copper is purified by an acid.
The divine (daiva) sacred site is at the base of the little finger.
On the finger-joints, [the marks] of the sages.
Human [beings] are on the tips of the fingers.
The middle of the palm is sacred to Agni.
The region between the forefinger and the thumb is for the ancestors (pitrya).
One should honor the foods for the morning and evening meals by saying, "It is pleasing."
"In the rite for the ancestors, [the response is] 'It is well-eaten' (svaditam)."
"In the rites for prosperity, [the word] 'it is prepared' is used at each of the rites for prosperity.
(VaDhS 3.71) "The four castes are distinguished by their origin and by specific sacramental rites. (VaDhS 4.1)
"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya was made from his arms;
that which was his thighs became the Vaiśya; from his feet the Śūdra was born.
Thus also there is a Vedic verse (nigama).

With the Gāyatrī he created the Brāhmaṇa, with the Triṣṭubh the Rājanya, and with the Jagatī the Vaiśya; he created the Śūdra with no metre at all—thus he is known to be one who is not to undergo the sacraments.
For all [these castes], truthfulness, freedom from anger, generosity, non-violence, and procreation [are duties].
"Even in the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and guests, one may kill an animal"—this is the teaching of Manu.
"Manu has declared that one may kill an animal only on these occasions— the honey-mixture offering, a sacrifice, and rites for the ancestors or deities— and not otherwise."
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings; and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven. Therefore, in a sacrifice, killing is no killing at all.
Moreover, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Rājanya should arrive as a guest, one may cook for him a large bull or a large goat, thinking, "In this way we shall provide hospitality."
The water-rites and purification apply from the second year onwards.
Some say [the period of impurity lasts] until the eruption of teeth.
Having consigned the body to the fire, they enter the water without looking back.
They should perform the water-rite with both hands, the left and the right, facing south on odd-numbered days;
for this direction toward the south belongs to the ancestors.
Having gone to their houses, they should remain for three days on a bed of grass, fasting.
In the event of incapacity, they should subsist on what has been purchased or produced.
Impurity on account of a death is ordained for ten days among the sapinda relatives.
Sapiṇḍaship is understood to extend up to the seventh person.
And for women who have been given away in marriage, it is known that [the impurity lasts] for three generations.
The others [the sons] shall perform [the rites] for those who have been given away [in marriage], and they [the married daughters] shall do so for them.
The same rule applies at birth as well for those who desire complete purity.
Or from his mother and father.
"Because she is the cause of that [conception], some say it belongs to the mother."
Moreover, they also cite this:

"There is no impurity for a man during childbirth, provided he does not come into contact [with it]. In that case, it is the menstrual flow that should be known as impure, and that is not found in a man."
If that [impurity] should occur again within [the period], they shall be purified by the remainder [of the original period].
If it is the remainder of the night, [he should perform it] with two [verses].
At dawn, [he should bathe] with three [verses].
A Brāhmaṇa [is purified] in ten nights.
A Kṣatriya [becomes pure] in fifteen nights.
A Vaiśya [is purified] in twenty nights.
A Śūdra becomes pure after one month.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, or even during a birth-impurity,
shall go to a terrible hell and is born among the animal species."
If a twice-born man eats meat from an animal that has died within ten days of slaughter, even by command,
he becomes a worm at the end of his body and consumes its excrement.
It is traditionally taught that one becomes purified by studying the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months.
When a child less than two years old has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the period of impurity for the sapinda relatives is three nights.
Gautama says that there is immediate purification.
If the deceased is in another country, one shall observe impurity for one night upon hearing of it after the ten days have passed.

If one who has maintained the sacred fires should die while away from home, Gautama says that after performing the cremation rites again, the purification is to be carried out as in the case of a corpse.

Having touched a sacrificial post, a funeral pyre, a cemetery, a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, or anyone who is impure, one should bathe with one's head immersed in water—yes, in water.
A woman is not independent; she has man as her primary authority.
It is known from tradition that those who maintain no sacred fire and women who have not reached their menses are "immortal" (amṛta).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence."
Regarding her husband's practice of malevolent magic, the expiation has been stated among the secret rites.
For month after month, their menstrual flow indeed carries away their misdeeds.
A woman in her menses remains impure for three nights.

She shall not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself; she shall not bathe in water, she shall sleep on the ground, and she shall not sleep during the day; she shall not touch fire, nor let go of a rope, nor clean her teeth, nor eat meat, nor gaze at the planets, nor laugh, nor perform any such action; she shall not run, but drink from a vessel that is not small, or drink with her joined palms, or from a vessel of red iron.

For it is known from tradition: Indra, having slain the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was seized by evil and thought of himself thus: "I am bound by great unrighteousness. All beings reviled him, crying out, "Foe of the embryo! Foe of the embryo! He ran to women, saying, "Accept a third part of this guilt of killing the embryo for me. They asked, "What shall be ours? He said, "Choose a boon. They said, "May we obtain offspring during the fertile season; may we unite with our husbands according to our desire until the birth of a child. "So be it," he replied, and they accepted. This very guilt of killing the embryo manifests itself month after month; therefore, one should not eat the food of a woman in her courses, for she remains assuming the form of the guilt of killing the embryo.

Regarding this, they say: "One must not accept from her even eye-salve or ointment, for that is the food of women; therefore, people feel disgust toward her and toward that [act], thinking, 'She has come to this.'"
Those among whom women remain menstruating, those who are without sacred fires,
and those whose lineage lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
"All of them follow the dharma of Śūdras."
"Good conduct is the highest dharma for all; this is the settled conclusion.
One whose soul is overwhelmed by deficient conduct perishes both in this world and after death."
Neither austerities, nor sacred knowledge, nor the Agnihotra sacrifice,
nor sacrificial gifts can ever rescue one who has fallen away from this [duty] due to deficient conduct.
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied together with the six auxiliary sciences;
at the time of death, the Vedic hymns abandon him, just as birds with grown wings leave their nest.
But for a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of proper conduct, even the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs and all the sacrifices are unable to produce any joy,
just as beautiful wives are of no avail to a blind man.
The Vedic meters do not rescue this deceitful man from his wickedness while he persists in deception;
however, even two syllables, when properly studied, purify that sacred knowledge (brahman), just as clouds [purify] the earth with rain.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly experiences suffering, is afflicted by disease, and is short-lived.
From good conduct, righteousness bears fruit; from good conduct, wealth bears fruit.
Through good conduct one attains prosperity; good conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who follows the conduct of the virtuous,
who is full of faith and free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
One who knows the Dharma must ensure that his eating, excretion, and movements are well-restrained;
likewise, his speech, mental activities, ascetic practices, as well as his wealth and lifespan, must be kept most strictly guarded.
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day;
at night, however, one should do so facing south, for in this way one's life-span is not diminished.
Facing the fire, facing the sun, facing a cow, facing a Brahmin,
facing Soma, water, or the twilight— wisdom perishes for one who urinates toward these.
One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor in ashes;
nor on cow dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in sown ground, nor in the shade of trees that provide livelihood or are grassy meadows.
In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction he finds comfortable, as well as when there is danger to his life.
One should perform [ritual] acts with water that has been drawn up [from a vessel].
Bathing may be performed even with water that has not been drawn up [from a well].
A Brahmin should fetch clay from a riverbank that contains sand.
The five types of earth that should not be used are: earth from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, from a mouse-hole, or what remains after one has already performed purification.
One application of clay is prescribed for the penis, three for the hands—thus two [applications] are traditionally taught;
five for the anus, ten for one [hand], and seven applications of clay for both [hands].
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Eight mouthfuls are the meal for a sage, sixteen for a forest-dweller,
thirty-two for a householder, and an unlimited amount for a student.
The maintainer of the sacred fires, the bull, and the student—these three succeed only while eating;
for them there is no success while fasting.
In the observances, the restraints, and the duties of sacrifice and study.
Yoga, austerity, self-control, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, compassion, knowledge,
discernment, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
One should recognize long-standing enmity, envy, untruthfulness, reviling Brahmins,
backbiting, and cruelty as the characteristics of a Śūdra.

Those Brahmins who are tranquil and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, who abstain from killing living beings, and whose hands are restrained from accepting gifts— they alone are capable of delivering others across [the ocean of existence].
One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity;
but among all vessels, that is the true vessel whose belly does not contain the food of a Śūdra.
If a twice-born man dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach,
he shall be born as a domestic pig or is born into that [Śūdra's] family.
For one whose limbs are nourished by the food of a Śūdra, even if he constantly studies the Vedas,
performs sacrifices, or recites prayers, he does not attain the higher goal.
But he who engages in sexual intercourse after having eaten the food of a Śūdra—
his sons belong to the one whose food he ate, and he himself shall not ascend to heaven.
One who has risen through Vedic study, possesses a noble birth, is tranquil, established in the sacrificial fires, fearful of sin, and possessed of great knowledge;
one who is patient toward women, righteous, a refuge for cows, and exhausted by religious observances—they say such a person is a worthy recipient.

Just as milk, curd, clarified butter, or honey placed in an unbaked earthen vessel would perish due to the weakness of the vessel— neither the vessel nor those liquids would remain— so it is with [the food].
In this way, an ignorant man who accepts cows, gold, clothing, a horse, land, or sesame seeds is reduced to ashes like a piece of wood.
One should not practice fingernail-scratching on the body.
And one should not eat with the fingernails at the beginning of a meal.
And one should not drink water with the hollowed palms.
One should not strike the water with the foot or with the hand.
Nor [should one touch] water with water.
One should not gather fruit with bricks.
One fruit is not [to be exchanged] for another fruit.
One should not be deceitful nor fraudulent.
One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes; one should not be fickle with speech or limbs—this is the sphere of conduct for the disciplined."

Those Brāhmaṇas to whom the Veda, along with its supplements, has been handed down through traditional succession, are to be known as the cultured (śiṣṭas), who have the revealed scripture as their direct authority.
He whom no one knows— whether he exists or does not exist, whether he is unlearned or deeply learned, whether he is well-conducted or ill-conducted— that man is a Brāhmaṇa.
"He is a Brāhmaṇa. Thus [it is said].
There are four stages of life (āśramas).
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant.
Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas among them, and having maintained his vow of studentship without breach, he may dwell with whomever he wishes.
A student of sacred knowledge shall serve his teacher until the liberation from the body.
And when the teacher has died, he should tend the sacred fire.
For it is known: "The teacher is indeed Agni for you."
Restrained in speech.
He should eat at the fourth, sixth, and eighth meal-times.
He should practice begging for alms.
He is dependent on his teacher.
He should wear matted hair, or have a single lock of matted hair on the crown of his head.
One should follow a teacher when he is walking; if he is sitting, one should stand; and if he is lying down, one should sit beside him.
He shall study when called upon.
Having offered everything he has obtained, he should eat with their permission.
He should avoid using a bedstead for sleeping, brushing his teeth, washing [the face], applying collyrium, anointing [the body with oil], shoes, and an umbrella.
He should stand during the day and remain seated at night.
Three times a day he should approach water, saying "Apaḥ! Apaḥ! (O Waters! O Waters!).

A householder, having subdued anger and joy and being permitted by his teacher, should bathe and take a wife who is of the same lineage as himself, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger in age, and who is of equal status.
The fifth [generation] on the mother's side and the seventh on the father's side.
He should kindle the nuptial fire.
One should not turn away a guest who has arrived in the evening.
No one shall stay in his house without eating.
If a Brahmin seeking lodging comes to one's house and does not eat,
he departs taking with him whatever merit that person has acquired.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even one night is traditionally known as a guest (atithi);
because he stays for an indefinite period, he is therefore called a guest.

A Brahmin who is a resident of the same village, as well as one who is merely a casual acquaintance, is not considered a guest; even when the proper time has arrived, he should not stay in one's house without eating, whether that time be the right or wrong hour.
One who is faithful, free from covetousness, and capable of maintaining the sacred fires should not fail to establish those fires.
And it is sufficient for Soma, but not for one who does not sacrifice with Soma.
He should be devoted to Vedic study, sacrifice, and procreation.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at one's house by rising from one's seat, offering a seat, speaking kind words, and being free from envy.
And one should satisfy all beings with food according to one's ability.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity. Among the four stages of life, the householder is indeed preeminent.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
so do all those in the [other] stages of life find their resting place in the householder.
Just as all living beings live by depending on their mother,
so do all mendicants live by depending on the householder.
A Brāhmaṇa who constantly offers water, constantly wears the sacred thread, constantly studies the Veda, avoids the food of outcasts,
approaches his wife during her season, and performs oblations according to the rule, does not fall from the world of Brahman.
"From the world of Brahman," so it is said.
The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) has matted hair and wears garments of bark or skins.
And he shall not enter a village.
One should not stand upon land that has been ploughed by a plow.
He should gather uncultivated roots and fruits.
One whose vital energy is drawn upward;
one whose disposition is patient.
One should honor a guest who has arrived at the hermitage with alms consisting of roots and fruits.
One should only give; one should not accept.
He should touch water at the three periods of the day.
Having established the fire according to the Śrāmaṇaka rite, he shall become one who has maintained the sacred fires.
Having his dwelling at the foot of a tree, after six months he shall be without fire and without a fixed abode.
He who gives to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings shall go to eternal heaven; thus it is "eternal."
The wandering mendicant, having given the gift of fearlessness to all beings, shall depart.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The sage who wanders about after having granted freedom from fear to all beings— for him,
too, there is never any fear from any being."
But he who, having granted safety to all beings, turns back from his vow, kills both those born and those unborn, as does one who accepts gifts for the sake of ritual fees.
One should renounce all ritual acts, but one must not renounce the Veda;
by renouncing the Veda one becomes a Śūdra, therefore one must not renounce the Veda.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
begging is superior to fasting, and compassion excels giving.
Shaven-headed, free from the sense of "mine," and without possessions.
He should go for alms to seven houses that have not been previously designated.
When the smoke has subsided and the pestle is at rest.
He should be clothed in a single garment.
Or, having covered his body with a deerskin or with grasses plucked by cows.
He should sleep on the bare ground.
He should dwell in a transient abode.
At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the foot of a tree.
One who studies while knowing [the text] with the mind.
He should be constantly dwelling in the forest.
One should not walk about while looking at domestic animals.
For one who is constantly dwelling in the forest, whose senses are conquered, who has turned away from the gratification of all the senses,
whose mind is absorbed in reflection on the inner self, and who is equanimous— certainly, for such a person, there is no returning [to worldly existence].
He should have unmanifest signs and unmanifest conduct.
One who is not insane but wears the garb of a madman.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"There is no liberation for one who is devoted to the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in acquiring worldly possessions;
there is none for one intent on food and clothing, nor for one who is fond of beautiful dwellings."
He should never seek alms by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology and bodily marks,
nor by teaching or by engaging in debate.

If he does not obtain [alms], he should not be despondent; if he obtains them, he should not rejoice. He should take only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, remaining free from attachment to material things.
He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three sacrificial fires,
nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food— he indeed is a knower of liberation.
In the house of a Brāhmaṇa, he should eat as much as he may obtain, both morning and evening, excluding honey and meat.
And he should not eat to satiety.
Or he may live in a village.
One who is not crooked, not deceitful, not seeking refuge [in the wrong], and not fickle.
And he should not engage in sexual intercourse with anyone.
He should be indifferent toward all living beings by avoiding both injury and favor.

The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, lack of faith, dishonesty, self-praise, disparagement of others, hypocrisy, greed, delusion, anger, and malice is held to be the duty for all stages of life.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, with a water-pot in his hand, pure, and avoiding the food of a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa does not fall from the world of Brahman—yes, from the world of Brahman.
There are six who are worthy of the guest-offering (argha).
The officiating priest, the father-in-law, the king, the paternal uncle, the Snātaka, and the maternal uncle [are to be honored].
One should offer the prepared Vaiśvadeva oblation in the domestic fire every evening and morning.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the household deities.
Having given the first portion to a *śrotriya* or to a student (*brahmacārin*), he should thereafter offer it to the ancestors.
Then he should feed the guest, each more distinguished than the last, in successive order.
Among those belonging to one's own *gṛhya* tradition, [the duties apply] to maidens, children, the elderly, the young, and women who have recently given birth.
Then [he should perform] the other domestic rites.
One should cast [the food] on the ground for dogs, Cāṇḍālas, outcasts, and crows.
One should give the remains of one's food, or that which is not the remains, to a Śūdra woman.
The remaining portion of the food, husband and wife, should eat together.
VaDhS 11.12: If, after the Vaiśvadeva offering has been set aside, a guest should arrive, one should cook again using all available means and provide him with special food.
For it is known: "A Brāhmaṇa guest enters as Vaiśvānara; therefore they bring water and food from the rain-vessels, for people know this to be the propitiation."
Having fed him, one should attend upon him.
One should follow [the teacher] as far as the boundary of the village, or until one receives permission to depart.
In the dark fortnight, after the fourth day, one should offer [the śrāddha] to the ancestors.

On the previous day, having assembled Brāhmaṇas—ascetics, householders, or virtuous men who are not of advanced age, who do not follow improper occupations, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are neither pupils nor resident students.
One should also feed disciples who possess good qualities.
One should exclude those who are naked, those with white leprosy, eunuchs, the blind, those with black teeth, those with skin diseases, and those with deformed nails.
Moreover, they also cite this:

"But if one who is learned in the mantras is disciplined, even if he possesses bodily defects that defile the company, Yama has declared him to be undefiled; he is indeed a sanctifier of the company."
At a Śrāddha, the remnants of the food must not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of nectar drip from them, which those who have not yet offered water for the dead drink.
One should not wipe away the remnants [of the food] until the sun has set;
then those who partake in the distribution of the leftovers go to inexhaustible streams of milk.
For those of one's own lineage who have died before their sacraments, this is the established rule:
Manu has declared that both the leavings of food and the scrapings from the dish are their allotted share.
One should offer the remnants that have fallen on the ground, the scattered grains, and the water used for washing to those deceased who were childless and short-lived.
Food offered to the ancestors that has been released from both hands—
during that interval, indeed, the Asuras of evil intent watch for it.
Therefore, one should not approach food with empty hands;
nor should one stand while touching either food or drink, until both have been consumed.
Two [invited] for the rite for the gods, three for the ancestral rite, or one for each of the two.
Even if he is very wealthy, he should feed [the guests] but should not be attached to an extensive display.
Hospitality, the proper place and time, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five things are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should avoid it.
Or else, one should feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning and good character, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the portion for the gods (daiva) be provided?
Having set aside a portion of all the food prepared in a vessel, [one should offer it].
Having performed [the ritual] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the *śrāddha*.
One should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (*brahmacārin*).
As long as the food remains warm, as long as they eat in silence,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been mentioned, for so long do the ancestors eat.
The qualities of the sacrificial offering should not be mentioned as long as the ancestors have not been satisfied;
once the ancestors have been satisfied, one may afterwards say that the offering is excellent.
But an ascetic who, when appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods, should consume meat,
goes to hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body.

At a *śrāddha*, three things are purifying: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, they praise three qualities in this context: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
When the sun grows dim in the eighth part of the day, that time should be known as *kutapa*; what is given to the ancestors at that time becomes inexhaustible.
If one engages in sexual intercourse after having given or eaten at a *śrāddha*,
his ancestors become consumers of that semen for an entire month.
The offspring born from such a person, having given away or consumed the paternal inheritance,
does not attain sacred knowledge and is born with a diminished lifespan.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather wait upon the son when he is born,
like birds upon a peepal tree.
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the *śrāddha* during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism."
The ancestors rejoice in a son who increases the lineage, who is diligent in the duties toward his father, and who is endowed with devotion to the gods and Brahmins.
His ancestors rejoice, just as farmers do at well-tilled fields;
for when one staying at Gayā gives food, his ancestors thereby become possessed of a true son.
One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇī, as well as on the Anvaṣṭakā day.
When the materials, the location, and the Brahmins are available, there is no restriction regarding time.
A Brāhmaṇa must necessarily establish the sacred fires.
And he should sacrifice with the New- and Full-Moon sacrifices, the Āgrayaṇa offering, the Cāturmāsya offerings, the animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice.
For this is both a constant obligation and is described as a debt.

For it is known from scripture: "A Brāhmaṇa is born burdened with three debts: to the gods by sacrifice, to the ancestors by progeny, and to the seers by the life of a student. Thus, he who has performed sacrifices, who has a son, and who has observed the life of a student is free from debt.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception;
a Rājanya in the eleventh year from conception.
A Vaiśya [should be initiated] in the twelfth year from conception.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Palāśa wood.
Or a *naiyyagrodha* staff for a Kṣatriya.
Or the staff of a Vaiśya may be made of Udumbara wood.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be equal in length to his hair.
For a Kṣatriya, it should reach up to the forehead.
The sacrificial cord of a Vaiśya reaches as far as the nose.
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass.
The bowstring is the [sacred thread] of the Kṣatriya.
The garment of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads.
The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa shall be a black antelope skin.
The Raurava [chant] is for a Kṣatriya.
For a Vaiśya, the skin of a cow or a goat [should be used].
The garment of a Brāhmaṇa shall be white and unwashed.
The garment of a Kṣatriya should be madder-red.
For a Vaiśya, [the garment] shall be yellow or made of silk.
Or, for all [of these], it may be woven cloth that is not dyed.
A Brāhmaṇa should ask for alms using a formula beginning with "bhavat."
A Kṣatriya [should address his teacher] as "bhavat" placed in the middle.
A Vaiśya [attains equality] with one whose husband is alive.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the time [for initiation] does not expire until the sixteenth year.
For a Kṣatriya, [the period extends] until the twenty-second year.
For a Vaiśya, [the period lasts] until the twenty-fourth year.
From this point forward, they become those whose Sāvitrī has been lost.
One should not initiate them, nor teach them, nor officiate sacrifices for them, nor should one have marriages performed with them.
One whose *sāvitrī* has been lost shall perform the *uddālakavrata*.

For two months he should subsist on barley-gruel; for one month on milk; for half a month on *āmikṣā*; for eight nights on clarified butter; for six nights on food obtained unasked; for three nights he should subsist on water; and for a day and night he should fast.
He should go to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
Or he should perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice; "he should sacrifice, or he should sacrifice"—so it is said.
Now, therefore, follow the observances of one who has completed his Vedic studies (the *snātaka*).
He shall not beg from anyone, except from the king and his attendants.
But when overcome by hunger, he may beg for just a little—be it prepared or unprepared food, a field, a cow, a goat or sheep, or at the very least, gold, grain, or cooked food.
But the instruction is that a *snātaka* must not suffer from hunger.
One should not live together with one who wears soiled garments.
Nor with a woman in her menses.
Nor with an unqualified woman.
One should not be a "family-to-family" practitioner.
One should not step over a stretched-out calf-rope.
One should not look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun.
One should not void urine or excrement in water.
One should not spit.

Having wrapped his head and covered the ground with grass unfit for sacrifice, he shall void urine and feces facing north during the day; at night, facing south; and during the morning and evening twilights, sitting facing north. Moreover, they quote this:
"For those who have completed their studentship (*snātaka*), there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one."
Two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water.
In water, in the hand, and in wood, as well as when declared pure by fire;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water.
For Manu Prajāpati has declared this to be the "circumambulation with fire" (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the necessary duties, one who is most skilled in the knowledge of purification should sip water for rinsing the mouth.
One should eat food facing the east.
Silently, he should swallow the entire morsel together with the thumb.
And he should not make a sound.
He should approach his own wife during her fertile period, avoiding the forbidden lunar days.
He should approach her without crossing over [her].
But he who performs sexual intercourse in the mouth of his wedded wife—
his ancestors become consumers of that semen for an entire month.
That pleasure which arises from unchaste conduct is based on a violation of dharma.
Moreover, it is known from the *Kaṭhaka*: "May those among us who are to be born tomorrow lie with their husbands"—this is the boon granted to women by Indra.
One should not climb a tree.
One should not descend into a well.
One should not blow upon the fire with the mouth.
One should not pass between the fire and a Brāhmaṇa.
Nor [should one study] while standing between two fires.
Nor [should one eat] from two Brāhmaṇas, even after having obtained their permission.
"One should not eat together with one's wife; for it is known in the Vājasaneyaka that [otherwise] the offspring will be lacking in vigor."
One should not point it out by the name "Indra’s bow."
One should say, "It is a jeweled bow."
One should avoid a seat made of *pālāśa* wood, sandals, and a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*.
One should not eat from one's lap.
One should not eat on a couch.
He should carry a staff made of bamboo.
And [he should avoid] wearing golden earrings.
One should not wear a garland outside [the body], except for one made of gold.
One should avoid assemblies and public gatherings.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The invalidation of the Vedas, the reviling of the sages,
and a lack of settled conduct in all matters— this is the destruction of the self."
One should not go to a sacrifice unrobed; if one should go, one should return by walking around it clockwise.
One should not set out on a journey when the sun is directly overhead the trees.
And one should not board a boat that is in a state of uncertainty.
One should not cross a river by means of one's arms alone.
Having risen during the latter part of the night and studied, he should not go back to sleep again.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, a Brāhmaṇa should observe certain restrictive rules; he should observe them, indeed, he should observe them.
VaDhS 13.1: Now, therefore, follows the commencement of Vedic study (svādhyāyopākarma), on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or of Prauṣṭhapada.
Having kindled the fire, he offers fried grains mixed with unhusked rice.
"To the gods, to the seers, and to the meters."
Having caused the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing and having consumed curds, they should then commence the study of the Vedic texts.
For four and a half months, or five and a half months.
From this point forward, he should study during the bright fortnights.
But one may study the Vedāṅgas at will.
Its days of non-study are as follows.
[One should not study] during the twilight or when there is thunder.
During the twilights.
In cities where there is a corpse inside or which are unfit to be proclaimed [as inhabited], [one should not enter].
If desired, [one may eat] on ground that has been soaked with cow-dung or swept clean.
At the edge of the cremation ground.
[The same applies] for one who is lying down.
[This applies] to one who performs a *śrāddha* ceremony.
Regarding this, they cite a verse of Manu:
"Having accepted fruits, water, sesame seeds, food, or whatever else may be offered at a *śrāddha*, there is no suspension of Vedic study; for Brāhmaṇas are said to have their hands as their mouths."
For one who runs, there is [the loss of merit] such as the stench of rot and so forth, as well as [falling] upon barren soil.
[The same applies] to one who has climbed a tree.
Nor [is it forbidden] on a boat or in an army.
And [one should not study] after eating while the hands are still wet.
[One should not study] when there is the sound of an arrow.
On the fourteenth day, on the new moon day, on the eighth day, and on the Aṣṭakā days.
And [the same applies] to one who has leaned against him with his feet and genitals extended.
In the presence of the teacher.
In the case of a woman who has abstained from sexual intercourse.
[He shall not eat] with a garment used for sexual intercourse that has not been washed.
At the edge of the village.
[The penance for] that which has been vomited.
[This applies] to one who has urinated or evacuated [feces].
And [the same applies] when there is the sound of the *Ṛg* and *Yajus* verses, or the sound of the *Sāman*.
[One should not study] when there is indigestion.
[The same applies] in the case of a thunderclap.
In the case of an earthquake (VaDhS 13.33).
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
In the event of a thunderous roar from the quarters, a mountain collapse, or a fall of stones, blood, or dust, the impurity lasts until the same time the next day.
In the event of a conjunction of a meteor and lightning, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
A meteor and lightning [are auspicious] as long as they are accompanied by light.
If [the moon] has not risen, the impurity lasts until the same time [on the following day].
When the teacher has died, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
In the case of the wife of a teacher, a son, or a pupil, [the impurity lasts] for one day and night.
One should rise to greet and salute the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the paternal uncle, and the maternal uncle, if they are of an age not inferior to one's own.
And those who are to be approached by the feet, as well as the wife of one's teacher.
And [he should honor] his mother and father.
He who knows how to greet [an elder] should approach him, saying, "I am so-and-so, sir."
And he who does not know [the sacred texts].

In the case of a return greeting (*pratyabhivāda*) addressed to one who has been called by name, the final vowel undergoes prolation (*plava*); a non-pragṛhya diphthong (*sandhyakṣara*) becomes *āy*, as in the example: "O Bhāu! (*bho bhāv iti*).
A father who has fallen [from his caste] is to be abandoned, but a mother does not fall because of her son.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Ten teachers are equal to one sub-teacher (upādhyāya), and a father exceeds a hundred teachers in dignity; a mother exceeds a thousand fathers in dignity."
A wife, sons, and disciples who have associated themselves with those who commit sinful deeds should be rebuked and then abandoned; he who abandons them otherwise [becomes guilty].
If one abandons a sacrificial priest or a teacher who has not performed the sacrifice or taught the Veda, he falls from his caste, except in the case of abandonment due to a grave offense.
"Those who have been born from one who has fallen [from his caste] become fallen themselves," they say, "except in the case of a woman."
For she indeed goes to another.
He should approach her as one who does not inherit property.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one’s conduct toward him is required to be as toward the teacher;
the sacred tradition (śruti) states that one should behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher himself.
A weapon, poison, and liquor are not to be accepted by a Brāhmaṇa.
Learning, wealth, age, relationship, and ritual action are grounds for respect.
Each preceding one is more serious than the following.
When meeting on a path, way must be yielded one after another to the elderly, the young, the sick, those burdened with loads, women, and those riding in vehicles.
When a king and a *snātaka* meet, way must be yielded by the king to the *snātaka*.
All [these verses] are for the bride while she is being led away.
Grass, ground, fire, water, kind speech, truthfulness, and freedom from envy—these are never lacking in the houses of the virtuous, never at any time.
VaDhS 14.1: Now, therefore, we shall describe what may and may not be eaten.
The food of a physician, a hunter, an unchaste woman, a staff-bearer, a thief, one accused of a crime, a eunuch, and an outcast is not to be eaten.

[One should not eat the food] of a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, a prisoner, one who is ill, a seller of Soma, a carpenter, a washerman, a vintner, an informer, a usurer, and a leather-cutter.
And [the same applies] to a Śūdra.
And those who bear weapons [are likewise excluded].
And he who considers his paramour to be a paramour.
And he who burns houses.
And he who does not strike down those deserving of death.
Or that which has been proclaimed by word of mouth, such as "Who shall eat? (VaDhS 14.9).
The food of a group and the food of a courtesan—these are [forbidden].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The gods do not eat the food of one who keeps a dog, nor of the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, nor of one conquered by his wife, nor of him in whose house lives a paramour."
One may accept these things: fuel, water, fodder, *kuśa* grass, parched grain, what is offered, a vehicle, a dwelling, *śapharī* fish, *priyaṅgu* seeds, garlands, perfumes, honey, and meat.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"One who wishes to support his wife for the sake of his teacher, or who intends to honor the deities and guests, may accept gifts from anyone; yet he himself shall not find satisfaction therein."
The food of a hunter who moves about with arrows is not to be avoided.

For it is known from tradition: "Agastya engaged in a hunt during a thousand-year sacrificial session (*sattra*); for him, the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) consisted of the flesh of excellent wild animals and birds, prepared at the time when no other food was available. Moreover, in this regard, they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"Alms that are offered up, brought forth, and given before one has asked—"
Prajāpati considered even those who have committed evil deeds to be worthy of being fed.
One may eat the food of a person who has faith, especially even that of a thief; but never the food of one who performs many sacrifices for others, nor of one who initiates many pupils.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, if he treats her with contempt.
The food of a physician, a hunter, a surgeon, a sinner, a eunuch,
and an unchaste woman, even if offered, is not accepted.
The leavings of one who is not one's guru are not to be eaten.
One's own leavings, and that which has been defiled by the leavings of another.
And that which has been defiled by cloth, hair, or insects.
But if he so desires, having removed hair or insects, sprinkled it with water, or scattered ashes over it, he may use that which has been commended by word.
For on this point they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by speech."
In a temple courtyard, at weddings, and at established sacrifices,
food touched by crows or dogs should not be discarded. Therefore, having removed that food, the remainder deserves purification.
For liquids, purification is by means of pouring [into water], while for solids, it is by sprinkling.
For that which has been touched by the mouth of a cat shall indeed remain pure.
Food that has stood overnight, food corrupted by its nature, food containing hair or insects, food cooked again, and raw meat or cooked meat [are forbidden].
However, he may at will consume it when it has been sprinkled with curd or ghee.
For on this matter they cite these verses concerning Prajāpati:
"If a Brahmin eats ghee or oil that has dropped from his fingernails,
Yama declared that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh."
But those fats, salts, and condiments which are given with the hand do not reach the giver; the eater consumes the sin.
One should give [the gift], but never with one's hand nor with an iron vessel.

In the case of eating garlic, onions, leeks, *gṛñjana*, *śleṣmāntaka*, the resin of trees, blood, things cut with a weapon, what has been licked by a dog or a crow, or the remnants of food left by a Śūdra, an *atikṛcchra* penance is required.
The milk of a cow in heat and the milk of a cow whose calf has not yet been born [are forbidden].
[The same applies] to cows, buffaloes, and goats that have not passed ten days [since birth].
Water within a boat is [pure].
One should avoid cakes, fried grains, *karambha*, parched barley flour, *vaṭaka* balls, oil, milk-rice, vegetables, and anything that has turned sour.
And other products made from milk and barley flour.
The porcupine, the hedgehog, the hare, the tortoise, and the monitor lizard are among the five-toed animals that may be eaten.
Among animals, camels and those with teeth only on one side are [unfit].
Or among fish, the following are edible: the ceṭa, gavaya, śiśumāra, crocodile, and crab.
Those with deformed shapes and those with serpent-like heads [are excluded].
The white ox, the gavaya, and the śarabha as well.
Likewise, those who have not been specifically designated [as guests].
And [the meat of] cows and oxen whose teeth have not yet fallen out.
But in the Vājasaneyaka it is known that the cow and the bull are fit for consumption and are pure.
But regarding the rhinoceros and the non-domestic pig, there are conflicting opinions.

And among birds, those born from eggs, those with webbed feet, the *kalaviṅka*, the *plava*, the swan (*haṃsa*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), the *bhāsa*, the crow (*kāka*), the pigeon (*pārāvata*), the osprey (*kurara*), the *sāraṅga*, the white dove (*pāṇḍukapota*), the curlew (*krauñca*), the *krakara*, the heron (*kaṅka*), the vulture (*gṛdhra*), the hawk (*śyena*), the crane (*baka*), the *balāka*, the cormorant (*madgu*), the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the *māndhāla*, the night-prowler (*naktañcara*), the woodpecker (*dārvāghāṭa*), the *cakaṭara*, the *elātaka*, the *hārītaka*, the *khañjarīṭa*, the domestic cock (*grāmyakukkuṭa*), the parrot (*śuka*), the *śārika*, the cuckoo (*kokila*), and carnivorous birds that frequent villages—these are the ones [whose meat is forbidden]. And those that frequent villages [are also forbidden]. Thus it is said.
A person arises from the union of blood and semen, having the mother and father as its cause.
In the giving away, selling, or abandoning of that [son], the mother and father have authority.
But one should neither give away nor accept an only son.
For he exists for the sake of the continuity of his ancestors.
A woman shall neither give away nor accept a son as an adopted child without the permission of her husband.

One who intends to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen and inform the king; then, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* formulas in the middle of his house, he shall adopt one who is not distant in kinship, that is, one who is closely related by blood.
And when a doubt arises, he should treat him as a distant kinsman or like a Śūdra.
For it is known from scripture that by means of one person, many may be saved.
If, after he has been adopted, a son should be born to him from his own body, the adopted son shall be entitled to a fourth part of the inheritance.
If he should not be engaged in rites for prosperity (nābhyudayika).
A violator of the Vedas, one who officiates at sacrifices for Śūdras, and those who have fallen from the ranks of the highest varṇa—these are the ones from whose vessels [the water] is poured out.

Due to the mixing of unworthy recipients, having taken up an incomplete vessel, a slave, or the son of a woman of a different caste, or a kinsman who is dissimilar or devoid of good qualities, shall strew upon it *darbha* grass with their tips pointing forward or red flowers using his left foot, and pour out the full vessel for him.
And his relatives, with their hair disheveled, should touch the one who leads him away.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, they may enter their homes at will.
From that point onward, they should not subject him to judicial proceedings.
Those who possess his qualities and practice that dharma [are called *dharmavatsa*].
But for those who have fallen [from their caste], once they have performed the penance, there is restoration.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"He who lifts [the food] first should go as if playing, as if laughing;
he who causes it to fall behind should go as if grieving, as if weeping."
For those who have killed their teacher, mother, or father, purification occurs through their favor or by being banished from them; this is their restoration.

VaDhS 15.20: Having filled a golden vessel or one made of clay from a sacred pool or from flowing water, they sprinkle him with these waters while reciting the *apohiṣṭhā* verses. {cf. 9.1: *obhūr jñātana | mahnāya ca*}. VaDhS 15.21: The entire restoration of one who has been consecrated is explained by the [ceremony] for the birth of a son; it is explained.
VaDhS 16.1 Now, the legal procedures.
The king or the minister shall perform the duties of the assembly.
When two people are disputing, he should not take the side of one against the other.
According to the seat [occupied], there is indeed an offense; for the offense is determined by the end [of the row].
He should be impartial toward all beings according to their station; for the first two castes, however, there is an offense [if he fails to do so], up to the point where knowledge is attained.
And he should protect what has been acquired.
The property of kings and minors [is protected].
[This applies] to those who have not attained legal capacity.
But when the time has arrived, that which [is prescribed] should be done.
VaDhS 16.10: Writing, witnesses, and possession are declared to be the threefold means of proof;
first, by the acquisition of wealth, the owner shall recover his property.
From roads and fields, there is likewise the right to discharge [waste] and to turn [the plough].
In the houses of the young and in other matters, [the fine shall be] three quarters of a pāda.
In a dispute concerning a house or a field, the testimony of the neighbors is decisive.
In a dispute with neighbors, documentary evidence is the means of proof.
In case of a contradiction with a counter-document, the decision shall depend on the testimony of the elders and guilds of the village or city.
Moreover, they also cite this:
paternal property, that which is purchased, that which is inherited, that which is received as a gift,
that which is acquired through sacrifice, the "tress" (veṇī), and likewise the "smoke-crested" (dhūmaśikhā) as the eighth.
In that case, [the impurity lasts] ten years for one who has eaten and then stopped eating.
Furthermore, they cite this:
"A pledge, a boundary, the property of a minor, a deposit, an open deposit, women,
the property of the king, and the wealth of one learned in the Vedas are not lost through adverse possession."
Property that has been abandoned belongs to the king.
Otherwise, the king, together with his ministers and the citizens, shall carry out the affairs of state.
Or rather, a king who is a creator (Vaśiṣṭha) is superior; he may have a retinue of vultures.
Or, surrounded by vultures, the king is better off.
One should be a vulture surrounded by a retinue of vultures; one should not be a vulture with a retinue that is not of vultures.
For indeed, faults arise from one's retinue.
And [the rite] for the destruction of theft and seizure.
Therefore, he should first ask about his family lineage.
