Now, concerning the witnesses. VaD
Witnesses should be those who are learned in the Vedas, handsome, virtuous, meritorious, and truthful.
In all [these cases], either all [the ancestors] or indeed everyone [is to be honored].
One should appoint women as witnesses for women; for the twice-born, similar twice-born men; for Śūdras, virtuous Śūdras; and for those of the lowest castes, those born of the lowest wombs.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"A gift promised in jest, that which is due to gambling, that which is due to a tavern,
and what remains after fines and taxes— the son is not liable for these debts of his father."
"Speak the truth, witness; your ancestors are hanging [in suspense]. Waiting for your word, they rise up and fall down."
Naked, shaven-headed, carrying a skull-bowl, and tormented by hunger and thirst,
he who gives false testimony shall go blind to the house of his enemy.
One kills five by lying about a maiden; one kills ten by lying about a cow;
one kills a hundred by lying about a horse; one kills a thousand by lying about a human being.
When her husband has died during a legal dispute, an expiation must be performed by the woman of the family;
for by those who bring false accusations here, their previous acquisitions are cut off.

At the time of marriage, during sexual intercourse, when life is at stake, when all one's wealth is being seized, and for the sake of a Brahmin—one may speak untruth; they say that these five types of untruth do not cause a fall from dharma.

If, for the sake of their own kin, or for the sake of wealth, or by relying on a partisan faction, they speak against what ought to be done, they cause even those ancestors of their lineage and family who reside in heaven to fall.
"They even cause [the fetus] to fall," so it is said.
When a son is born, if a father should behold his living face, he discharges his debt to him and attains immortality.
Infinite are the worlds for those who have sons; there is no world for one who has no son.

"May the devourers be childless"—this is a curse. There is also a Vedic verse: "O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality. [As it is said in the Ṛgveda: "O Jātavedas, bestow glory upon us; O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality. Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity.
Now, through a grandson of a son, one attains the world of the sun, according to the verse: "He reaches the realm of the sun."
Regarding the son of a woman who has been given in marriage, they dispute whether he belongs to the owner of the field (the husband) or to the progenitor (the biological father).
Regarding this, they cite both [traditions]:
"If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of another, those calves belong to the owner of the cows; the bull's seed was in vain."
"Be vigilant; guard this lineage so that others do not sow their seed in your field. In the hereafter, the son belongs to the progenitor; thus the sower makes his lineage fruitless.
Among many who are born of one father, if even one man has a son, the sacred tradition (*śruti*) declares that they are all possessed of a son by virtue of that one son.
If among many wives of one husband, one has a son,
the Vedic revelation states that they all become possessed of sons through that son.
There are exactly twelve sons as seen in the ancient tradition.
The first [type of son] is one begotten by oneself upon one's own consecrated wife.
In the absence of that, a son born of a wife duly appointed [to bear a child] is the second.
VaDhS 17.15: The third [type of son] is the appointed daughter (putrikā).
It is known from tradition: "A woman without brothers goes toward the ancestors of her husband; she goes back to the state of being his son."
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"I shall give you this sisterless maiden, adorned;
whatever son is born of her, let him be my son."
The fourth is the paunarbhava (the son of a remarried woman).
VaDhS 17.19: She who, having abandoned her husband from her youth and having lived with others, returns to his very household, becomes a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). VaDhS 17.20:

And she who, having abandoned a husband who is impotent, fallen, or insane, finds another husband, or [does so] when he has died, becomes a *punarbhū*. VaDhS 17.21: The son born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*) is the fifth [type of son].
They say that a son whom a woman, being uninitiated, bears in her father's house out of desire, belongs to her maternal grandfather.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If the unmarried daughter of one should obtain a son from a husband of equal status,
by that son the maternal grandfather shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth."
And the one secretly born in the house is the sixth.
"These are the heirs, the kinsmen, and the protectors from great fear," so they say. (VaDhS 17.25)
Now, among those who are neither heirs nor kinsmen, the son born of a pregnant bride (*sahoḍha*) alone is the first.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, the son born is a *sahoḍha* (one taken with the bride).
The adopted son is the second.
That which the mother and father may give.
The third [type of son] is the purchased.
That has been explained by Śunaḥśepa.
King Hariścandra indeed purchased the son of Ajīgarta Sauyavasi.
One who comes of his own accord is the fourth [type of guest].
This has been explained by Śunaḥśepa.

Śunaḥśepa, having been bound to the sacrificial post, praised the deities. Thereupon the deities released his bonds; but the officiating priests (ṛtvij) said, "Let this man be the son of me alone! He did not agree with them. They then reached an agreement, saying, "Let him be the son of whomever he desires. Viśvāmitra was his *hotṛ* priest, and thus he attained the status of his son.
The fifth is the *apaviddha* (abandoned).
One who might adopt a son who has been abandoned by his mother and father.
"The son of a Śūdra woman alone is the sixth," so they say; these are the non-heirs and non-relatives.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If none of the six preceding [relatives] should be an heir for anyone, these [others] shall take his inheritance."
Now follows the division of the inheritance among brothers.
And for those who are childless, [the rule applies] until they obtain a son.
The eldest shall take two shares.
And for a cow or a horse, it is one-tenth less than ten years.
Goats, sheep, and the house belong to the youngest brother.
Iron and tools for household protection belong to the middle son.
The women shall divide the mother's dowry among themselves.
VaDhS 17.47: If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons by a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā;
The son of a Brāhmaṇī woman shall take three shares.
The son of a Kṣatriya wife shall receive two shares.
The others shall divide [the estate] equally.
And he by whom any of these [sons] has been begotten by himself shall take two shares.
But those who have entered other stages of life are not entitled to a share.
And those who are impotent, insane, or outcasts.
The maintenance of those who are impotent or insane [is the duty of their kin].
The wife of a deceased man shall observe a vow for six months, eating food that is neither pungent nor salty, and sleeping on the ground.

After six months have passed, having bathed and offered the *śrāddha* for her husband, and having assembled those related by learning, occupation, teacher, or birth, the father or brother shall arrange the *niyoga*.
He should not, however, appoint a woman who is insane, lacking self-control, or diseased.
Even if she is older [in age].
Sixteen years.
Unless he should be afflicted by illness.
During the *muhūrta* sacred to Prajāpati, he should behave toward her as if she were his wife, except for laughing with her, harshness of speech, and physical violence.
In matters of food, clothing, bathing, and the application of unguents, she should take the initiative.
Regarding one born of a woman not authorized [to bear a son], they say that the son belongs to the progenitor.
If there should be two appointed [officiants], it should be so.
There is no appointment [of a widow] out of greed for the inheritance.
Some say that one should also appoint him after instructing him in an expiation.
A maiden who has reached puberty shall wait for three years.
After three years, she should find a suitable husband.
Moreover, they also cite this: "If,
through the father's negligence, a girl here is given away after she has passed the proper age,
she destroys the giver while waiting, like an excessive fee for a teacher paid late."
Out of fear that her daughter might reach puberty, the father should give away the maiden while she is still pre-pubertal;
for if she remains until she has reached her menses, the fault falls upon the father.

As many menstrual periods as touch a maiden who, being of equal status and desirous [of marriage], is being solicited by suitors—for that many embryos have been killed by those two, the mother and the father; such is the declaration of the Dharma.
If the bridegroom should die first after the girl has been given by water and word,
but she has not yet been led away by the sacred mantras, she belongs to the father alone.

If a maiden has been forcibly abducted, provided she has not been consecrated with the sacred mantras, she should be given to another according to the prescribed rule; for she remains just as a maiden as before.
If the husband dies while the young woman has been consecrated solely by the sacred mantras,
she, provided her virginity remains intact, deserves to undergo the marriage rite once again.
A wife whose husband has gone abroad shall wait for five years.
After five years, she should go to her husband's presence.
If she is not inclined toward living abroad for the sake of dharma or wealth, she should behave as if she were already dead.

Thus, for a Brāhmaṇī woman, there are five [years of impurity] after giving birth and four after not giving birth; for a Rājanyā, five after giving birth and three after not giving birth; for a Vaiśyā, four after giving birth and two after not giving birth; and for a Śūdrā, three after giving birth and one after not giving birth.
From this point forward, among those who share the same purpose, birth, funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), water-offering (udaka), and lineage (gotra), each preceding one is more venerable than the next.
But indeed, while a man of noble birth is available, she must not go to another.
If among his six ancestors there should be no heir whatsoever, his *sapiṇḍas* or those who stand in the place of sons shall divide his wealth.
In the absence of these, the teacher and the pupil shall take them.
In the absence of those two, the king shall take it.
But the king shall not take [the property] of a Brāhmaṇa.
But the property of a Brahmin is terrible poison.
They say that poison is not truly poison; the property of a Brahmin is called poison.
Poison kills only a single person, but the property of a Brahmin destroys sons and grandsons.
He should bestow [it] upon those who are learned in the three Vedas and are virtuous; he should bestow it. Thus [it is said].
They say that one born of a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother becomes a Caṇḍāla.
From a Kṣatriya woman, a Vaiṇa is born.
From a Vaiśya woman, an Antyāvasāyin is born.
They say that one born of a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is a Rāmaka.
From a Kṣatriya woman [by a Śūdra father], a Pulkasa is born.
They say that one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother becomes a Sūta.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Whosoever are born in secret and possess the qualities of those born in the inverse order of castes—
one should recognize them by their actions, due to their deviation from virtuous conduct."
Those born from women one, two, or three classes lower than the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya fathers become Ambaṣṭhas, Ugras, and Niṣādas respectively.
Among Śūdras, the Pāraśava is [the son born of a wife of the same caste].
Regarding the Pāraśava, they say that even while still alive, he is as good as a corpse.
"Some say that those who are Śūdras are this cremation ground."
Therefore, one should not study in the vicinity of a Śūdra.
Moreover, they cite these verses sung by Yama:
"This cemetery is manifest before our eyes—those Śūdras who act wickedly.
Therefore, one must never study in the vicinity of a Śūdra."
One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor what has been prepared for sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharma, nor prescribe a vow for him.

"He who teaches him the Dharma and he who instructs him in his vow—both of them enter together with him into a terrible, unending darkness. (VaDhS 18.15) "He in whose wound an insect might ever arise... (VaDhS 18.16)
One is purified by the Prājāpatya penance; the sacrificial fee consists of gold, a cow, or a garment.
Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a beautiful woman.
A woman who is dark-complexioned is for pleasure alone, not for dharma; she is for pleasure alone, not for dharma.
The specific duty of a king is the protection of all beings; his success comes from the performance of that duty.

The learned say that this sacrificial session (*sattram*) lasts from old age until death, during which fear and compassion are abandoned. Therefore, one should appoint a domestic priest for the obligatory rites of the householder stage.
It is known from scripture: "The kingdom prospers when the Brahmapurohita sacrifice is performed."
Because he protects both.
And also because of incapacity.
Having thoroughly entered into all these local, regional, caste, and family customs, the king shall establish the four social orders in their respective duties.
If they act improperly toward them, he should inflict punishment.
But the punishment for injury and verbal abuse must be determined according to the specific circumstances of place, time, social duty, age, learning, and station in life.
On account of traditional authority and because it is observed.
One should not harm trees that bear flowers and fruit.
And he may kill [an animal] for the purpose of providing the means for cultivation.
And the measures and weights used for the requirements of the householder's state shall be kept protected.
There is no concealment of one's own purposes through deception.
The value of the measure should not be taken for one's own personal use.
In the case of the two great festivals (Mahāmahas), the road [should be cleared] from the site.
In a journey, a force consisting of ten draft animals shall be double the effective capacity.
There should be water-stalls at every [stage].
And he should cause men of less than one hundred years of age to be sacrificed.
Women should not be barren.
A hand, a pebble, a māṣa bean, water from the middle of a *śara* reed, and a foot [as measures of value] should be equivalent to one *kārṣāpaṇa*.
A tree that has no water nearby should be plundered.

A person who does not know the syllable *oṃ*, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), a king’s man, and those who are helpless, wandering mendicants, children, the elderly, and young women [are exempt from fines].
Girls who have already gone [to their husbands] and women whose husbands are maintained by others [are not eligible].
With his two arms, he should give a hundredfold more than that.
The burning of rivers, thickets, and forests, as well as the utilization of mountains, shall be free of taxes.
Or those who live off that [property] shall pay it.
But he should cause the one who provided the bride-price to be brought back every month.
And when the king has died, one should give what is incidental [to the occasion].
By this, the conduct toward one's mother is explained.
The king shall maintain the paternal uncle and the maternal uncle of the queen.
And [he should offer] to his relatives and others as well.
The wives of the king shall receive food and clothing.
Or they may go forth [into the religious life] even against their will.
The king shall maintain those who are impotent or insane.
Because the inheritance goes to him.
Regarding the toll, they also cite this verse of Manu:
"There is no toll on a broken kārṣāpaṇa coin, nor on one engaged in a craft, nor on an infant, nor on a messenger;
nor on what is obtained as alms, nor on the remnants of what was stolen, nor on a Śrotriya, nor on a wandering ascetic, nor at a sacrifice."
A thief does not incur guilt if he enters [the house] unobserved.
One who bears arms, one who was seized together with the woman, one who has wounds, or according to some, one who has been designated [as her husband].
Upon releasing one who deserves punishment, the king shall fast for one night.
The domestic priest shall observe a fast for three nights.
The domestic priest shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for failing to punish one who deserves punishment.
The king [observes] a three-night [period of impurity].
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The killer of an embryo transfers his guilt to the one who eats his food; an unfaithful wife transfers hers to her husband;
a pupil and a sacrificer transfer theirs to their teacher; and a thief transfers his guilt to the king."
But men who have committed sins and have been punished by kings go to heaven stainless, just like virtuous people who have performed meritorious deeds.
The sin overtakes the king who releases a guilty man; but if the king should have him executed, he destroys the evil deed through righteousness.
For kings, immediate purification is prescribed in the case of urgent business;
likewise, it is not so in non-urgent matters, for in this case, time alone is the determining factor.
Regarding this, they cite a verse sung by Yama:
"There is no fault today for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor for those performing long sacrificial sessions;
for they are ever become Brahman, seated in the station of Indra."
"For they are indeed always [present]," so it is said.
There is an expiation for an offense committed unintentionally.
Some [hold that it is a sin] even when committed intentionally.
The teacher is the instructor for those who possess self-control; the king is the instructor for the wicked;
and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, is the instructor for those whose sins are concealed.
And in that case, if he has been overtaken by sunrise while still impure, he should remain standing during the day and mutter the Sāvitrī.
Thus he remained through the night, having turned away from the sun.
One with deformed nails or black teeth, however, shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights.
One who has been superseded by a younger brother, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, may enter the household and marry that very woman.
Now, one who has superseded a younger brother by marriage shall perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penances, give [the property] to that brother, and then marry again, taking her as his wife.
The husband of an *agredidhiṣū* shall perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance, marry her, and then enter into household life.
The husband of a *didhiṣū* shall perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances, give [the girl] back to him, and then marry again.
We shall explain the slayer of a hero later on.
One who has forsaken the Veda shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then receive the Veda again from his teacher.

One who has violated the teacher’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, hold them in his cupped hands, and walk facing south; wherever he meets with an obstacle, there he shall remain until his body perishes.
"Or, having been stripped of his clothes and smeared with clarified butter, he should embrace a red-hot iron image; it is known from tradition that he becomes purified by death."
And the same applies toward the wife of a teacher’s son or a pupil.

Having had sexual intercourse with a woman of high birth, a female friend, the wife of a teacher, one who has lost her caste, or an outcaste woman, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one quarter of a year.
VaDhS 20.17: This same [penance] applies to eating the food of a Cāṇḍāla or an outcast; after that, there is a second initiation, but with the exclusion of shaving and the other [rites].
Regarding this, they cite a verse from the *Mānava*:
"Shaving, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows—
these are indeed discontinued upon the performance of the rite of re-initiation."

If one intentionally drinks intoxicating liquor other than *asurā* or *surā*, or drinks them unintentionally, one must perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances respectively, consume clarified butter, and undergo the rite of re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*).
And likewise in the case of consuming urine, feces, or semen.
If any twice-born man should drink water that has stood in a vessel for liquor, he becomes pure after three nights by drinking water from the Udumbara, Bilva, and Palāśa trees.
But in the case of repeated consumption of *surā*, a twice-born man shall drink it when it is red-hot like fire; he becomes purified through death.
We shall now declare the penance for the slayer of a learned Brāhmaṇa (bhrūṇahan). One becomes a bhrūṇahan by killing a Brāhmaṇa or an embryo whose sex is unknown.

"For embryos are indeed unknown as to whether they will become males; therefore, one offers oblations with rites intended for males. Having kindled the fire, the killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan) should offer these [oblations].

"I offer the body hairs to Death; through the body hairs, I clothe Death"—this is the first [offering]. "I offer the skin to Death; through the skin, I clothe Death"—this is the second. "I offer the blood to Death; through the blood, I clothe Death"—this is the third. "I offer the flesh to Death; through the flesh, I clothe Death"—this is the fourth. "I offer the sinews to Death; through the sinews, I clothe Death"—this is the fifth.

"I offer fat to Death; with fat I clothe Death"—this is the sixth [offering]. "I offer bones to Death; with bones I clothe Death"—this is the seventh. "I offer marrow to Death; with marrow I clothe Death"—this is the eighth.
For the sake of the king or for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, one should cause oneself to be slain facing the enemy in battle.
It is known from tradition that one who has failed three times, even if unconquered [in battle], becomes purified.
"For when a sin is declared, it becomes less," so it is said.
Moreover, they cite this:
"If one says of an outcast, 'He is an outcast,' or of a thief, 'He is a thief,' by such speech one incurs an equal guilt; if the statement is false, one incurs double the guilt."
Likewise, having killed a Kṣatriya woman, one should perform this penance for eight years.
A Vaiśya [should wait] six [days].
For a Śūdra, three [years].
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī, or having killed a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a Soma sacrifice;
We shall now discuss the *ātreyī*. They call a woman who has bathed after her menses and is in her fertile period an *ātreyī*.
For in this case, it is said: "the offspring yet to come."
In the case of harming a Kṣatriya who is not an Ātreyī woman, [the penance is] as prescribed.
In the case of injury to a Vaiśya woman by a Kṣatriya.
In the case of injury to a Śūdra committed by a Vaiśya woman, [the penance is as follows].
Having killed a Śūdra woman, [one must perform penance] for one year.

VaDhS 20.41: Upon stealing gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one should dishevel his hair, run toward the king, and say, "I am a thief, sir; may your majesty punish me. The king should give him a weapon made of Udumbara wood, with which he should take his own life; by death, he becomes purified—so it is known. VaDhS 20.42: Or, having removed all clothing and being smeared with clarified butter, he should burn himself with a fire of cow-dung, starting from the feet; by death, he becomes purified—so it is known.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"Listen to how the body of those who died long ago due to evil and various kinds of actions becomes [reconstituted] when they have again obtained a body."

A thief becomes one with deformed nails; a killer of a Brahmin becomes one with white leprosy; a drinker of spirituous liquor has black teeth; and one who violates the teacher’s bed suffers from skin disease.

And in the case of association with outcasts—whether through Vedic study or through marriage—one must abandon those portions of the inheritance received from them, and one must not live together with them.
It is known from tradition that by going toward the northern direction and studying the Saṃhitā while fasting, one becomes purified.
Moreover, they cite this:
"By mortification of the body, by austerity, and by study, the doer of evil is released from evil; and by giving, he is likewise liberated."
Thus it is known; thus it is known.

If a Śūdra should have sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in vīraṇa grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the Brāhmaṇa woman's head to be shaved and having smeared her all over with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a black donkey and cause her to be paraded along the high road. Thus she becomes purified—so it is known.

If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red darbha grass and cast him into the fire; having caused the shaving of the Brāhmaṇa woman’s head and having anointed her all over with clarified butter, one should place her naked upon a bull and a donkey and cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known.

If a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed-leaves, drench him in clarified butter, cast him into the fire, place the naked woman upon a white donkey, and cause her to be led along the high road; thus she becomes purified—so it is known.
In this same way, a Vaiśya [begets] on a Rājanyā woman.
And a Śūdra [is the son] of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman.

VaDhS 21.6: In the case of transgression against her husband through the mind, she should eat barley-gruel or rice with milk for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, while submerged in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the *sāvitrī* mantra for each head [of the mantra]. It is known from tradition that she thus becomes purified. VaDhS 21.7: In the case of verbal intimacy, having performed this same penance for one month, after the month she should, while submerged in water, offer oblations with four sets of one hundred and eight repetitions of the *sāvitrī* mantra for each head [of the mantra]. It is known from tradition that she thus becomes purified.

In the case of sexual intercourse, however, one should wear a cloth soaked in ghee for a year and sleep on a bed of kusha grass in a pit filled with cow dung; after a year has passed, one should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra while submerged in water, using one's own head as the ladle; thus it is known that she becomes purified.
In sexual intercourse and in visiting sacred fords, however, he turns away from his religious duties.
But four [wives] must be abandoned: one who has gone to a pupil, one who has gone to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has approached a degraded man.
The gods do not lead that Brahmin woman who drinks liquor to the world of her husband; having exhausted her merit, she wanders right here [in this world], becoming a water-snail or a pearl-oyster.
The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; the others [wives of lower castes] are not.
Those women who have intercourse in the reverse order [of castes] shall perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.

For those women who are devoted to their husbands, who maintain the household, who are true to their vows, and who are pure in their conduct, their worlds are equal to those of their husbands; but for those who are unchaste, their worlds are like those of jackals.
Half of the body of that man falls [from grace] whose wife drinks liquor;
for one whose half-body has fallen, no expiation is prescribed.
If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally approach the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he must perform the Kṛcchra penance if she has not ceased her religious duties, and the Atikṛcchra penance if she has ceased them.
The same applies for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
If he should kill a cow, he shall remain for six months wrapped in her wet hide, performing either the Kṛcchra or the Taptakṛcchra penance.
The rule for these two is as follows.
He eats during the day for three days, and indeed eats at night for another three days;
he observes the vow of not asking for food for three days, and does not eat for three days—this is the Kṛcchra penance.
For three days he should drink warm water; for three days he should drink warm milk;
having drunk warm ghee for three days, he should subsist on air for the final three days.
Thus ends the *taptakṛcchra* penance according to VaDhS 21.21.
And one should give a bull and a cow.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"In ancient times there were only three diseases: envy, fasting, and old age.
By killing a *pṛṣadvastra* [spotted] goat, one may bring back ninety-eight [years of life]."
Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a snake, a frog, or a rat, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some small gift.
But having killed a heap of boneless creatures as large as a cow, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and give some small gift.
But for those with bones, however, it is one [day] for each.
He who should cast away the sacred fires shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then have them re-established.
If one persists in falsehood toward a teacher, he should bathe with his clothes on and propitiate the teacher; it is traditionally taught that through the teacher's favor, he becomes purified.
An atheist, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism.
But for one who lives as an atheist, the atikṛcchra penance is prescribed.
By this, the seller of Soma is explained.
A forest-dweller who has violated his initiation vow shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then increase the growth of the great thicket.

Beggars (bhikṣukas) shall follow the rules of forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas) regarding the increase of the Soma-plant during its growth, as well as the refinement according to their own scriptures; and [the same applies to] the refinement according to their own scriptures.

Now, indeed, this man gives false testimony, or he officiates at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed, or he accepts what should not be accepted, or he eats what is unfit to be eaten, or he practices what should not be practiced.
Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation, or should one not?"
"One should not do so," they say.
"For indeed, action is not exhausted."
Therefore, one should simply perform [the rite], because of the evidence of the revealed scripture (śruti).
"He who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice overcomes all evil and overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.
And one who has been accused [of such a crime] should perform the Gosava and the Agniṣṭut sacrifices.
The means of expiation for that are recitation, austerity, burnt offerings, fasting, and giving gifts.

The Upaniṣads, the beginnings of the Vedas, the Vedāntas, all the Vedic meters, the Saṃhitās, the Madhu-hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Atharvaśiras, the Rudras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Rājana and Rauhiṇa Sāmans, the Kūṣmāṇḍa hymns, the Pāvamānī verses, and the Sāvitrī—these are the purifiers.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"By performing the Vaiśvānarī, the Vrātapatī, and likewise the Pavitreṣṭi sacrifice once during the [proper] season, one purifies ten generations of one's lineage."
According to the rule for fasting, the following are purifying: subsisting on milk, eating fruits, consuming a handful of barley-gruel, swallowing gold, and drinking soma.
All mountains, all rivers, sacred lakes, holy fords, dwellings of sages, cow-pens, and sacred enclosures—these are the [auspicious] places.
The years, the months, twenty-four days, twelve days, six days, three days, and a day and night—these are the periods of time.
In the absence of a specific injunction, these very [rites] may be performed optionally.
In cases of heavy sins, the penances are heavy; in cases of light sins, they are light.
The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and the Cāndrāyaṇa constitute the universal penance; this is the universal penance.
If a student of sacred knowledge should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice an ass as an animal dedicated to the Rakṣas deities in a common fire at a crossroads in the forest.
Or he should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) to Nirṛti.
For him, he should offer oblations with: "To Desire, svāhā! To the one who desires desire, svāhā! To Nirṛti, svāhā! To the deities of the Rākṣasas, svāhā!"
This same [penance] applies for the intentional emission of semen during the day while dreaming, or during other observances prior to the *samāvartana*.
In the case of sexual intercourse with an animal, one should give a white bull as a gift.
Having approached a cow, the guilt is explained as being equal to that of killing a Śūdra.
For a religious student (brahmacārin) performing the funeral rites for a corpse, there is a cessation of his vows.
Except in the case of his mother and father.
If he should fall ill, he may at will eat all the remains of his teacher's food for the sake of medicine.
VaDhS 23.10: If one commissioned by his teacher should die, the teacher shall perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
VaDhS 23.11: If a student (*brahmacārī*) should eat meat, or food that is the leavings of another, he shall perform a twelve-night *kṛcchra* and then complete the remainder of his vow.
And the same applies to eating at a śrāddha or during periods of ritual impurity due to birth or death.
In the Vājasaneyaka it is known: "Honey that is obtained unintentionally does not cause defilement."
If one who has attempted suicide is accused [of a grave crime], the performance of the funeral rites for his sapinda relatives is interrupted.
He who destroys himself by means of wood, water, clods of earth, stones, weapons, poison, or ropes becomes a self-killer (ātmahā).
Moreover, they also cite this:
"If a twice-born man, out of affection, should perform the funeral rites for one who has committed suicide,
he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra penance."
We shall explain the Cāndrāyaṇa penance further on.
In the case of a resolve to commit suicide, [the penance lasts] for three nights.

VaDhS 23.19: One who attempts suicide while still alive shall perform a *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights; he shall fast for three nights, always wear an oily garment, restrain his breaths within himself, and recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times.
VaDhS 23.20: Or else, according to this same procedure, he may recite the *gāyatrī*.
Or alternatively, having kindled the fire, he should offer clarified butter with the Kūṣmāṇḍa verses.
And whatever else besides the great sins (mahāpātaka) there may be, all that is purified by this.

Furthermore, having mentally contemplated evil, one should sip water while reciting, "May Agni and Manyu [purify me]," and then mutter the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*, or recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn.
Having touched a human bone that is still moist, there is impurity for three nights.
But if it is not oily, [the penance lasts] for one day and night.
And the same applies when following a corpse.
If one enters while those who are studying are engaged in their lesson, there shall be a fast of one day and night.
For three nights there shall be ritual sprinkling and mutual dwelling apart.
For dogs, cats, mongooses, and swift-moving creatures, the period of impurity lasts one day and night.

For eating the flesh of a dog, a cock, a village pig, a heron, a vulture, a kite, a pigeon, a human, a crow, or an owl, there shall be a fast for seven nights, becoming free of excrement, consuming clarified butter, and undergoing the purificatory rite again.
But a Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows into the ocean and performed one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), becomes pure after consuming clarified butter.
It is known from tradition that upon touching a dog, a *caṇḍāla*, or an outcaste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing with one's clothes on.
Upon hearing the cry of an outcaste or a *caṇḍāla*, they shall remain silent and fasting for three nights.
It is known from tradition that those who practice this up to ten thousand times become purified.

By this very same [rule], those who teach what is censurable and those who perform sacrifices for such persons are explained; it is known that they become pure by abandoning the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
By this very [rule], the accused person is explained.

In the case of killing an embryo, one should subsist on water for twelve nights and fast for twelve nights. Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a crime entailing loss of caste or of a lesser crime, one should subsist on water for a month and repeat the Śuddhavatī verses.
Or he should go to the final purificatory bath of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By this very same [rule], sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is explained.
Now follows another general rule for the performance of the Kṛcchra penance in its expanded form.
One day [of fasting] in the morning, one day at night, and one day [of fasting] without soliciting food;
one day of the *parāka* penance—this constitutes one cycle, and two further cycles in this manner [make up the full penance].
For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, Manu, the best among the upholders of dharma,
prescribed the *śiśukṛcchra* penance in this manner for children, the elderly, and the sick.
Now follows the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
increasing the number of morsels as one eats, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
For thus, at the beginning of the bright fortnight, he should eat one morsel;
eating with a reduction of morsels, he should complete the remainder of the fortnight.
In this very situation, he should sing the Sāman chants, or else mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
This is the Cāndrāyaṇa rite for a month, a purifier praised by the seers;
it is prescribed as the expiation for all those [offenses] not specifically mentioned.
"It is prescribed," so it is said.
Now follows the Atikṛcchra penance.

Eating only in the morning for three days, likewise in the evening for three days, and eating only what is unasked for for three days—this is the *parāka* penance; this constitutes the *kṛcchra*. Eating only as much as one can take in a single mouthful, as described previously, is the *atikṛcchra*.
Subsisting on water for one day is the *kṛcchra*; that same [practice] repeated for three days is the *kṛchrātikṛcchra*.
These are the forms of the vows for the *kṛcchra* penances.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha says: He should have his beard and hair shaved, except for the eyebrows, the eyelashes, and the topknot; having clipped his nails, wearing a single garment, eating blameless food [obtained by begging once], bathing three times a day, carrying a staff and a water-pot, avoiding conversation with women and Śūdras, and habituated to standing during the day and sitting at night—this is the rule.
He should not give this Dharmaśāstra to one who is not his son, nor to one who is not his disciple, nor to one who has not lived with him for a year.
The sacrificial fee is a thousand [cows], with a bull as the eleventh, or it is the favor of the teacher; indeed, it is the favor of the teacher.
I shall describe in its entirety the purification for great sins whose faults have not been publicly proclaimed, as well as for all minor offenses.
For one who has maintained the sacred fires, who is disciplined, aged, or learned, the penance prescribed in secret applies; for other people, that which was stated previously applies.
Those who are constantly disciplined through breath-control, purificatory rites, gifts, burnt offerings, and likewise recitations, are liberated from their transgressions; of this there is no doubt.
With purifying grass in hand, seated, one should practice the daily Veda-recitation, as well as breath-control exercises, the purifiers, the Vyāhṛtis, and the Praṇava.
Constantly engaged and repeatedly performing breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
let him practice supreme austerity from the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails.
From cessation wind is born; from wind, indeed, fire is born;
from heat water is then born; thus, through these three, one becomes pure within.

Neither by intense austerity, nor by Vedic study, nor by sacrifice are the twice-born able to attain that goal which they reach through yoga. Through yoga, knowledge is attained; yoga is the defining characteristic of dharma.
Yoga is the supreme austerity; therefore, one should always remain disciplined in it.
One should be constantly engaged with the *praṇava* and the seven *vyāhṛtis*, as well as with the three-footed *gāyatrī*; for such a person, no fear exists anywhere.
From the *praṇava* proceed the Vedas, and they are established within the *praṇava*;
the *praṇava* is the entirety of speech. Therefore, one should practice the *praṇava*.
The single syllable is known as the supreme Brahman, the highest purifier.
When a mixture of all sins has occurred,
the great purification is the recitation of the Sāvitrī ten thousand times.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.
"He is called [thus]," it is said.
He who, unwearied, performs three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the rule,
destroys at that very moment the sin committed during a day and night.
Whatever sin has been committed during the day by deed, thought, or word, one sitting for the evening twilight rite dispels it through breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin has been committed during the night by deed, thought, or word,
one dispels it by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) upon rising for the morning twilight devotion.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the praṇava,
performed day after day, purify even the slayer of a learned Brahmin within a month.

Having recited the *Kautsa* hymn and this three-verse section of the *Vāsiṣṭha*—namely, "O Agni, drive away our sin with your light; shine forth wealth upon us" (RV 1.97.1) and "The wise Vasiṣṭhas, the first singers, have awakened the Dawn with their hymns and songs" (RV 7.80.1)—even a drinker of *surā* is purified by the *Māhitra* hymn and the *Śuddhavatī* verses.
By reciting the Asyavāmīya and the Śivasankalpa even once,
one becomes stainless in an instant, even after having stolen gold.
Having repeated the *haviṣyantīya* hymn, the triplet beginning with "na tam aṃhaḥ" (RV 10.126.1–3),
and having recited the *puruṣasūkta*, one who has violated the teacher’s bed is liberated from that sin.
Alternatively, while submerged in water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
Manu has declared that it is equal to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a horse sacrifice.
The sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (*ārambhayajña*);
that which is performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*) is a hundred times superior, and that which is performed mentally (*mānasa*) is remembered as being a thousand times superior.
Those four *pākayajñas* together with the *vidhiyajñas*—
all of them are not worth even a sixteenth part of the *japayajña*.
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
He may perform other rites or he may not; one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.

Sins do not dwell with those who recite prayers, those who perform fire-sacrifices, those who practice meditation, those who reside at sacred fords, and those who have performed ritual ablutions accompanied by head-vows.
Just as fire, fanned by the wind and fed with oblations, blazes up,
even so a Brahmin who is constantly devoted to the recitation of prayers shines brightly.
For those who constantly study their own sacred texts, who are ever self-restrained,
and who likewise recite prayers and offer oblations, no downfall exists.
One desiring purification, even if situated in all manner of sins, should employ the divine [Gāyatrī] mantra consisting of a thousand at most, a hundred in the middle, and ten at the least.
A Kṣatriya should overcome his own adversity through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through recitations and burnt offerings.
Just as horses would be without a chariot, or as a chariot would be without horses; so it is with these means.
Thus, austerity is useless for one who lacks knowledge, and knowledge is likewise useless for one who lacks austerity.
Just as food combined with honey, or honey combined with food,
so too are austerity and knowledge, when united, a great remedy.
Sin does not attach itself even to a Brāhmaṇa who is constantly engaged in sinful deeds, provided he is endowed with learning and austerity and is devoted to the recitation of sacred texts.
"Sin does not attach itself," so it is said.
If even more than a hundred forbidden acts have been committed, yet the Veda is retained in memory,
the fire of that Veda consumes them all, just as fire consumes fuel.
Just as a fire that has gained strength burns even moist trees,
so does the fire of Vedic knowledge burn away the defects of one's own actions.
Even having slain these worlds and consuming [their wealth] from here and there,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.
One should not take delight in sinful actions by relying on the power of the Veda;
for it is only through ignorance and negligence that one is consumed by the consequences of action, and not otherwise.
The sage who performs austerities in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits,
and he who studies even a single verse of the Rigveda— these two are equal.
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will strike me."
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability and the performance of the sequence of the great sacrifices quickly destroy all sins, even those born of the most heinous crimes (mahāpātaka).
One should perform, without sloth, one's own duties as prescribed by the Veda;
for by performing them to the best of one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
From officiating at sacrifices for others, from teaching, from matrimonial alliance, and likewise from accepting improper gifts—
no fault shall accrue to Brahmins [in these acts], for they are equal to fire and the sun.
When a doubt has arisen concerning whether food is fit to be eaten or unfit to be eaten, I shall declare the purification of food; listen to me as I speak it.
A Brāhmaṇa should drink the pungent and saltless *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*,
and for three nights he should drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with milk.
Having boiled the leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, as well as *kuśa* grass, lotuses, and *udumbara* fruits, one should drink the water; thus one becomes pure in three nights.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a one-night fast, would purify even an outcaste dog-eater (*śvapāka*).
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise ghee—
if one subsists on these for five nights, one is purified by the *pañcagavya*.
One who consumes barley according to the prescribed rule becomes purified by direct perception itself;
when the state [of the recipient] is pure, they are pure, but if it is impure, they remain stained with passion.
Three morning meals of sacrificial food (haviṣya), and likewise three evening meals;
in the same way, there should be [three meals] of unsolicited food—this constitutes a three-day fast.
Now, if he is in haste to perform [the penance], he should subsist on air during the day;
having fasted at night by a body of water, that is equal to the Prājāpatya penance.
But by reciting the Sāvitrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is released from all sins, provided that one is not a slayer of a Brahmin.
Indeed, whether one is a thief, a drinker of spirituous liquor, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed,
by merely studying this treatise on Dharma, he is liberated from all sins.
For misfortunes, ill-performed rites, and likewise for great sins,
the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances are the destroyers of all evil.
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
on the new moon day one should not eat at all—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"Thus is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa."
A woman is not defiled by an adulterer, nor a Brahmin by his Vedic rites;
water is not defiled by urine or feces, nor fire by the act of burning.
Whether she has herself consented, or has been driven away,
or has been enjoyed by force, or has even fallen into the hands of thieves;
A woman who has been defiled must not be abandoned; her abandonment is not ordained. She should wait for her period; she becomes pure through the menstrual flow.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their evil deeds.
Formerly, women were enjoyed by the gods—by Soma, Gandharva, and Agni;
they go to men afterwards, and thus they are not tainted according to dharma. To them, Soma gave purity, and Gandharva taught speech.
And because fire makes everything pure, women are therefore free from blemish.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three heinous crimes for women in this world:
the murder of her husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus.
A calf is pure when causing milk to flow; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual intercourse; and a dog is pure when seizing game.

Goats and horses are pure in their mouths; cows are pure in every part. (VaDhS 28.9) Hereafter, I shall declare all the purifiers of the Vedas, by the recitation and burnt offerings of which people are purified; there is no doubt in this matter. (VaDhS 28.10)
The Aghamarṣaṇa, the Devakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, the Taratsamās,
the Kūṣmāṇḍas, the Pāvamānīs, and the Durgā-sāvitrī.
The *atiṣaṅgas*, the *padastobhas*, the *sāmans*, and likewise the *vyāhṛtis*; the *bhāruṇḍa* *sāmans*, as well as the *gāyatra* and the *raivata*.
The Puruṣavrata, the Bhāsa, and likewise the Devavratas; the Abliṅga, the Bārhaspatya, the Vāksūkta, and the Madhvṛcas.
The Śatarudriya, the Atharvaśiras, the Triṣuparṇa, the Mahāvrata, the Gosūkta,
the Aśvasūkta, and the two Sāmans, the Śuddha and the Aśuddhi.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agner Vrata, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these, when recited, purify living beings; if one so desires, one obtains the memory of former births.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are the daughters of the Sun.
He who gives gold, a cow, and land shall enjoy infinite fruit.
A cow, a horse, gold, or land,
if given to a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas and whose hands are empty of sacred knowledge, bring ruin upon the donor.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, however, one should [feed] seven or five Brāhmaṇas with black sesame seeds or others, mixed with honey.
"May the Lord of Dharma be pleased"—or whatever else dwells in one's mind;
by this, the sin committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment.
Having fashioned a black antelope with its hooves intact and a golden navel,
and having covered it with sesame seeds, listen to the fruit of the merit for him who should give it as a gift.
By him, the earth—with its gold mines, its mountains, forests, and groves, and its four faces—is as good as given; of this there is no doubt.
"Having placed sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin, he who gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds. (VaDhS 28.22)
"He overcomes all evil deeds. Thus it is said.
Through giving, one obtains all desires.
A celibate student (brahmacārī) becomes long-lived and handsome.
One who does not harm living beings attains heaven.
By entering the fire, one attains the world of Brahman.
Through observing silence, one attains good fortune.
The lord of the *nāgas* [is the deity] because of his dwelling in the water.
Free from disease and with his treasury exhausted.
The giver of water prospers in all his desires.
The giver of food becomes one with clear vision and a retentive memory.
One who is wise and a giver of safety from all quarters.
In the case of a carriage drawn by oxen, one should perform ablutions at all sacred bathing places.
By the gift of a bed and a seat, one attains sovereignty over the inner apartments.
From the gift of an umbrella, one obtains a house.
One who bestows a house attains a city.
The giver of shoes obtains a vehicle. Furthermore, they also cite this:
"Whatever sin a man afflicted by his livelihood commits..."
One is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
One should give a full water-pot to a Brahmin for the purpose of sipping;
having attained supreme satisfaction after death, he is born again as a drinker of Soma.
The gift of thousands of oxen, capable of bearing the yoke,
given according to rule to a worthy recipient, is equal to the gift of a daughter in marriage.
They say there are three supreme gifts: cows, land, and the *sarasvatī* (the Veda).
Indeed, among all gifts, the gift of knowledge is the supreme gift; it is even greater than those.
He who, being free from malice and possessing knowledge, follows this code of conduct, attains the gift of the ultimate fruit— the liberation from saṃsāra.
One who is faithful, pure, and self-controlled should either uphold or even hear this;
having abandoned all sins, he is glorified in the highest heaven.
"He is honored on the back of the vault of heaven."
Practice dharma, not adharma; speak the truth, not falsehood.
Look to the long-term, not the short-term; look to the beyond, not the immediate.
The Brāhmaṇa becomes Agni.
For there is a Vedic revelation stating, "The Brahmin is indeed Agni."
And how is that so?

In this regard, for a Brāhmaṇa, the sacrificial hall (*sadas*) is the body, the altar (*vedi*) is the resolve (*saṃkalpa*), the sacrifice is the self (*ātman*), the animal victim (*paśu*) is the intellect (*buddhi*), the sacrificial post-girth (*raśanā*) is the seat (*sadas*), the mouth is the *āhavanīya* fire, the navel is the *gārhapatya* fire, the stomach is the fire itself, the *adhvaryu* priest is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *hotṛ* priest is the down-breath (*apāna*), the *brahmā* priest is the middle-breath (*vyāna*), the *udgātṛ* priest is the pervasive-breath (*samāna*), the self and the senses are the sacrificial vessels. He who, knowing thus, offers the objects of the senses with the senses—this is also known in the *Kāṭhaka*.
Moreover, they also cite this:
"The giver protects and saves both himself and the recipient from sin,
when an oblation is poured into the fires that are the mouths of Brahmins, which are enriched by the fuel of the Vedas."
That which is offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is superior even to the Agnihotra; it does not spill over, it does not cause distress, and no sin adheres to it.
Having made meditation the fire, truth the altar-mound, patience the oblation, modesty the sacrificial ladle, non-violence the sacrificial cake, contentment the sacrificial post,
and the granting of fearlessness to all beings the priestly fee, the wise man performs a mental sacrifice that does not go to ruin.
The hair of an aging man decays; the teeth of an aging man decay.
But the hope for life and the hope for wealth do not decay, even as one grows old.
"That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
that thirst which is a disease ending only with life— for him who abandons it, there is happiness."
"Salutation be to Vasiṣṭha, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa and of Urvaśī, who has a hundred ways [of departing], to Vasiṣṭha, to Vasiṣṭha!"
Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra (i.e., Vaikhānasa Smārtasūtra 8–10)
