Now, regarding the duties of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma):
the four classes were born from the mouth, the arms, the thighs, and the feet [of the Creator],
for the Vedic revelation states, "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."
For the first three [classes], the purificatory rites beginning with impregnation (*niṣeka*) are prescribed.
For those twice-born ones, there is the entitlement to the Vedas.
Therefore, for a Brāhmaṇa, there are six duties: studying and teaching, sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices, and giving and receiving gifts.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the duties are] sacrificing, studying, and giving gifts. For the Kṣatriya, [in addition,] protecting the subjects, restraining the wicked, and fighting.
For the Vaiśya, [the duties are] cattle-rearing, money-lending, and trade.
The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born and agriculture.

There are four stages of life (āśramas) for a Brāhmaṇa, the first three for a Kṣatriya, and only two for a Vaiśya. Those belonging to these stages are four: the student (brahmacārī), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the mendicant (bhikṣu).

Having been initiated, the religious student (*brahmacārī*), wearing a girdle, a sacrificial thread, a deerskin, and carrying a staff, shall bathe, perform the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) both morning and evening, and the fire-oblation with fuel-sticks (*samiddhoma*). Having clasped the feet of his teacher and saluting him constantly, he shall study the Veda according to his vow. While the teacher stands, he should remain standing; when the teacher rises, he should rise before him; when the teacher walks, he should follow behind him; and when the teacher sits or lies down, being so directed, he should sit or lie down at a lower level.
He shall not perform any action that has not been prescribed. Even if not specifically told, he should perform his daily recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) and his obligatory duties.

Having avoided bathing in hot water, cleaning the teeth, applying collyrium, ointments, perfumes, flowers, shoes, umbrellas, sleeping during the day, emission of semen, looking at or touching women, sexual intercourse, as well as desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, violence, and so forth, he should always be intent on service and perform those actions that are pleasing and beneficial to his teacher.
Free from malice and agreeable in speech and mind, he speaks what is pleasant and true;
even when distressed, he does not utter untruth, what is unpleasant, or slander.

Avoiding the consumption of honey, meat, fish, broth, fermented liquids, and other forbidden foods, he should practice begging for alms and, having been permitted by his teacher, eat the food obtained through those alms.
One should not utter the names of one's guru, elders, or those initiated for sacrifice (dīkṣita).
In the absence of the guru, one should perform the duties toward his son as one would toward the guru himself.
There are four types of religious students (brahmacārins): the Gāyatra, the Brāhma, the Prājāpatya, and the Naiṣṭhika.

After the initiation (*upanayana*), for three nights he shall abstain from pungent and salty food; having studied the *Gāyatrī*, he remains a student of vows until the completion of the *Sāvitra-vrata*. Thereafter, being a Brahmin, he shall practice begging for alms in the houses of householders who are neither accused of sin nor fallen, and perform the observances of the Vedas. Having stayed in the teacher’s house for twelve years or twenty years, and having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas together with the *Sūtras*, he may enter the life of a householder.

The Prājāpatya [student], having bathed, being devoted to his daily duties and the practice of celibacy, and being intent upon Nārāyaṇa, reflects upon the meaning of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and then performs the taking of a wife. Regarding the Prājāpatya, the sages declare that he should not remain [in that state] for more than three years.

The lifelong student (naiṣṭhika), having donned a saffron-colored garment, a raw silk cloth, an antelope skin, or a bark garment; wearing matted hair or a top-knot, a girdle, and a staff; carrying the sacred thread and an antelope skin; remaining chaste, pure, and abstaining from pungent food and salt; stays in the teacher’s household until his own death, subsisting on alms-food that has been announced to him.

Having taken a wife, the householder—observing the rules of conduct such as ritual bathing and performing the daily *aupāsana* fire sacrifice and the *pākayajña* offerings—should rise to greet a teacher (*guru*) or a *snātaka* who has arrived at his home at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* oblation; having saluted them and offered a seat, water for the feet (*pādya*), and water for sipping (*ācamana*), he should present the *madhuparka* mixed with ghee, curd, and milk, and feed them with various foods according to his ability.

He should honor, according to their merit, mendicants, celibate students, guests who are knowers of the Vedas and learned in the scriptures, paternal uncles, teachers, officiating priests, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and others who have arrived, as well as children, the elderly, the helpless, the afflicted, and those exhausted by travel.
Even if he is unable [to provide much], he should eat only after giving the first portion or alms-food along with water.

Endowed with compassion, truthfulness, purity, and right conduct, he should constantly worship the sages through Vedic study and libations; the gods with sacrifices, offerings, oblations, water, flowers, and the like; the ancestors with *śrāddha* rites and sons; and all beings with sacrificial food; and men with gifts of food and other necessities.

Thus, being freed from the three debts, he becomes debtless. Householders are of four types: those who subsist by their own labor (*vārtāvṛtti*), those who live as householders (*śālīnavṛtti*), those who wander for alms (*yāyāvara*), and those who follow severe ascetic practices (*ghorācārika*).
One who subsists by the *vārtā* way of life is one who makes his livelihood through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.

One who follows the *śālīna* way of life is endowed with restrictive observances (*niyamas*); having performed the *pākayajñas*, he establishes the sacred fires; he performs the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices every fortnight, the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices every four months, the *paśubandha* sacrifice every six months, and the *soma* sacrifice every year.

The *yāyāvara* performs sacrifices with *havis*-offerings and *soma*-sacrifices; he officiates as a priest for others, studies, teaches, gives gifts, and accepts gifts; devoted to these six duties, he constantly attends to the sacred fires and provides food and sustenance to guests who arrive.

The Ghorācārika, endowed with restrictive observances, sacrifices but does not officiate at sacrifices for others; he studies but does not teach; he gives gifts but does not accept them; he subsists on the *uñcha* mode of gathering grain. Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, having performed the morning and evening *agnihotra* oblations, he performs the *asidhārāvrata* during the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Jyeṣṭha, tending the sacred fire with forest herbs.

A householder together with his wife, whether he maintains the five fires or the three fires, when intending to depart from the household to the forest hermitage, should—whether he is one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) or one who has not (*anāhitāgni*)—place the *aupāsana* fire upon the two kindling woods (*araṇi*). Having churned it out in the house and established it according to the rules for the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, and having offered the *āghāra* libation, he should take the *śrāmaṇaka* fire and proceed to the third stage of life (*āśrama*). As before, he should perform the rites such as sprinkling and scraping the fire-chamber.

Having wiped the third altar as well, and having prepared a grass mat (*kūrca*) for spreading—measuring thirty-six *aṅgulas*, made of *darbha* grass, threefold and knotted like a rope at its base, and tied six *aṅgulas* below the fire—he spreads it around the middle altar for the *Śrāmaṇaka* rite.

Having invoked the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice with the formula ending in "yajñadaivaviśvān devān," and having set aside the clarified butter (ājya), he should offer oblations ending with the formulas: "To the Śrāmaṇaka, svāhā! To the Śrāmaṇaka sacrifice, svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, the deities of the sacrifice, svāhā! Then he should offer the cooked rice-oblation (caru); such is the specific rule for the supporting libations (āghāra).
Furthermore, the upper altar (ūrdhvavedi) of the Śrāmaṇaka fire is thirty-two finger-breadths long, four finger-breadths wide, and four finger-breadths high.
The middle [altar] is surrounded by that [first one], measuring five *aṅgulas* in width and four *aṅgulas* in height.
The third altar is situated below, with its width and elevation equal to those of the upper altar.

Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) provided with three altars and a depression in the center measuring twelve *aṅgulas*, the forest-dweller, having established the fire, should daily offer the morning and evening oblations as in the *aupāsana* rite, and then sacrifice into the *śrāmaṇaka* fire with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
One who has a wife may go to the forest with his wife but without the sacred fires. Vānaprasthas are both those with wives and those without wives; those with wives are of four kinds.

The Audumbara, the Vairiñca, the Vālakhilya, and the Phenapa—of these, the Audumbara subsists on uncultivated grains, cultivated grains, or herbs, or eats roots and fruits; he avoids onions, asafoetida, garlic, honey, fish, meat, stale food, fermented grain-liquor, contact with others, and food cooked by others; he worships the gods, sages, ancestors, and men; he lives in the forest, excluded from the village; and having performed the morning and evening *agnihotra* as well as the *śrāmaṇaka-agnihoma* and the *vaiśvadeva-homa*, he practices austerity.

Having established only the single *śrāmaṇaka* fire, some say he offers oblations. The follower of Vairiñca gazes toward the eastern direction; having gone to that direction, he nourishes his own guests with whatever is obtained there, such as *priyaṅgu*, barley, *śyāmāka*, and *nīvāra*. Devoted to Nārāyaṇa and characterized by austerity, he performs the *agnihotra*, the *śrāmaṇaka*, and the *vaiśvadeva* oblations.

The *vālakhilya* ascetic, wearing matted hair and garments of bark or rags, maintaining the fire of the sun, should discard abundant food on the full moon day of Kārttika and thereafter subsist on the remainder for the rest of the months while performing austerities. Regarding him, they declare that his fire becomes the sun itself.

The *phenapa* (foam-drinker), the *uddaṇḍaka*, the *unmattaka* (one who acts like a madman), the *nirodhaka*, and he who subsists on withered and fallen leaves—practicing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, sleeping upon the earth, and meditating on Nārāyaṇa—seeks liberation alone.
There are many kinds of men who are without wives.

It is known that there are various modes of conduct, such as: those who eat at fixed times; those who wear their hair in tufts; those who live with their bodies covered; those who grind their food with stones; those who subsist on wild fruits; those who use their teeth as a mortar; those who live by gleaning grains; those who live by showing themselves to others; those who live like pigeons; those who follow the path of deer; those who take food directly from the hand; those who use rocks as their bowls; those who eat only what is scorched by the sun; those who eat only bilva fruit; those who eat only flowers; those who eat only pale leaves; those who eat at intervals of time; those who eat once a day; those who eat four times a day; those who sleep on thorns; those who sit in the *vīrāsana* posture; those who sleep in the midst of five fires; those who inhale smoke; those who sleep on stones; those who immerse themselves in water; those who live in water-jars; those who observe silence; those who sleep face-down; those who face the sun; those who keep their arms raised; and those who stand on one foot. Thus it is understood.
Now, mendicants seeking liberation are of four kinds: the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*.

Among them, the *kuṭīcakas*—who know the reality of the path of yoga and seek only liberation—subsist on eight morsels of food in the hermitages of [sages] such as Gautama, Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, and Hārīta.

The Bahūdakas, carrying three staffs, a water-pot, and garments dyed with ochre minerals, and assuming that outward appearance, frequent the houses of Brahmanical sages and other people of virtuous conduct; avoiding meat, salt, and stale food, they collect alms from seven houses and seek only liberation.

Those called *haṃsas* dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a town; not dwelling longer than that, subsisting on cow’s urine and cow dung, or fasting for a month, or constantly performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, they always pray for spiritual awakening alone. Those called *paramahaṃsas* dwell at the root of a single tree, in an empty house, or in a cremation ground; they are clothed in a garment or are naked.
For them, there is no duality such as merit and demerit, truth and falsehood, purity and impurity, and so forth.
Equal toward all, with their whole selves, regarding a clod of earth and gold as the same, they practice the mendicant’s round among all social classes.

For Brahmins, the four stages of life (āśramas) are prescribed; for Kṣatriyas, three stages; and for Vaiśyas, two stages. Indeed, the fruit of that [practice] is twofold: with desire and without desire.

In this world, "with desire" (*sakāma*) refers to the longing for the attainment of a son and so forth, or the longing for other fruits such as heaven, once one has recognized the increase [of worldly existence] within this *saṃsāra*.

"Without desire" (*niṣkāma*) refers to the performance of prescribed duties without longing for anything whatsoever. Among these, that which is without desire is of two kinds: engagement (*pravṛtti*) and renunciation (*nivṛtti*).

"Pravṛtti" (the path of worldly engagement) refers to that which, disregarding the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), relies upon immeasurable knowledge and—being joined with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), posture (*āsana*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—effects mastery over the vital air (*vāyu*) and attains the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) such as atomization (*aṇimā*).
However, because it leads once again to rebirth due to the exhaustion of merit from austerity (*tapas*) and because of the abundance of diseases, the supreme sages do not honor it.

Renunciation (*nivṛtti*) is known as follows: having realized the impermanence of the worlds and that nothing exists apart from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), one disregards the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and severs the bond consisting of a wife. Having become a master of the senses and abandoned the body, one effects the union (*yoga*) of the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self. Thus it is understood as the entry into the supreme light—which is beyond the senses, the seed of the entire universe, devoid of all particularity, eternal bliss, like drinking the nectar of immortality, always providing satisfaction, and the means of liberation.

Indeed, due to differences in their conduct regarding withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), yogins are of three kinds: *sāraṅga*, *ekārthya*, and *visaraga*. The *sāraṅgas* are of four types: those who do not restrain [the senses], those who restrain them, those who follow the path, and those who follow a wrong path. The *ekārthyas* are of five types: those who go far, those who do not go far, those whose gaze is fixed between the eyebrows, those who are undivided, and those who are divided.
The *visaraga* (those who have gone forth) are not numbered.

Among them, the *sāraṅga*s—so called because they go toward the essence (*sāra*), which is the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field)—are those who move about having meditated, "I am Viṣṇu, the unobstructed. For them, there are no breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth.
However, for those who are obstructive, there exist the sixteen digits (*kalā*), beginning with breath-restraint, withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
For those who follow the path, there are only six [limbs], beginning with *prāṇāyāma* (VaikhDhS 01.10).

For those who follow the wrong path, they conceive of eight limbs—*yama*, *niyama*, *āsana*, *prāṇāyāma*, *pratyāhāra*, *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*—and thus they also alter the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). Now, regarding the single-seeded state (*ekārṣyā*).
Those who have but one seer (*ṛṣi*) are the *ekarṣis*. For those among them who travel by the distant path, this is the way:

they enter the solar orb through the *piṅgalā* channel and, having united with the Person (*puruṣa*) residing there, they proceed to the lunar orb and unite with the Person residing there; from there they go to lightning and unite with the Person residing there; then, in due order, they attain union (*sāyujya*) with Vaikuṇṭha.
This is the duty for those who are not far [from the goal]:

having brought about the union of the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) and the supreme self (paramātman) by means of the knower of the field, and having meditated upon the total dissolution therein, they meditate, "I am existence alone, like space."

Those known as the *bhrūmadhyaga*s lead [the vital breath] to the space between the eyebrows through the door of the fire consisting of *sattva* during the union of the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); they effect its withdrawal from the five locations beginning with the big toe, and then its exit through the *piṅgalā* channel until the end of dissolution (*pralaya*), or until the conclusion of the yoga of the *kṣetrajña*.
Those known as the *asaṃbhakta*s perform meditation with the mind;
they hear the scripture that establishes that [truth] with their ears.
With the eye they behold the form of the deity;
with the nose they experience fragrance;
with the hand they pay homage to the deity.

The one called Saṃbhakta is the Brāhmaṇa; because he pervades everything, whether it be appropriate or inappropriate, that Supreme Self remains pervading all like space. Therefore, apart from that Brahman, one does not perceive a self anywhere else.
Even regarding that which resides between the eyebrows, it has been stated that doubt is entirely without foundation.
Therefore, nothing other than Brahman is logically possible.
Because they follow various paths, hold various views, and travel along wrong ways, they are called *visaraga*.
In ancient times, Prajāpati perceived the faction of the *visaragas* for the purpose of concealing the true instruction.
Seeing him, even the sages fell into a state of delusion, let alone ordinary men.
For those who possess egoism and are like beasts, there is no liberation in this life, but only in future births. Therefore, the side of the beast-like should not be practiced.

Some [attain liberation] through the renunciation of bodily exertion; some through the recitation of mantras; some through a particular form of meditation; some through a particular syllable; others through the conquest of the vital breath (*vāyu*). Others, having united the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), meditate; these do not desire union with the Supreme Self at all, but rather maintain that the Person resides within the heart. Some, understanding that yoga is simply the performance of what has been prescribed and that there is no other meditation whatsoever, desire liberation.

For those who follow the path of releasing animals (*visarjana-paśu*), there is no liberation in this birth. Therefore, one who desires liberation in that very life should not practice the release of animals.

It is known from scripture that one should first fix the intellect upon Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*) and subsequently exert effort by taking refuge in the attribute-less Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*).
Now follows the rule for the *śrāmaṇaka* (the life of a forest-dweller) for one who has retired from the world.

A householder who has performed the *soma* sacrifice, having seen his son and grandson and having established their sons and so forth in the household, shall shave his head and perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
In the spring, during the bright fortnight, at a sacred site (*puṇyakṣetra*), he goes to the forest hermitage together with his wife.

On the preceding day, having bathed and made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), he should drink water with *kuśa* grass and observe a fast. Having performed the *aupāsana* oblation, he should consign the fire into the two kindling woods (*araṇi*) with the verse, "This is thy womb. Then, according to the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, having gathered *darbha* grass and other materials, he prepares as before the ritual seats (*paristaraṇa-kūrca*), the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), the fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and the bamboo staff, sacred thread, water-pot, bark garment, and so forth.
One should construct the fire-pit according to the previously stated rule.

On the following day, having churned the fire with the Vaiśvānara-sūkta and kindled it, one should place the fire [in the pit] with the mantra "āgneyāhi | upāvaroha. Having thus established the fire, one performs the *āghāra* libation for the *śrāmaṇaka* fire as before.

Having bowed to the fire and sprinkled water around it, and having offered the five-fold expiatory oblations with the mantra "O Agni, you are the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitte tvam*), he should sprinkle himself with the *āpohiraṇya* verses and worship the principal deities—those dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa—concluding with the *vyāhṛti*s.

To the west of the fire, having placed two *kuśa* grass blades with their tips pointing eastward and having set a stone upon them, he should step upon the stone with the tip of his right big toe while reciting, "That excellent splendor of Savitṛ... Having put on a bark garment, an antelope skin, or a tattered rag while reciting, "Possessing brilliance... as before, he takes up the girdle and the other three items—the sacred thread, the upper garment, and the black antelope skin.
Having sipped water (ācamana), saying "May the gods grant well-being," and having circumambulated the fire while bowing to it, he should sit down.

Having sprinkled water on his own head with the mantra "May the altars be auspicious to us," and having offered the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, *rāṣṭrabhṛt*, and *vyāhṛti* oblations, he should consume the remainder of the clarified butter by means of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Having sipped water twice with the mantra "In every union," and reciting "A hundred autumns indeed," he should perform a prostration; then, with the mantras "The guest has come" and "We have united with the great one," he should circumambulate the sun.
With the mantra "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom" (*rāṣṭrabhṛd asi*), he should take up a seat with its tip pointing upwards.

Having recited the *Sāvitrī* verse—part by part as divided into quarters: "Oṃ bhūs tat savituḥ," "Oṃ bhuvo bhargo devasya," "Oṃ suvar dhiyo yo naḥ"; then half-verse by half-verse: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvas tat savituḥ," "Oṃ suvar dhiyo yo naḥ"; and finally the whole verse: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvas tat savituḥ"—and having entered the forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*), he should formally resolve upon the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*).
His wife likewise shall remain a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇī*).

Having himself circumambulated the fire from left to right, he offers clarified butter with the *Prājāpatya* [mantra], the *dhātā* verses and so forth, the *mindāhutī*, the *vicchinna*, the *Aindra*, the *Vaiśvadeva*, the *Vaiṣṇava*, the *Bāhya*, the *viṣṇornuka* verses and so forth, the *Prājāpatya-sūkta*, and the *tadvratabandha*. Having again offered these principal oblations, he binds the *Prājāpatya-vrata*.

Having stood [in place], with the two mantras "devasya tvā" and "yo me daṇḍaḥ," he takes up the *vaiṣṇava* double-staff (*dvidaṇḍa*), which is joined with five, seven, or nine joints, reaching to the hairline, and straight;
then, with the mantra "yena devāḥ," he takes up the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the staff for holding earth (*mṛdgṛhiṇī*), as well as the sandals and the umbrella, as before.

Having kindled the fires, beginning with the Gārhapatya, and having performed the Agnihotra sacrifice, he offers the Prājāpatya oblation and the Viṣṇu-sūkta into the Āhavanīya fire; then, having offered everywhere with the formulas "Svāhā to Agni," "Svāhā to Soma," and "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," he consigns the fires into the two kindling woods (*araṇī*).

In a forest, on a mountain, or on a secluded riverbank, having prepared a forest hermitage (*vanāśrama*), he should construct the fire-pits as prescribed. Taking the fires along with his wife, and equipped with the vessels and other necessary implements, he enters the forest hermitage.
Having sprinkled water at the site for the fire-altar, having dug it up, and having drawn six lines, he should place a piece of gold and grains of rice and establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire.

He collects wild materials: earthen items, products of trees, bamboo shoots, old *śaṇa* fibers, ancient *kuśa* and *darbha* grasses, a tuft of wool, the tip of a *plakṣa* tree, fragrant reeds, *guggulu* resin, pieces of gold, and a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*).

Having chosen the forest-dwelling sages as his officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), having churned the fire, and having established the three sacred fires—namely the *gārhapatya* and the others—or the five fires according to the procedure for the formal setting up of the fires (*agnyādheya*), he offers two oblations each time; thereafter, he constantly performs the fire-oblation twice daily using only forest-grown materials.

The sage belonging to the forest hermitage (*vanāśramī*) practices these ten observances (*niyamas*): bathing, purification, Vedic study, austerity, charity, sacrifice, fasting, restraint of the sexual organ, vows, and silence. He also practices these ten restraints (*yamas*): truthfulness, compassion, straightforwardness, patience, self-control, friendliness, clarity of mind, gentleness, non-violence, and sweetness of speech. He observes all of these.

Meditating upon Viṣṇu with devotion, he does not neglect the two daily offerings to the *agnihotra* and the *śrāmaṇaka* fires. Having abandoned food grown in villages, he resolves upon forest herbs, fruits, roots, or vegetables as his constant diet. Having fetched [the fuel] with the mantra "Tirodhā bhūḥ," he himself, or accompanied by his wife, cooks the sacrificial oblation in the afternoon.
At the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, having fed the guests and visitors who have arrived, he eats an unlimited amount.
He shall not eat at night.

Having spread *darbha* grass, ordinary grass, or leaves beneath him, the man of firm vows should sleep alone, even if his wife is likewise firm in her vows. She shall perform service for him; he should not approach her.
Free from desire, with his vital energy drawn upward and his senses conquered, he should regard her as his mother.
He should perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Cāturmāsya, the Nakṣatreṣṭi, and the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi with wild herbs, following the previous sequence.

Sustaining his life with roots, fruits, leaves, or flowers that have ripened in their respective seasons and fallen of their own accord, he should practice an ever-increasing application of austerity, distinguished by the excellence of the fruits and other such offerings.

Now, one who maintains the sacred fires (vaikhānasa), having consigned all his fires into the two kindling woods (araṇis) and having gathered together all the terrestrial and arboreal fires with the *saṃvāpa* formulas, should churn out fire according to this procedure and, by means of all the mantras prescribed for the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*), establish the *śrāmaṇaka* fire in the place of the *sabhya* fire.
They say that the *śrāmaṇaka* fire is a modification of the *sabhya* fire.

And one who is without a wife, having performed the fire-oblation like a mendicant, having discarded the vessels for forest-gathering and the like, having entrusted his wife to his son, and likewise having internalized the sacred fires within himself, should take up a bark garment, a sacred thread, and other such items, as well as an alms-bowl; then, being without fire and without a wife, he should go and dwell in the forest.
This is the root of all ascetic practices (*tapas*); therefore, Vikhanas said that this rule and this fire are called "the Śrāmaṇaka."

Regarding the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*): when a man is aged beyond seventy, childless, or incapacitated, and having reflected upon birth, death, old age, and so forth, becomes desirous of yoga, then—alternatively, having entrusted his wife to his son and fixed his mind upon the Supreme Self—he should go from the forest to renunciation.

Having shaved his head according to the rule and bathed outside the village, he should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. In the forenoon, having gathered a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*), a sling (*śikya*), a saffron-colored garment (*kāṣāya*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), a water-strainer (*appavitra*), a vessel for taking earth (*mṛdgrahaṇī*), and an alms-bowl, and having consumed the three-fold mixture (*trivṛt*) and observed a fast, he should bathe again in the morning on the following day, offer the *agnihotra* and the *vaiśvadeva* oblations, and then prepare an offering of twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) to Vaiśvānara.

Having prepared clarified butter (*ājya*) in the *gārhapatya* fire and having offered two full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the *Puruṣasūkta* in the *āhavanīya* fire, he offers with the formula: "To Agni, to Soma, to Dhruva, to Dhruvakaraṇa, to the Supreme Self Nārāyaṇa, svāhā! (VaikhDhS 02.06).
Having taken four portions into the *sruk* ladle by means of the *sruva* spoon, he should offer them into all the fires with the formula: "Oṃ svāhā! (VaikhDhS 02.07).
He throws the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle into the *āhavanīya* fire, and other vessels made of clay or stone into the *gārhapatya* fire.

A householder who has not maintained the sacred fires, as well as a forest-dweller, having offered the oblation in the *aupāsana* fire or the *śrāmaṇaka* fire, should cast away his ritual vessels. Having recited the *sāvitrī* verse foot by foot, half-verse by half-verse, separately, and then in its entirety, he enters the stage of mendicancy, saying, "I enter the mendicant order.

Standing within the sacrificial altar (*vedi*), he should smell each of the fires, beginning with the *gārhapatya*, three times with the mantra, "O Agni, that which is yours, worthy of sacrifice," and then consign them into himself with the mantra, "May you two be of one mind toward us."

Having uttered the call "bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, may it be renounced by me" three times, both in a low voice and aloud, and having drunk water once with the right hand and sipped it, and having spoken in the same manner again, he should release three handfuls of water.
He gives his girdle, four sacred threads or one sacred thread, a black antelope skin, and an upper garment as before.

With the three mantras, "Of the god thee," "The staff which is mine," and "May my friend protect [me]," he should take up the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*); with "That which is on the further shore of the darkness," the sling (*śikya*); with "By which the gods [purify] with the filter," the water-strainer (*appavitra*); and with "By which the gods [attain] light," the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and the clay-receptacle (*mṛdgrahaṇī*).
Having bathed, he should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*.

Having sipped water (ācamana) and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and having recited the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand or a hundred times, he takes up an alms-bowl made of gourd, wood, or clay.

Having offered libations of water to the gods with the seven vyāhṛtis, each preceded by the syllable *Oṃ* and followed by the words "I satisfy," he should then offer libations to the ancestors with the first four [vyāhṛtis], using the word "svadhā.
He should then worship the sun with the verse beginning, "Upwards from the darkness... (*ud vayaṃ tamasaḥ*).
Having offered a handful of water, he should grant fearlessness to all beings.
The ascetic, devoted to the inner self, subsisting on alms, practicing the restraints and observances, with his senses controlled, perceives the Supreme Self through the yoga of meditation.
[He should follow] the righteous conduct of the virtuous.

Wearing the sacrificial thread over the right shoulder (nivītin), having placed it around the right ear, sitting in a squatting posture (utkaṭika), facing north during the day and south at night, he should void urine and feces on ground covered with grass.

He should not do so in a river, a cow-pen, on a path, in the shade, on ashes, in water, on kuśa grass, or on darbha grass. Without looking at cows, Brahmins, water, fire, wind, the sun, or the moon and stars, he should perform these acts.

Having grasped the penis with the left hand and risen, sitting by the side of water, the student (*brahmacārī*) and likewise the householder (*gṛhastha*) should perform purification with water drawn up [from the source], applying earth twice to the penis, twice to the hands, and six times to the anus.
He should wash the left hand ten times and both hands likewise with earth and water.
For the forest-dweller (*vanastha*) and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*), this is doubled.

At night, one may perform half of what has been prescribed. In the case of the emission of semen, purification should be performed as in the case of urine; some say that for semen, it should be done three times.

Wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), facing either the east or the north, and having sat down elsewhere, he washes his feet and hands with earth and water as before, sips water (*ācamana*), and then sips water again while reciting the mantra.
A Brāhmaṇa should sip water that reaches his heart, a Kṣatriya water that reaches his throat, and a Vaiśya water that reaches his palate.

Having sprinkled himself with water, having cast the water away toward each sun, and having circumambulated the sun, he should restrain his breaths on the left side of either the water or the fire, and recite the Gāyatrī—preceded by the seven vyāhṛtis beginning with *oṃ* and including the *śiras* at the end—three times. This is *prāṇāyāma*. Having performed three or one such *prāṇāyāmas*, he becomes purified.
Having performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) at dawn and dusk, one who recites the Sāvitrī one hundred, ten, or eight times wipes away the sin committed during the night and the day.
A twice-born man who neglects the twilight devotions becomes equal to a Śūdra.
A religious student (brahmacārī), having announced his own name, should offer a salutation, saying: "I, O venerable sir."
Having touched his ears and the teacher’s feet—grasping the right foot with his right hand and the left with his left, alternating them down to the ankles—and bowing his head, he greets him.
The teacher should say to him, “May you be long-lived, gentle one. One who does not utter such a blessing is not to be saluted.
The mother, the father, the guru, and learned men are to be saluted every day.
Other relatives are to be saluted upon returning from a journey.

An elder brother, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, and a father-in-law are to be honored like a father; likewise, a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, an elder sister-in-law, and an elder sister are to be honored like a mother.
For all [these], the mother is most excellent, and the teacher is even more excellent. When touching a young woman who is another's wife, one should salute her while remaining on the ground.
Through saluting those worthy of veneration, longevity, knowledge, strength, health, and auspiciousness arise.

One should not wear a sacred thread, girdle, deerskin, or staff that have been worn by another. Having performed the initiatory rite (*upākaraṇa*), being free from laziness and pure, one should study the Veda beginning with the *praṇava*; however, one should not study on the new moon day, the full moon day, the two fourteenth days, the two first days of the lunar fortnights, or the two eighth days. There is no prohibition against study during the daily recitation (*japa*) or the fire-oblation (*homa*).

If a cat, mongoose, frog, dog, snake, donkey, pig, or other such animal passes between [the teacher and student], there shall be no study for a day and a night; likewise during the impurity caused by birth or death (*sūtaka* and *pretaka*), for as long as that period of impurity lasts; and for three nights during the three *aṣṭakā* festivals and when the teacher has died. Upon the death of his wife or son, or the death of one's own pupil, there shall be no study for one day during the *manuṣyayajña* (offering to men) and while eating at a *śrāddha*. Furthermore, there is no study during times of distress or illness, or when one is in a state of ritual impurity (*aprāyatya*).

One should not study at the following times: when mounted on a tree, a boat, or a vehicle; with the feet outstretched; upon the voiding of urine, feces, or semen; while a corpse is within a village; when eating food that is unfit to be eaten; after vomiting; in a cremation ground or in a place where one has been; during the twilight hours; when there is thunder; during an earthquake; when there is a preternatural glow in the quarters of the sky; when lightning, thunderbolts, or meteors fall; during a rain of blood, stones, or dust; and during an eclipse of the sun or moon—at these respective times, one should not study.
The Veda brings about welfare both in this world and the next; therefore, it should be studied. At the conclusion, having uttered the *praṇava*, he says: "I have finished."
Having offered two fuel-sticks into the common fire, he should, observing silence, eat pure alms-food that bestows intelligence.

In the month of Pauṣa or Māgha, outside the village at the edge of water, having offered the oblation for the conclusion of the vow as before, and having ceased his private Vedic recitation, he should study the Veda during the bright fortnight and the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnight until reaching the end; then, having given a sacrificial fee to his teacher, he shall perform the rite of returning home (*samāvartana*).

At midday, having washed his feet and hands with clay and water in pure water, having sipped water (ācamana) and purified his limbs, he should immerse himself in the water while reciting, "May the waters purify [us].

Having sipped water again, having bowed to Viṣṇu with Vaiṣṇava mantras and to Varuṇa with the mantra beginning "Hiraṇyaśṛṅga," and having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the *aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*, he should bathe with the mantra, "O Waters, you are auspicious. The four types of ascetics (*āśramins*) perform this bath daily according to the previously mentioned rule, as well as for optional (*kāmya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) purposes.

Having covered himself with a washed garment and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) as before, having sprinkled himself with water, and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), he should, while either seated or standing, mutter the *Sāvitrī* and worship the sun.

Having gratified the kings and others with the *brāhma* (thumb-base) *tīrtha* of the right hand, Nārāyaṇa and others with the *daiva* (forefinger-base) *tīrtha*, Viśvāmitra and others with the *ārṣa* (middle-finger-base) *tīrtha*, and the ancestors and others with the *paitṛka* (palm-base) *tīrtha* using water, he should, intending to perform the *brahmayajña*, recite the *svādhyāya* as he desires—beginning with the first three sections (*anuvākas*) of the *Yajussaṃhitā* while reciting the formulas "To food thee! To strength thee!
(VaikhDhS 02.13). He may also study occasional hymns such as "Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca" and so forth, or the mantras beginning with the four Vedas.
The sacrifice to Brahman (brahmayajña) is the beginning of all sacrifices;
therefore, it must be performed by the twice-born starting from the very time of their initiation (upanayana).
One should perform one's bath in a river, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), in a natural pool dug by the gods, in a lake, or in a large reservoir.
In the water of another person, one should bathe after having extracted five lumps of earth;
at a well, one should sprinkle oneself three times with a jar on its bank.
One who is impure or naked should not bathe, nor should one sleep in such a state.
One who is afflicted by illness should not immerse himself in water.

When a sick person performs an occasional bath (*naimittika-snāna*), another person who is not ill should immerse himself in the water ten or twelve times, sip water (*ācamana*), and then touch him; thereupon he becomes purified.

Twice a day, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*), having washed his feet and sipped water, he should stand facing either the east or the west upon a square, smeared mandala and place a clean vessel there.
Having placed food therein, he honors it.

Placing two feet or one foot upon the ground, he sprinkles [the food] in the evening with the mantra, "I sprinkle thee, the gracious, with truth," and in the morning with, "I sprinkle thee, truth, with Ṛta. Having drunk the rinsing water with the mantra, "Thou art the under-layer for the nectar," and having offered the oblations to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhutis*) according to the rule, he eats the food without finding fault with it.
Having eaten, he should drink water with the mantra, "Thou art the covering of nectar," and having sipped water and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), he should rinse his mouth again.
Wearing only a single garment, while lying down, standing, not having bathed, not performing *japa*, *homa*, or eating, or with feet that are dry, or facing north, he does not eat.
He should not eat food from a broken vessel, nor food that is stale, nor food placed upon a bed, a seat, or one's lap.
One should not drink water with cupped hands (añjali).

One should not eat food that has been touched by those who are impure from remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa), those who are physically unclean (aśuci), those in a state of ritual impurity (āśaucin), outcasts (patita), or those who have undergone birth or death pollution (sūtakapretaka). Sesame, flour-meal, curd, and parched grain are not to be eaten at night.
Food that has stood overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with clarified butter or curd.
Food contaminated by worms, hair, or insects, smelled by a cow, or pecked at by birds becomes pure if sprinkled with ashes and water.

When a large quantity of food is defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, one should remove and discard only as much as would satisfy a person; then, having sprinkled it with ashes and water while reciting the verse "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," and having touched it with a firebrand of *darbha* grass, one may take it.

Within ten days of giving birth, one should avoid the milk of cows, as well as the milk of animals with uncloven hooves, camels, and women; likewise, onions, mushrooms, garlic, *gṛñjana*, and *viḍja* (if not specifically permitted), as well as fish and meat, are to be avoided.
Meat that remains from a sacrifice may be eaten. One should avoid food touched by a woman in her courses, or touched by those born of the *śūdra* and *anuloma* castes, as well as their food.
One may accept raw food from those Śūdras who follow their own specific duties and are born in the direct order (anuloma), provided one is hungry;
however, even when hungry, one should not with effort accept either raw or cooked food from any of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the intermediate castes, or the Vratyas.
Furthermore, one should renounce cooked food that has been touched by them or mixed with them.
Performing the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti through the actions of mind, speech, and body, he gradually practices righteousness.

The householder of the *gṛhastha* stage of life should carry two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), a bamboo staff, and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). Having bathed together with his wife, he should perform the domestic rites in the domestic fire and the Vedic rites in the Vedic fires.
In the evening, at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, having fed any guests who have arrived and having himself eaten a moderate amount, he should sleep with his wife.
With wet feet and with his head toward the west or the north, he should not sleep;
he should approach his own wife during her fertile periods.
At the outset, for three nights, she who has reached her menses should avoid sexual intercourse, sitting together, and sleeping together.
She must not consort with another's wife;
for from consorting with another's wife, one’s lifespan, prosperity, and Vedic luster perish.
He does not eat together with his wife; he should not look at her while she is eating, yawning, or naked;
he avoids speaking untruths.
There is no sin greater than untruth, and there is no virtue greater than truth.

A twice-born man should live for the welfare of all living beings by means of non-violence alone; he should be pure in his livelihood and possess sufficient wealth to maintain himself. He may be one who stores grain in a granary (*kusūladhānya*), one who stores grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*), one who gathers enough for three days (*aśvastanika*), or one who gathers only for the day (*aśvastanika*). A twice-born man should not touch those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) or those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*).
One should not look at the sun at its rising or its setting.
One should circumambulate to the right the gods, the teacher, a Brahmin, clarified butter, milk, curds, water, sacrificial fuel, *darbha* grass, fire, and trees.
Way should be yielded to a *snātaka*, a king, a teacher, an eminent person, a sick person, a burden-carrier, and a pregnant woman.
Roads are purified by the rays of the sun and the wind.
One should not use the seats or beds of another that have not been given. If one uses things that have not been given, he loses a fourth part of his own merit.
One should not wear clothes, garlands, sandals, or umbrellas that have been used by another.
One should not warm one’s feet over the fire; one should not blow upon it with the mouth, nor touch it with the foot. One should not place anything beneath the fire.
One should not throw fire into fire, nor into a temple, nor into water, nor urine, feces, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, food remnants, or bodily excretions into the fire.

One should not look at another man’s wife while she is naked, nor at feces or urine. While impure from eating, one should not look at the gods, the sun, the moon, the planets, the constellations, or the stars.
One should not step over the shadow of a deity, a teacher, a *snātaka*, one initiated for a sacrifice, a king, a cow, or a person of high standing.
One should not show a rainbow to another, nor speak of it;
one should not awaken a sleeping person;
and one should not travel on a road alone.
One should not prevent a cow grazing in another's field or a calf sucking, nor should one report it. One should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes;
one should avoid gambling with dice, the smoke from a funeral pyre, and warming oneself over a fire using hair.
One should not step upon hair, body hair, chaff, embers, potsherds, bones, feces, urine, pus, blood, semen, phlegm, or food remnants.
One should cleanse with earth and water any limb smeared with impurity until the smell of that substance is gone and no mental suspicion remains.
One should not dwell together with outcasts, those of the lowest castes, fools, unrighteous persons, or enemies.
While impure or defiled by food remnants, one should not touch gods, cows, Brahmins, or fires.
One should not show contempt for the gods, the Vedas, the king, teachers, parents, or learned Brahmins; nor should one revile them. For he who shows contempt and he who reviles perish.
One should not engage in reviling or striking any living being.

One should not carry out a dispute with one’s teacher, mother, or father; nor with their fathers and so forth, nor with brothers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, preceptors, officiating priests, and others.
Among all forms of purification, for a person, the purification of wealth, the purification of women, and the purification of food are the most excellent.

Among objects, those made of gems, gold, or silver he purifies with water, or he touches them in fire. Copper, tin, lead, iron, and the like [he cleanses] with acidic water; those made of wood or ivory by planing or scrubbing; and sacrificial vessels by wiping or washing with the right hand. He should sprinkle leather articles, woven fabrics, and vegetables, roots, and fruits; small quantities he should wash.

Having purified substances such as clarified butter and the like, one should examine them with a firebrand. Silk and woolen fabrics [should be cleaned] with alkaline salt; fine cotton cloths with *śrīphala* fruits; conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and cow-horns with mustard seeds mixed with water; earthenware by burning again; and a house by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and washing. One should purify the ground by digging it up, filling it with fresh earth, and having cows dwell upon it, as well as by sweeping and other such means.
Water that reaches the ground and satisfies the throat, which is free from defects and well-purified;
water consecrated by speech, water cleansed by a stream, and what is unseen [by the eye]; the mouth of a woman and the hand of an artisan with goods displayed for sale—these are always pure.

Fruit left over by birds is blameless; likewise, that which has been settled upon by mosquitoes, flies, or gnats, as well as their droplets, are not defiled. Furthermore, anything touched by wind, fire, or the rays of the sun is pure.
In the case of one who is ill, a child, or in a kitchen, purity need not be scrutinized; it should be maintained according to one's ability. Water that is abundant is not defiled by feces or urine.
One who is performing the ritual sipping (ācamana) does not become impure by drops of water from another person’s sipping that fall to the ground and rise back up, or by those touched by the feet.

A forest-dweller (vānaprastha) should constantly engage in Vedic study; he should gather *kuśa* grass, fuel, and the like for the sake of the sacred fires, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits grown in a pure place for his own food.
He should avoid what is dependent on others, what has been discarded by others, what is grown in an impure place, and cow's milk.
He should not accumulate grain or wealth.
He should not wear clothing.
When honey is mentioned, he takes water; when meat is mentioned, he takes that which is made from flour.

Compassionate toward all beings, impartial, patient, pure, free from malice, indifferent to pleasure, possessing auspicious speech, and avoiding envy and miserliness, he should renounce fish and other biting creatures, as well as plants grown in ploughed soil, bulbs, roots, fruits, vegetables, and the like. Wearing matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails, bathing at the three divisions of the day, dwelling on the ground, and subsisting only on forest products, he should offer sacrificial oblations of cooked rice (*caru*) and sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

He avoids onions and the like, tree resins, white eggplant (*śvetavṛntāka*), *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *śleṣmātaka*, *vrajakali*, *citraka*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), *bhūs-tṛṇa*, *kovidāra*, and radish (*mūlaka*).
For a sage, all meat is equal to beef, and fermented grain-water (*dhānyāmla*) is equal to liquor (*surā*).
He discards previously stored food and his former garments in the month of Āśvayuja.
A practitioner of meditation (*dhyānayogin*) who has mastered the Vedas and Vedānta performs austerity.

Being without a wife, without sacred fires, without a household, and without a fixed dwelling, he lives at the root of a tree or in the forest hermitages, or in the houses of householders; having begged for alms, he eats food sufficient merely for the maintenance of life on a clean leaf by the side of water, like a mendicant. Withering his body, he should perform increasingly intense austerity.

Having bathed daily, the mendicant should satisfy himself with the *praṇava*; he should offer salutation with that very same [syllable]. Having performed at least six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and having recited the *Sāvitrī* at least one hundred times, he should perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*).
One should sip water purified by straining it through a non-sacrificial filter.
One should practice wearing saffron-colored robes, renouncing everything, abstaining from sexual intercourse, and avoiding theft and other such acts.

Being without a companion, without a sacred fire, and without a fixed dwelling, free from doubt, equal in honor and dishonor, and avoiding dispute, anger, greed, delusion, and falsehood, one should dwell outside the village in a secluded hut, a temple, or at the foot of a tree.
Except during the four months of the rainy season, he should not dwell in a single place for more than one day.
During the rainy season, the autumn, and the four months [of the rains], he may stay in one place alone.

Having fastened the triple staff, the ochre garment, the strainer, and other implements, and wearing them with his left hand around his neck, holding the alms-bowl with his right hand, he should go for alms at one time to the houses of pure Brahmins at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Having looked at living beings on the ground, he should place his foot down while avoiding them;
standing with his face turned downwards, he should seek alms.
Having stood for the duration of milking a cow, or half that time, he should proceed.

Even when there is no gain or when he is treated with contempt, he should not be despondent; even upon obtaining honor, he should not be satisfied. He should not walk either too quickly or too slowly.
Except at the time for begging alms, he should not go to another's house.
He should not go more than a *krośa* to beg for alms.

Having wandered for alms, he should wash his hands and feet by the water’s edge, sip water (*ācamana*), and offer the first portion of the alms to the Sun with the mantra "ud u tyam," to Viṣṇu with "ato devāḥ," and to Brahmā with "brahma jajñānam. He should then cast the *bali* offering for all beings.

Having resolved upon the sacrifice to the Self (*ātmayajña*) according to the procedure for the *agnihotra*, he should eat eight mouthfuls—just enough for the maintenance of life—or he may eat at will, or not eat at all.
Having drunk water filtered through a cloth and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), he sips water again;
he should not engage in censure or abuse;
and he should abandon his kinsmen and relatives.
One should not speak of one's lineage, conduct, austerity, or learning.

Having abandoned attachment, practicing restraint and self-control, speaking what is pleasant and true, being non-hostile toward all beings, impartial, always devoted to the inner self, and a practitioner of meditation-yoga, one should maintain concentration while perceiving Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman;
thus one attains the imperishable Brahman.
"The supreme Brahman is Nārāyaṇa"—so says the Śruti.

When the body of a renunciant who has not maintained the sacred fires has died, his son or another person, having covered it with grass and having brought it near by means of a vehicle or with pure Brāhmaṇas, digs a pit in a river flowing toward the ocean or on a sandy bank, in such a way that it will be untouched by jackals and other such creatures.

Having bathed [the image] with the Gāyatrī, and having likewise caused it to rise or lie down, one should place the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) in the right hand with Vaiṣṇava mantras; the water-strainer (*śikya*) and the *appavitra* in the left with the verse "yad asya pāre rajasaḥ"; the alms-bowl (*bhikṣāpātra*) on the belly with the Sāvitrī; the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*), the earth-grabber (*mṛdgrahaṇī*), and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the private region with the verse "bhūmir bhūmim" (VaikhDhS 3.8). Having thus placed them, one should cover [the image].
If that [image] is touched by jackals or other such creatures, the one who performed that act becomes more sinful.

Having internalized the fires within himself, the renunciant whose fires have been maintained (āhitāgni) should, upon the death of his body, bathe it with the *gāyatrī*, carry it as previously described, and place it in a pure location. Having descended that fire into a common fire (*laukikāgni*) with the mantra "Descend into this fire" (*tadagnim upāvaroha*), and having poured clarified butter and milk into its mouth with the mantra "Thou art a purifier" (*pavitraṃ te*), he should arrange the triple staff and other implements as before. Then, by means of the *brahmamedha* or the *pitṛmedha*, using the mantras of one who maintains the sacred fires and those very fires themselves, he performs the cremation.
For these two [the renunciant and the householder], one should not perform the impurity rites, the water libations, the offering of funeral cakes (*balipiṇḍa*), the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha, and so forth.
He who performs the Nārāyaṇa-bali—
whether by digging up the vessel [containing the remains], covering it, cremating it, or performing the Nārāyaṇa-bali itself— shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Regarding the *Nārāyaṇabali*: "From Nārāyaṇa alone comes the accomplishment of all goals. One performs this for those killed by Brahmā and others, for suicides, for those who died from rope, weapons, water, lightning, fanged animals, beasts, serpents, and so forth, for those who died of every kind of sin, for other [uncremated] persons, and for a mendicant—after the eleventh day; and for the five types of great sinners (*mahāpātakin*)—after twelve years—in place of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for the sake of the deceased, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight or under the *Śravaṇa* asterism.

On the previous day, one should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas. On the following day, having prepared a fire-sanctuary near the temple of Viṣṇu, by a riverbank, or in the house, one should offer the *āghāra* oblation. Having strewn grass around the fire, one should place an image made of that [same material] or gold upon darbha grass in the north-western direction of the fire. Meditating on the Puruṣa, one should invoke the god Nārāyaṇa, facing eastward, with the mantra "Oṃ bhūḥ puruṣam" and so forth, and then offer a seat, water for the feet, and water for sipping.

Having bathed [the deity] with the *Puruṣasūkta*, or with the eight-syllable mantra "nārāyaṇāya vidmahe," he worships him with a garment, an upper cloth, ornaments, water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and further water for sipping.
He should satisfy [the deity] with water while reciting the twelve names beginning with Keśava.

Having sprinkled [the offering materials], he should offer clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the hymns beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and "viṣṇor nu kaṃ," as well as the twelve names.

Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with jaggery, ghee, and fruit as an oblation to the Lord of Gods with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should present water for the feet, water for sipping, and a mouth-freshener.

Having worshipped, beginning from the south, upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing northward to the south of the fire, he offers an oblation of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) with the following mantras: "To Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-headed, the thousand-eyed, the thousand-footed, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Light, the Supreme Brahman, the Unmanifest, the Cause of All, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Soul of Sacrifice; to the All-Gods; to all deities; to the Sādhyas. Having thus offered the oblation, he sacrifices clarified butter (*ājya*) with these same [mantras].

Having washed the feet of the Brāhmaṇas, having given them new lower garments, upper cloths, and ornaments, and having honored them with flowers and other offerings, he should feed them white food accompanied by side dishes, clarified butter, molasses, curds, and fruit while meditating upon the twelve forms [of Viṣṇu]. He gives gold as a sacrificial fee according to his ability.

Having praised [Viṣṇu] with the hymns beginning with "sahasraśīrṣā" and with the twelve names, he should prostrate himself and perform the concluding oblation (*antahoma*). Having attained the supreme goal desired by him, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Regarding those born from the intermixture of the four castes—namely the *anulomas*, *pratilomas*, *antarālas*, and *vrātyas*—their origin, names, and occupations [are as follows]:
One born from a man of a higher caste (*ūrdhvajāta*) and a woman of a lower caste (*adhojātā*) is an *anuloma*. One born from a man of a lower caste and a woman of a higher caste is a *pratiloma*.
From that, one born from a man of a higher class to a woman of a higher class is an *antarāla*;
one born from a man of a lower class to a woman of a lower class becomes a *vrātya*.
From the mouth of Brahmā arose the Brāhmaṇas and Brāhmaṇīs; the Brahman-sages became their wives.

Among them, one born from a limb-born [son] to a Brāhmaṇa woman of a different *gotra*, who has been taken according to the prescribed rite with mantras, shall be a pure Brāhmaṇa. One born by an improper rite to a woman who has had another husband before is a *golaka*; and one born to a woman who has not been married is a *kuṇḍa*. These two types of Brāhmaṇas are censured.
Therefore, one born according to the rite from a Kṣatriya father to a Kṣatriya mother, up to the level of the arms, is a pure Kṣatriya.

Of these two, the one born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*) who lacks the [proper] rite is impure and is called *abhoja*; he is not to be consecrated with the binding of the turban, yet he exercises the command of the king’s army.
In the absence of a pure [son], one who is not bound with the turban may protect men;
his conduct should be like that of a king.

From a Vaiśya born below the thighs, by a Vaiśya woman, likewise a Vaiśya is born; he is pure, except for the specific rules [of initiation]. A Maṇikāra is impure; he pierces gems, pearls, and the like, and works with conch shells and bracelets. Now, from a Śūdra born from the feet, by a Śūdra woman, a Śūdra is born according to the rule; he is pure.
A paramour, a Mālavaka, one who is censured, a Śūdra, a horse-keeper, and one who gathers grass for horses—
these are the [low-caste] persons belonging to the four varṇas.
All those born from their very sacraments (saṃskāra) are the anuloma and other [mixed castes].
One born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya daughter is a Savarṇa; among those born in the direct order (anuloma), he is the foremost.

His livelihood consists of the rites of the Atharvaveda, the driving of horses, elephants, and chariots, mounting [the king's elephant], serving as a general for the king, and the practice of Āyurveda.
One secretly born [to a Kṣatriya woman] is called an Abhiniṣakta.
If he becomes an anointed king, he should study the eight-limbed Āyurveda or the Bhūtatantra.
Following the conduct prescribed therein, endowed with compassion, and speaking the truth, he should act for the welfare of all living beings according to those injunctions;
or his additional occupation may consist of the calculation of the stars and so forth.

From a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya woman is born an Ambaṣṭha; he is a kakṣyājīvī, an Āgneya, a dancer, a herald, and a surgeon. From an old man [of this class] is born a potter, who follows the occupation of a *kulāla* (potter) and is a barber who shaves from the navel upwards.
From a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman is born a Madgu; having attained preeminence, he is known as the Mahānarma and follows the occupation of a Vaiśya, but does not perform the duties of a Kṣatriya.
From a hidden [union], the offspring is an Āśvika, who is a buyer and seller of horses.

From a Brāhmaṇa man and a Śūdra woman, a Pāraśava is born; his livelihood consists of the worship of Bhadrakālī, painting, knowledge of the limbs [of the body], sounding musical instruments, and massaging.
Born from an adulterous union, a Niṣāda is one who commits violence against beasts of prey and other wild animals.

From a Kṣatriya man on a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra, whose duty is to inflict severe punishment upon those who ought to be punished; from a paramour on a Śūdra woman is born a Śūlika, whose duty is to subject them to tortures such as impalement on a stake;
from a Vaiśya man on a Śūdra woman is born a Cūcuka, whose occupation is the buying and selling of betel nuts, betel leaves, sugar, and similar items.

From a *gūḍha* (secretly born) father, one becomes a *kaṭakāra*; and from a *kaṭakārī* mother, likewise. From that, one born in the direct order (*anuloma*) from an *anuloma* woman is an *anuloma*. He shall adopt the livelihood of either his father or his mother.

A *sūta* is one born from a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden through the performance of mantras; he is the foremost among those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*). Though initiated with mantras, he is devoid of the duties of the twice-born (*dvija*).
His livelihood consists of instructing others in their duties and preparing food for the king.

A Rathakāra, born from a man of lower caste by a woman of higher caste without the performance of sacred mantras, is excluded from the status of the twice-born; his duty is that of a Śūdra, and he lives by the service of tending and training horses.

From a Vaiśya father and a Brāhmaṇī mother is born a Māgadha, who is not to be fed by Śūdras, nor is he to be touched; he is a servant to all and subsists by praising, reciting, singing, and acting as a messenger.

From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born an Āyogava; he is a weaver, a maker of cloth, and one who lives by dealing in garments, bronze, and water-vessels. From a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is born a Puliṇda; he lives in the forest, subsisting by killing wicked beasts and wild animals. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Cakra; he is a seller of salt and oil. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Dhigvaṇa; he is a worker in leather and a carrier of the dead. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Pukkasa; he is a hunter of deer and a sweeper of streets. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Caṇḍāla; he is an outcaste, a dog-eater, and a remover of corpses. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Māgadha; he is a bard, a panegyrist, and a messenger. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Sūta; he is a charioteer, a genealogist, and a reciter of praises. From a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Rathakāra; he is a carpenter and a builder of chariots. From a Kṣatriya by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaidya; he is a physician and a counselor. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born a Mālava; he is a soldier and a servant. From a Vaiśya by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Tāpasa; he is a hermit and a practitioner of penance. From a Vaiśya by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha; he is a seller of cooked food and a cook. From a Śūdra by a Brāhmaṇa woman is born an Antyāvasāyin; he is a menial servant and a dweller in the outskirts of the village. From a Śūdra by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Niṣāda; he is a fisherman and a hunter. From a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Madgu; he is a boatman and a ferryman. From a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman is born a Kṣatta; he is a supervisor of cattle and a keeper of boundaries. From a Kṣatriya by a Śūdra woman is born an Ugra; he is a guard and a punisher of criminals. From a Brāhmaṇa by a Kṣatriya woman is born a Kṣatriya; from a Brāhmaṇa by a Vaiśya woman is born a Vaiśya; and from a Brāhmaṇa by a Śūdra woman is born a Śūdra. These are the mixed castes (varṇasaṃkara) produced through the intermixture of the four primary orders. From a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother is born a Pulkasa; having offered *surā* that is either artificially prepared or derived from the *arka* plant, he sells cooked food. From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Vaidehaka; he is untouchable even by Śūdras, his food is not to be eaten even by them, and he subsists by living in the forest, tending goats and buffaloes, and selling their products.
From theft, one becomes a *cakrika*, living by means of salt, oil, and oil-cakes.

From a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, a Caṇḍāla is born; he wears ornaments of lead and iron, has his neck bound with leather, carries a gong (*kakṣerī*) at his side, wanders here and there excluded from all activities, and having removed impurities elsewhere, he casts them out outside the village streets during the forenoon.
He shall dwell far outside the village among those of his own kind.
After midday, he does not enter a village. If he should enter, he is to be executed by the king;
otherwise, he incurs the sin of killing an embryo.
And those who violate the intermediate vows:

from a Brahmin woman, [the son of] a carpenter is untouchable, as is one with a hand-drum (*jhallarī*); [the sons of] a woodworker, a goldsmith, an iron-smith, or a brazier [are born from a Kṣatriya woman]. From a Kṣatriya woman, [the sons of] a fisherman and a fish-catcher [are born].

From a Vaiśya father and a Vaiśya mother, the Sāmudra shall live by sea-trade and by killing fish. From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Brāhmaṇa mother, the Nāvika lives by sea-trade and by catching fish; he navigates a boat that crosses the ocean. From an Ambaṣṭha father and a Kṣatriya mother, the Adhonāpita shaves the hair below the navel.
From a Madgu with a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Veṇuka, who plays the flute and the lute;
from a Kṣatriya woman, a Karmakara, who is a laborer;
and from a Vaidehaka with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Carmakāra, who lives by working with leather.
From an Āyogava and a Vaiśya woman is born a Sūcika, who works with needles and piercing;
from an Āyogava and a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Tāmra, who lives by working in copper; and from an Āyogava and a Kṣatriya woman is born a Khanaka, who lives by digging.

From a *Nṛpa* man and a *Vaiśya* woman is born a *Udbandhaka*; from a *Śūdra* man and a *Vaiśya* woman is born a *Vastraprasādhaka*, a washerman who cleanses clothes of dust. From a *Pulkasa* man and a *Brāhmaṇa* woman is born a *Rajaka*, a washerman of clothes. From a *Caṇḍāla* man and a *Brāhmaṇa* woman is born a *Śvapaca*. He is marked with the same signs as a *Caṇḍāla*, is eternally censurable, and must be excluded from all activities. Dwelling in cremation grounds, he removes filth from cities and other places; he collects discarded vessels and releases a corpse that has no relatives.

Having killed those who deserve death, he shall seize their clothes and other property, subsist on food dependent on others, eat from a broken vessel, consume dog-meat, and engage in the trade of skins and armor.
When such a base son is born, the father becomes fallen and ruined, and goes to terrible hells.
A virtuous son is a savior from the hells; having purified his ancestors, he leads them to auspicious worlds.
"Therefore, Brāhmaṇas and the others should procreate a son according to the rule upon a wife of their own caste," so says Vikhanas.
